- _ _ "THE SPINSTER'S SVVEET'ARTS." In Tennyson's new book is a humorous sketch of an (elderly spinster, who has given the names of her four suitors to her cats, and discourses to them of the failings of the prototypes whose names they bear. I e_alLs 'em arter the fellers ea once wos sweet upo' me, And Tommy the fust, an' Tommy the second, an' Steevie an' Bob have to reeeive her exhortations and her reminiscencPs as though in them were lodged the souls of their proto- types. The spinster has one immense satisfaction, and it is enough for '1 spite o' the men I' a kep' thruf thick and thin my two 'oondered a year to

mysen. To eacls " sweet'art" a turn she recalls incidents of her career which endangered her independence and her maoney. Especially to Rob does she relate her narrow escape -- D'va mind the mamia' when we was a-walkin' togither, an' stood By the elaay'd-oop peed, that the foak be sa scared at, i' Gigglesby Wood, i'Vheer the poor wench drownded hersen, black Sul, es 'ed been disgraced An' I fead the arm es I stood wur a-creeiipin' about my waaist ; An' me es wur lhs affear'd of a man's gittin' ower fond, I sidled awaay aa' awaay till I plumpt foot fust i' the pond; And. Robby, I niver 'a liked tha sa well as I did that daiy, Fur tha joompt ka thysen an' the,' hoickt my feet wi' a flop fro' the clear Ay, stick crop thy beck, an' set sop thy taail, tha may gie ma a kiss, Fur I walk'd the all the way hoarn, and wur niver sa nigh saayin' Yis. But wa boath was i' such a clat we AWLS shaamed to cross Giggiesby Greetin, Fur a cat may look at a king thou knaws, but the cat man be cleeara. Se we boith on us kep out o' sight o' the winders o' Gigglesby Hinn— Naar, but the claws o' tha! quiet! they pricks clean tbruf to the skin— Au' we boith slinkt 'oarn by the brokken shed i' the ladne at the back, Wheer the poodle runn'd at the,' once, and thou runn'd oop o' the thack ; An' the,' squeedg'd my 'and i' the shed, for theere we was forced to 'ide, Fur I seed that Steevie wur comin', 'an' one o' the Tominies beside. Rob, the original Rob, was within an ace of success, but he committed the unpardonable sin of coming in upon the brand-new carpet with unwiped shoes : An' I could 'a cried ammast, for I seed that it could'nt

be, An' Robby I gied tha a raatin' that sottled thy coortin' o' me. The general conclusion to which she has arrived on the subject of men's conduct in a house, and the superiority of single-blessedness on her own independent income, is thus summed up Theere ! I ha' master'd them ! Had I married the Tommies-0 Lord, To loove an' ok&ay the Toinmies ! I couldn't 'a stuck by my word. To be horder'd about, an' waaked, when Molly 'd put out the light, By a man coomia' In wi' a hiccup at ony hour o' the night! An' the taable staained wi' 'is aile, an' the mud o"is boots o' the stairs, Are the stink e"is pipe i' the 'ouse, and the mark o"is 'ead o' the chairs! An' nodan o' my four sweet'arts 'ad 'a let me a' hed my can way. Sa I likes 'em best wi' taails when they 'evn't a word to saiy. An' I sits i' my oin little parlour, an' sarved by my oda little lass, Wl' my oan little garden outside, an' my oan bed o' sparrow grass; An' my can doer-porch w' the woodbine an jessmine a-dressin' it greeian, Au' my can fine Jackman i' purple a roabing the 'house like a Queean. An' the little gells bobs to ma hoffens es I be abroad i' the laines, When I gods to eoomfut the poor es be down wi' their haiches an' their pains. An haalf-pot e' jam, or a morsel o' meat when it beant too dear, They ma,akes ma a paater Laady nor 'er i' the mansion theer, Hes 'es hallus to hax of a man how much to spare or to spend; An' a spinster I be an' I will be, if soi pieiise God, to the bend.

What the milkman seldom treats his customers to— The cream of the joke. The greatest sources of happiness and usefulness are open to rich and poor alike. A man in this city has got so deep in debt that not one of his creditors has been able to see him for months.
_ "Are ye needin' ony sticks the day, mistress?" said Robe, an itinerant timber dealer. "Sticks. Robie— what kind o' sticks ?" • " Wud sticks, to be shure."

Only the waters in the ship can sink the ship; but while kept outside all the heaving deep waters thunder- ing over three-fifths of the globe can work no ship- wreck. We can blindly follow frovidence'and ask no questions when we are led toward wealth, but when we are led toward poverty our theoloE gives way and we suddenly 'begin to doubt. A gentleman gave a penny to a beggar in the street. "Thanks for your kind intentions," replied the latter, "but I don't receive any coppers now. It was all very well at the start !" Young Housewife (consulting with gook about the dinner for a party) : As a second course we will have eel. Cook: How much ought I to get, ma'am? Young Wife: I fancy ten yards will be sufficient. "Curious world, this," said an old man to a fellow- traveller. "Very," was the laconic reply. "And it's strange," continued the venerable philosopher, "very strange that so few of us get out of it alive." "How things do grow this weather," said the deacon tea Brother Amos. "Yes, they do," replied the brother. "Last night I heard you say you caught forty fish, and this morning I heard you tell Mr. Smith it was one hundred and fifty." Women admire strength without seeking to imitate it men gentleness without bestowing it in return. Patience is strength; impatience is weakness. To sit quiet even though what is going on wearies you is a gain. Buds do not come up in a day, and if you wait you may find -flowers where only a little while ago you thought it was all barren waste. Your strength, as was Israel's, is to sit still. One day a man came to Khodshah, and said, "I need a denkey to-day; won't you lend me your's?" "I no banger own a donkey," was the answer. At the same moment the donkey began to bray in the stable. "Oh," exclaimed the man, "do I not hear the donkey's bray- ing "What !" retorted Khodshah angrily, "would yoz sooner believe a donkey than me ?" A MISSIONARY TRIUMPH.—Far away from this, near the southernmost point of South America, is a land called Terra del Fuego, and the people who lived'. in that had fifty years ago were in a very miserable condition. About that time they were visited by a young man called Charles Darwin, who had seen many lands and many tribes, and he said they were the poorest, the most miserable, the least like human beings of any he had seen. "Poor wretches ! " he called them. They had neither houses to live in nor clothes to wear; their speech was more like the cries of birds and beasts than the speech of human beings. Instead of clothes they daubed them- selves over with white paint. They were more like beasts of the field than men and women. There was found in the city of Bristol, :between two bridges, a poor infant, thrown out there to perish. He was found on St. Thomas's Day. Because he was found between the bridges he was called Bridges for surname, and because he was found on St. Thomas's Day he was called Thomas for Christian name. And by-and-by this deserted child became the Rev. Thomas Bridges, and set his heart on going out into the heathen world to save souls. And to this very land of Terra del Fuego, of which I have been speaking, he was sent. He listened to the strange speech of the wretched people; he caught the tones; he com- pared one with another; he made an alphabet of them. Then he made the letters into words; he wrote them down; he came to understand their speech, came to be able to speak to them. He told them the story of the love of- God, told them all about Jesus. He translated the Gospels into their language, and taught them to read them for themselves. Through his ministry they were lifted up out of their poor, wretched, lost condition. A new life entered into them; they became human beings again; they became Christian worshippers ; they built houses and dwelt in them- they were clothed and in their right mind. And it could be truly said of them, as of the prodigal in the parable, they were dead, and came to life again; they were lost, and were found.—Sanalay Mayazzne.

; Fannie is a little girl who has a big wax doll as a com- panion. A few days ago a new sister came to her house, and after a few days she went over to a neighbour's. "Well, Fannie," said the lady, "where's your wax doll?" "Oh," she answered, turning up her nose, "I don't have nothin' to do with wax babies any more. We've got a meat baby at our house now, and that takes up all my time now." A New York merchant who does business with Moses! Schaumburg, of Austin,,wrote to the latter asking him if a certain Austin lawyer was reliable. The same lawyer owed Mose 32 dols. for a suit of clothes. Mose turned to Jake Silv•erstone, his efficient clerk, and said, " Choost write to that man in Niel* Yorick dot it vas one of my pishness princibles never to say noddings pad of a man in mine own town, hence, for dot reason, I says noddings about dot schay-hawk lawyer." NAZARETIL—Naza,reth is at the present time a town, though not one of much importance. The valley of 1 Nazareth is about a mile long, and its wavy line is never more than a quarter of a mile broad, except at one place, where it enlarges itself into the shape of a basin, on the upper part of which the town is built. A more secluded and peaceful spot can scarcely be found than the hamlet 1 in which the infancy of Christ was passed, for in the days when Mary dwelt there it was only a small hamlet !or rustic village. Nazareth had no history till "the ' Annunciation" made it celebrated for ever over the civilised world. A very pretty description of the whole I little picturesque village has feen given in these words: —" Nazareth is a rose, and, like a rose, has the same I rounded form, enclosed by mountains as a rose by its ! leaves ;" and again, "fifteen gently rounded: hills rise 1 about it like the edge of a shell." These hills, with their round tops, are from four to five hundred feet high. The glittering limestone which forms them, and of which the 1 town also is built, would, like the chalk cliffs of Dover, be almost too bright to be pleasant to the eye if it were not for the fig trees, and olives, and pomegranates that ! grow there, and for gay wild flowers that flourish luxuriantly, amen., which the holly-hock, that favourite flower of our gardens, raises its bright head and shines conspicuous. T.e bullying manner of the German students is pro- verbial, as is also their mania for duelling. It was at Heidelberg that a quiet citizen leaving the cars said to a swaggering student, "Sir, you are crowding me. Keep hack a little bit, sir !" The student turned fiercely, and s iid in a low tone, "Do you not like it? Well, sir, lam at your service whenever you please !" "Oh, thank you," said the traveller; "your offer is very kind, and you may carry my valise to the hotel for me. The stu- *dent fled amid shouts of laughter. ONLY. • Only a single golden hair! How round one's heart it twines, Only a single golden hair! Clinging like claspy vines; Only a single golden hair! One's dream of love to utter, Only a single golden hair! And I found it in the butter! " Tlo.at boy a yours is not adapted for the undertak- ing business," explained an undertaker to the boy's father, who inquired why he had been discharged. "What's the trouble with him?" "He hasn't a realising; sense of what is due to the afflicted. Day before yester- day Mrs. B— buried her fourth husbana. I sent the boy up to learn at what hour she wished the ceremony to take place, and he asked her what her regular time of day was for burying husbands. I expect to lose her trade entirely." A LITERARY REMINISCENCE OF FIFrY YRARS AGO.— At The Elms, a little girl, the chosen playmate and coun- sellor of my younger children, Octa,via Hill, devised, even in their games, schemes for improving and brightening the lot of the poor and oppressed. And the retiring and meditative young poet, Alfred Tennyson, charmed our seclusion by the recitation of his exquisite poetry : Like an Xollan harp that wakes No certain air, hut overtakes Far thought with music that it makes. I may also mention in connection with this period of our life that my husband, on the announcement of his in- tended "Visits to Remarkable Places," received in 1838 a letter from Manchester, signed E. C. Ga.skell, drawing his attention to a fine old seat. Clopton Hall, near Strat- ford-on-Avon. It described in so powerful and graphic a manner the writer's visit as a schoolgirl to the man- sion and its inmates, that in replying he urged his cor- respondent to use her pen for the public benefit. This led to his receiving at The Elms for criticism the first volume of a novel, describing with great feeling and local knowledge the life of the Lancashire operatives. William, delighted by its perusal, bade Mrs. Gaskell go on and prosper; and in 1848 "Mary Barton" appeared. It immediately obtained a most cordial welcome from the reading world.—MAßY HowerT in Good Words. OUR INSULAR IGNORANCE—lnsularity is in Some re- spects a happy condition, but it fosters a strange blind- ness towards some very important polifical truths. Ido not now speak merely of its narrowing influence. We must all be more or less aware of this. We must be aware that we live in a kind of seclusion, in a kind of half-ignorance that other nations really exist, that other langueges are spoken. When a nation thus secluded arrives at great wealth and power, this narrowness blends with self-satisfaction, and the compound which results is that peculiar character which foreign politi- cians know by the name of John Bull. They think him very conceited, very self-satisfied, and they are astonished If centuryw i th important.la l tago,his "what at his ignorance ot all the affairs which seem to them mostf ignorance`'l t i st pb ortoshedei gEEinonguglsil,si's; Englishmen id Prince Kaunitz penrodspoenroatnkd grnowow." eriocuhn, tray is ndktereopddaenn iantvitoilma tees soil,b y foreignw h when almost, every country cannot help respecting so much success ;* but yet they do'not admit the explanation of it which com- mends itself to us; they do not think we are prosperous simply because we are wise and virtuous, for they hold to their opinion that we are ignorant, but they think that our insularity, the cause of our ignorance, is also the principal cause of our prosperity, since it keeps off enemies and diminishes the difficulties of foreign policy. It is not precisely this narrowness upon which I would dwell, nor even this ignorance, which, if it only con- cerned the diplomatic secrets of military Governments, such secrets as for a Kauniti or a 'Metternich were the sum of knowledge, might be esteemed happy. But in- sularity such as ours has another result which is too little remarked. As we have practi.cally no frontier to protect, and at home at least no enemy to fear, and as ilbthing forces us to think of foreign nations, and as our education at the same time does not introduce us to foreign literature, we live almost as if we were alone in the world. Our American cousins, it is true, are in mere position more isolated even than we, but this is com- pensated to them by the fact that they read more foreign literature—for English literature is foreign literature to them—than any other nation. They at least know that, besides the United States, there is England; but we know of no countiy but our own.—Professor Seeley, in the Nineteenth Century. THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY, 16, 1886:
SCIENCE, ART, &c.

At the meeting of the French Academy of Sciences this week M. Manseron claimed that the first experiments in the transmission Of motive power by electricity were made by him in 1873 and in 1876, by means of apparatus which can still be seen at work in the Saint Thomas d'Anquin Artillery Museum. The Amateur Photographer says that the Czar of all the Russias has taken to photography, and, through the Russian Embassy in London, has ordered an English photographic outfit. This is a distinct compliment to English manufacturers, and we trust his Imperial Majesty will be successful in his endeavours. Mr. James Russell Lowell has presented to the Massa- chusetts Historical Society an original letter of Robert Burns, which was given to him by the widow of "Barry Cornwall." It was addressed to her mother when a little girl. It is a characteristic letter, and' is dated " Dumfries, 21 Mar., 1793." Mr. Lowell has also been the medium of adding to the society's library copies of a rare and valuable collection of letters of early Spanish

discoverers. The incident narrated in the Poet Laureate's Irish poem " To-morrow "is exciting some discussion. Mr. William Allingliam, in the Ath"enaitin, mentions that in 1850 he began a poem on the same theme, but with the scene in Cornwall, and changed it into a prose story. "The Wedding Ring," to meet a request of Leigh Hunt, in whose London Journal (the new series) it appeared early in 1851. His authority, he thinks, was an old newspaper cutting, but neither before nor since has he dreamed of looking on the subject as other than common property in the world of imagination. Mr. Hamilton Aide having had his attention called to a paragraph in the Pall Mizfl Ga:ette, pointing out the similarity of subject between Lord Tennyson's " To-morrow " and his own poem of "Lost and Found," writes to say that the story dates from the last century, and is claimed alike by Germany, Scotland, and Wales. Dr. Cantani, an Italian savant, has applied the doctrine of the survival of the fittest in combating zymotic dis- eases ; that is, he is endeavouring to destroy pathogenic microbia by means of microbia which are harmless under the given conditions. He. claims to have obtained re- markably favourable results by administering Bacterium termo (the agent of putrefaction) in cases of tuberculosis. The organism in question, he maintains, is innocuous to the patient, but it destroys the tubercle bacillus. The results which Dr. Cantani reports are certainly encourag- ing, though there is still room for question as to whether they are actually due to the Bacterium ternio as he sup- poses. Meanwhile it will be remembered in this connec- tion that it has been asserted by some of the Paris doc- tors that smallpox cures tuberculosis. The theory is the same as that applied to account for the ravages of phylloxera in France, for instance. In America there is an insect which preys upon the phylloxera and keeps it in check, and the spread of the pest in France is attri- buted to the absence of its natural enemy. THE PLANET VENUS.—A correspondent writes: During this month Venus will be a very conspicuous object in the evening twilight. She is rapidly approaching her inferioeconjunction with the sun, consequently she is ap- proaching the earth at the daily rate of 581,250 miles. About six in the evenings at an altitude of 13 deg. she is S.W. by S., near a small star of the fourth magnitude, marked on the star maps by the Greek letter lota, in the haunch of the constellation Aquarius. The variations in brightness of Venus in various parts of her orbit are re- markable. These are caused by the varying proportions of the visible illuminated area of the planet's whole disc. Dr. Halley was the first to point out the method of find- ing the times at which Venus arrives at her greatest bril- liancy. This situation happens about 36 days before and after inferior conjunction with the sun, the first occasion being the 13th of January. Venus then appears a little more than on3-fourth illuminated, and answers to the ap- pearance of the moon when five days old. She is then bright enough to cast a shadow at night. When she attains her:greatest north latitude she is brightest, and can be seen with the naked eye during the day. In consequence of the near commensurability of the periods of Venus and the earth, there occur certain remarkable inequalities in the motions of both planets. It may be mentioned that eight periodical revolutions of the earth are equal to 13 periodical revolutions of Venus, and 24 periodical revolutions of the earth to 15 synodical revo- lutions of Venus. In calculating the places of Venus Baron de Lindenun's tables were formerly used,but they have been superseded by those of Le Verrier, because among other causes of error there existed a long inequality, occasioned by the periods above mentioned., discovered by Sir G. B. Airy in 1846, affecting the places of the earth and this planet, if the planets were seen from the sun, to a very sensible extent. This inequality goes through all its changes in 239 years, and affords a striking ex- ample of the precision of our knowledge in the planetary motions by the application of the principles of the theory of gravitation. THE SUBMARINE GREAT GUN.—The special wonder at the Royal Arsenal at Woolwich is just now a monster weapon intended to fire projectiles or torpedoes under water. It is the invention of Captain Ericssen, the well- known scientific American, and it was made in the United States, partly under the supervision of Lieutenant Glad- stone, of Her Majesty's Navy, who was sent over for the gun, and has now brought it to England. It reached the Arsenal only this week, and now lies at the inspection branch of the Royal Gun factories, whence, after some preliminary tests, it will be sent on board ship, probably at Portsmouth, for trial at sea. The cannon and the projectile are almost of equal length, and, as they lie side by side, painted a bright red, are formidable objects to look at. No fewer than 40 tons of steel are used in the construction of the gun, which is 30 feet long, and has a bore of 18i inches. It is a breech-loader, and closes at the stern by an arrangement of a very simple and effed- tual character, much resembling that of the great guns which were displayed at the Inventions Exhibition. The vent, which is axial, is sealed, and said to be effectual in preventing the escape of powder gases. The projectile measures 25 feet, which is only s'feet less than the gun, and is guaged to pass freely along the bore, which is unrifled. It is hollow, and, notwithstanding its great length, weighs only one ton. The proposal is to fit the gun in the bow of a ship 9 feet under the water-line, so as to fire straight ahead from the cutwater. A dia- phragm of india-rubber is fixed over the muzzle to exclude the water, but is blown away at the first puff of the discharge. The projectile is inserted from the mar, and is stopped by a pin a few inches short of the diaPliragin, for it has a short rod projecting from its nose, which is to act by percussion on the charge within, and must be protected from all risks of prema- ture explosion. Its safety at this stage is, however, to some extent guaranteed by the action of a strong spring which prevents the rod from being driven back by any force short of a thousand pounds. A charge of 201bs. of powder is all that is thought necessary for propulsion, and this being placed behind the projectile, the breach is closed, and the gun is ready for firing. The only other requisite is something to aim at; and when a hostile ship can be got within a convenient distance, the monster gun lets fly. It is asserted that a range of 300 'yards under water may be relied upon, but it is consi- dered doubtful whether the shot can overcome the resist- ence of the water and retain an effective striking power for half the distance. The inventor, however, has tried his device, and he says he ought to know. To preserve the lateral position and uniform depth of his submarine missile, he has weighted it to the gravity of water, and, while he keeps one side under by the preponderance of weight, lie has a steering-plate on the upper side which opens only after leaving the mouth of the gun, and acts as a rudder in keeping the projectile in its course. Until the gun is tried the authorities are loth to express an opinion upon it, but it is regarded at least as an honest attempt to establish a new principle in gunnery, in which it is quite unlike the wonderful breech-loaders which were obtained from America during the Crimean war, which were contracted for at so much per pound, and sent in with such a mass of metal piled upon them that they were too heavy to be moved or to work, and have never been fired to this day.

DESTRCCrIVE MILL FIRE - bout nine o'clock on Wed- nesday night a fire broke out in the third storey of a spin- ning mill belonging to Messrs. John Walmsley and Sons, Holme Mill, Darwen, and despite the efforts of the Dar- wan and Blackburn Fire Brigades the mill was totally de- molished. The damage is estimated at from £35,000 to £45,000. .

. Inm STonm.—Early on Wadnesday morning a etorm, brief in duration but almost reaching a hurricane force, passed over the Midland counties. Great damage was done to buildings and other property, and at Wolverhampton a man was killed by the overthrow of a tall crane. Extensive floods are reported as the result of the heavy rainfall and melting snow. The railway station at Stratford-on-Avon was unroofed by a gnat of wind.

THE STATE OF IRELAND.—The Premier has arranged to -receive a deputation from the Irish Defence Union on Tues- day next. The Bishop of Down has desired the clergy of his diocese to use in morning and evening service a prayer for deliverance from the " threatened calamity impending" over Ireland. The prayer is substantially that which ,tands in the Book of Common Prayer "to be said before a Fight at Sea against an Enemy." The Irish papers pub- lish many reports of resistance to the payment of rent. Az New Ross (county Wexford), on Tuesday, a man was com- mitted to prison for three months for having induced a cle.-k in a coal merchant's office to refuse to sell coal to a woman who was boycotted. Mr. Goldwin Smith, in a further letter on the Irish question, says it cannot be doubted that an Irish Parliament means separation. He contends tbat it is "somewhat i4nominions " in Britons to fling-klif3mselves at Mr. Parnell's.feet before he has "even condescended to tell them his wishes." MEDICINES. ELASTIC STOCKING'. Mr. Allan Munnock, Dairy, has sold a pedigree Ayr- shire bull to Mr. F. Beresford Wright, of Wootton Court, Warwick, for the purpose of crossing with Brittany

. . . _ cattle. At Muir of Ord Market, a lot of forty Highland cows fromH,ord Dunmore's well-known herd at Harris, have been4sold by public auction. The highest price obtained , was 13k guineas. 1 The Messrs. Leonard Brothers, of Missouri, have ob-

tamed £5,400 from the Lake Erie and Western Railway Company for damages to a large shipment of polled cattle, injured on the company's line. The Council of the Yorkshire Agricultrr,al Society have sanctioned three classes for Aberdeen cattle to be added to the prize list of their show to be held at Shef- field in the first week of August, 1886. There is a class for bul!s, one for cows, and one for heifers. The number of pure-bred rams sold in Scotland dur- ing the past year was 10,637, at an average price of £4 is. 70. per head, the total amount realised being £43,401 Bs. id. Blaekfaces stand. highest in point of numbers, _ _ . .

and Border Leice,sters higheSt, in price. Earl Cawdor has issued a circular to the members oi the South Wales Black Cattle Herd-book Society, calling attention to the fact that at present there are only fifty entries for the fourth volume, and urging the advan- tages of registration to breeders of Welsh cattle. Mr. Jas. M'Corquodale, tenant of the farm of Cuthlie. near Arbroath, has just left for Buenos Ayres, where he owns large flocks and herds, taking with him from Kin- nochtry two promising polled Angus bulls, a nice cow, and eight:first-class specimens of Border Leicester sheep from the same place. The declining state of agriculture in Germany has been the subject of discussion by the Central Agricul- tural Society, and: a committee has been chosen to inquire into the causes. Where is agriculture prospering at the present time? A Hampshire Down shearling ram, which was sold last spring by Mr. W. Parsons. of West Stratton, to Mr. Wood, of Mount Kisco, U.S., took first prize at the recent show at New York. Mr. Wood, writing of him, says "the ram has done splendidly, and I am delighted with him. I should have shown him at other places, but needed him to use with my flock." The experiences of a farmer near Penrith in regard to pleuro-pneumonia are attracting much attention in Cumberland. Twelve months ago the disease broke out upon his farm, and several animals were slaughtered. In October last it reappeared, some of the cattle on the farm having formed part of the stock on the first out- break. Another outbreak is now reported, and two animals slaughtered. The germs of the mischief seem to have preserved an extraordinary vitality. A committee appointed by the British Dairy Farmers' Association to consider the frauds in spurious: com- pounds purporting to be butter has recommended that, a law be passed compelling the registration of all estab- lishments manufacturing butterine in the United King- dom, that all such compounds should be branded with a Government mark, and that the offering for sale any package not so branded shall be punished by a heavy penalty. The final official estimate of the wheat crop of the United States is 357,000,000 bushels, grown on 34,000,000 acres; that is, an average yield of 10q bushels an acre. Supposing that the growers have received 3s. a bushel, a liberal assumption, considering how much' of the crop is of low quality, they are not likely to grow rich on an average return of 31s. 6d. an acre, which would be ne more than a living profit if it were all profit, instead of none of it. The maize crop is set at 1,936,000,000 bushels on 73,000,000 acres, or 26- bushels (26.52) an acre. Maize is very low in price; but it is more than half the value of wheat, and the yield is considerably more than double that of wheat. The daddy-longlegs, or tipula grub, is one of the most destructive of farm pests. It has been discovered that the tipula grub has a rooted aversion to heat and light. and that he disports himself above ground with greatest frequency at night in cool weather. Heavy rolling of the soil at night is suggested, but for the benefit of farmers loving early hours for themselves and men, the Royal Society recommend certain preparations which are at once fertilising to the soil and destructive to the grubs. Guana and salt equally mixed, and applied at the rate of 4cwt. to the acre is one mixture, 1 cwt. each of kainit and:superphosphate is another, while a".good third is found in nitrate of soda, dissolved bones, and gas lime. FARMERS AND BIITCHERS.—The ag,itation7against but- chers' " rings "• commenced by the farmers of Kent, Yorkshire, and other counties, continues to spread. A farmer sent round the Grimsby town crier to announce that he would sell beef at cheap' rates. When all his meat was ditposed of the farmer calculated that he had made more by £8 than lie would have received for the beast had he sold it by auction in the cattle market. The example of this farmer is being followed by others. A number of farmers in North Bedfordshire are making arrangements to kill their own sheep, and sell the meat in Bedford and other towns at 7d. per lb. At Biggles- wade the butchers are endeavouring to checkmate this move by introducing New Zealand mutton, which they are retailing at 6d. and 6id. per lb. THE NATIONAL FOOTPATH PRESERVATION SOCIETY.— The first annual report of this very useful association has just been published. It contains a list of subscribers. a list also of footpath "cases" dealt with or reported during the year, and a long list of testimonies to the ser- vices rendered by or to be expected from the society. These lists are all of them important. In the first we find many influential names; in the second, ample proof of the need of a Society for the Preservation of Foot- paths; and in the third, overflowing testimony to the welcome which such a society everywhere receives. Than Mr. Henry Allnutt, the energetic secretary, who is the heartiest, least quarrelsome, and youngest man of his years upon our " list " of friends, there could not be a better secretary; and we are certain that landowners and farmers will do well to join all others in the defence of the rights of property—even property in footpaths, nuisances though they imagine them to be. Anyhow the society is doing good work, has done good work, and has lots of good work to do.—Agricultural Garetie. Rimer OP WAY.—" Todbere" says e" For over 20 years I I have had a right of war through another man's field into my own field. Over 20 years ago this man threw down the hedge on his side of the way, leaving his corn- field open. Consequently, when I drive my sheep into my field they run over a part of his field. He says that I am obliged to put up hurdles to keep in my sheep as they pass to and fro through his field. IS this so ?" You' must not allow your stock to trespass whether your I neighbour fences his land or not. It is your duty to Ireep Tour sheep on yeur own land. Whether this rule applies ' in the special case of a right of way, with the inevitable and habitual incidents of traffic, we do not know. JERSEY CATTLE.—The great favour which this breed , of dairy stock has found in this country and the United States, has caused an unprecedented competition forl the animals which are of the best milking strains and of, the most fashionable colours. The milking and butter- making traits consist, of course, in the quantity and I quality of the milk yielded. This can only be 'deter- mined by the weighing machine first, and the churn afterwards, and by keeping a record of results, which American breeders are 'eery careful in doing. The fashionable colours are silver-fawn bodies, with black points. Colours very often, fortunately for sellers, are taken more into account than. the milk and butter pro- duce. For the ladies very often have a large share in I making selections, and as profit scarcely enters into the I calculation, a heifer or cow that is "very beautiful," or "sweetly pretty," excites very active competition. These animals are, in fact, largely kept as bovine pets for the families Of the rich men of New York, and/other cities; and its the heads of families in these instances are not particular to a few hundred dollars, more or less, prices have risen till there is no pretence for saving that the Jersey cattle in America are now profitable as yielders of milk and butter to sell at so much .per pound. But this fashionable demand has greatly encouraged practi- cal and professional breeders, who therefore have been keen competitors for what are looked upon as the best animals. DRYING OFF Cows.—The loss of a teat so impairs the usefulness of a cow that it seldom pays to retain one in the dairy after she has met with such a misfortune, so that such an accident is pretty nearly equivalent to dropping a cow out of the herd. It is an important item, therefore, in the economy of dairy farming to see that such occurrences should be avoided as far as possible. No human foresight is clear enough or watchful enough to guard against an occasional accident of this kind, but most of the numerous mishaps which spoil the teats of cows can be avoided by proper care. Ninety per cent, of the spoiled udders are destroyed by bad management in drying off cows at the close of the milking season. When they are giving so little milk that it is not deemed advi- sable to milk regularly to save it, they are pretty apt to be neglected and to go so long between milkings ae to induce inflammation in one or more quarters of the udder, and when inflammation is once established there, it is a pretty difficult matter to counteract it. The milk thickens in the reservoirs of the udder, and as the curd cannot pass out through the small tubes leading into the teats, it remains there to irritate and keep up inflamma- tion until the part of the udder involved is spoiled beyond remedy. Milk should, therefore, be drawn often enough to keep the bag limp and cool. The time between milk- ings may be more and more extended, but the watchful- ness should be constant, and at the first indication of any extra warmth or thickening of any part of the bag, the milking had better be done daily, or twice or. thrice daily, until all danger from an accumulation is past. Attention to no detail in the management of a herd is more essential than this item of care in drying off cows at the close of the milking season. Inflamina,tion to any extent ought to be prevented if possibfe; for if it 'is not severe enough to ruin any part of the udder entirely, it always impairs the activity of the inflamed part for the following season. A lack of proper care in this matter is often the mysterious cause which makes cows Vary in their messes in different seasons, when food and other I surroundings seemed equally favourable. • Better by far to keep up 'milking until the next 'calf is dioppeci than to hiinch mind are 'e allow any leverishness or sevellingl'ef the udder to occur dkryeepin tgho is off matter cowsw from an accumulation of retained milk. div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING.
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING.

DISEASES OF FRUIT TRERS.—MOSS and lichen, which grow on the stems of fruit trees, may be regarded as diseases. Some take the trouble to scrape these parasites away, and then scrub the trees with a hard brush and soapy water. But we think the quickest and most effec- tual method of destroying them is to wash the trees with newlyslacked lime. 'Stagnant moisture is probably the prevailing cause of trees being affected with these low forms of vegetation, but we have seen apples and pears as bad as they could be on land where the limestone and the chalk were near the surface, and the only remedy was carting suitable soil from other parts to give suffi- cient depth to the roots. Moss and lichen covered trees in wet soils have recovered after draining has taken place, and have cast the parasites off, as well as some of the injured bark. There are several species of scale that attack the different kinds of fruit trees, but they may all be destroyed by applying a mixture of soft soap and ' paraffin as described in a previous paper on American blight. Birds have from some inexplicable cause already attacked the buds of currants and gooseberries. Scarcity of other food might attract our sympathy towards them, but as yet there is no lack Of that, and the recklessness with which the contents of the buds are scattered on the ground supplies ample proof of this. The tomtits are the principal offenders at the present time, so much so that we have during the past week wished that every one of them adorned some female head gear. As they are not deterred by the usual bird scarerA, and as shoot- ing at them would. damage the trees, we have determined to trap them. Seeing that it was estimated last year that £lO worth of damage was done by them on about an acre of fruit trees, we feel justified in taking this step, and we would advise others to secure a few small iron traps and bait them with a crust secured with a piece of string. If the traps are elevated on a;stand such as a tub or box turned bottom upwards, these übiquitous little creatures will show their appreciation of this arrangement by paying an earlier visit to the traps than if placed on the ground. THE FRONT GARDEN.—Resuming our remarks on gar- den walks, it will be as well to state that before much is done to the walk itself the edgings will have to be put in order, as it is almost impossible to fix or repair them after it is finished. After the width of a new walk is decided upon, pegs about eight inches long should be driven into the ground on either side to indicate the outline, and the ground at the back of these should be well trod and its surface levelled, and if the pegs are of uniform height and,representing the height of the edg- ing, the soil may be regulated to within a couple of inches of their apex. It is not an easy task to lay even a few yards of edging accurately without these prepara- tory measures, and to attempt to do so without making the ground firm would result in the edging, whether dead or alive, showing all kinds of irregularities, and the most experienced walk-maker would hesitate to proceed unprovided with pegs, line, and level. • THE GREENHOUSE.—FuIfiIIing a promise made last week in reply to a correspondent, we offer our first re- marks on the Greenhouse, and it is our intention to give its management a fair share of notice in this column. We pass over for the present such questions as the most suitable position, elevation, form of house, and method of heating, and pounce at once on the best method of dealing with the occupants of the Greenhouse, which at this season of the year are likely to suffer from excess of artificial heat, which is productive of distended growth destitute of fibre and practically worthless. :.With the view of pushing the plants, the ventilators are not opened except on fine days, and the plants kept in a continued state Of excitement, much to their injury.7.Every.Green- house should have a thermometer in it, which should in- dicate a temperature of 40deg. at night, with a rise of sdeg. or 10deg. by day, dependent on whether there is sun or not. When the weather is frosty by day as well as night 40deg. will be high enough till there is a change, and occasionally the temperature may go as low as 35deg. at night, without any harm being done. ~When the ex- ternal air is below 40deg. the ventilators of the house need not be opened, as sufficient air will-be admitted through the interstices of the laps of the glass. ...When the weather is damp and dull for successive days a little fire heat should be applied in the daytime, so that the ventilators may be opened and the damp dispelled. The fire should be lighted early in the day, and at the time the house is closed it should be allowed to go out.

AN ENGINEER'S THRILLING EXPERIENCE. The Liverpool Daily Post says :—" A day or two ago a gentleman, wtrfle in conversatiora with a prominent army officer, wee made acquainted with A most thrilling account of prolonged suffering and ultimate rescue experieeced by one of the oldest engineers in Liverpool. The name of the latter gentleman is Mr. William Buchanan. who, upon being visited, made the following statement: I have been twenty-four years in the service of the Cunard Steamship Company, and 1 reside at 8. St. John's road, Kirkdale, Liverpool. Two years ago, while attendiug church one day, I was suddenly attacked wi:h a most excruciating pain in my head, which so completely prostrated me that I had to be conveyed to my home. Then followed twelve months of agony, which it is utterly impossible to describe. I had to resign my position, being entirely incapacitated from work. Medical opinion was divided as to what my malady really was. One doctor decided that I was suffering from rheumatic election of the brain, another that it was an overflow of ntooa to the brain, Ana a third that it was acute aeuralgia of the head. All agreed, however, that it would lead to softening of the brain. Six•of the most eminent physiciams in Liverpool attended me, and afforded me no :elle. My case was regarded as incurable, and my suffer- ings were so greet that I often became uneonscious and fairly crazy from pain. I could neither see nor bear for days at a time, and during the fearful attacks of pain my cries often attracted the attention of the neigh- bours. My house was pointed out as one in which a man lay at death's door, and some of my paroxysms of pain were so great that it required two and sometimes three strong men to hold me in bed. My physicians held consultations, but all of no avail. My suf- ferings remained the same. My family were in despair, and at ene time they regarded me so near death that in ad- dition to three physicians who were in attendance, twe clergymen were summoned to my bedside. At that time my wife's attention was called to a new remedy which was then being introdaced, and which claimed to be a cure for rheumatism and neuralgia. She procured a bottle and ap- plied the contents to my head. !Neither she nor I had any confidence in the remedy, but it was like a drowning man catching at a straw, and it looked like the last hope. The remedy acted like magic. It saved my life. I feel sure, my family and my friends feel sure, that had I not used it I would be dead, instead of alive and hearty and in perfect health, as you see me here. All other treatment had en- tirely faile:, and wonderful to relate, I have never had the slightest return shine I was cured some months ago. My friends and neighbours know all about it, and are like- wise familiar with my terrible sufferings, and my former helpless and hopeless condition. My care was considered 80 marvellous—it has become much talked over and is welt- known—that I have received over 200 visits and letters on the eabject. To all of tliese I have simply stated the facts as I have related them to you.' "A call was then made upon Messier,. Budden and Co.. THE CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT.-013 Wednesday, at the Buckinghamshire Assizes at Aylesbury, Sam Taylor Mendel, aged 37, was brought up to receive sentence, hay- ina pleaded guilty to charges of unlawfully taking a girl named Helen Line, aged 14, out of the possession of her father, and of criminally assaulting her. MendC, who re- sided with his wife at Great Horwood, made the acquaint- and of the girl, and persuaded her to go away with him. They went to London and other places, and lived together. Counsel addressed the Court in favour of leniency, but Air. Justice.Mitnisty, who said the case was " fearfully disgrace- ful," passed sentence of 15 months' imprisonment with hard labour.

MGCRACK EN'S BABY.

They had a baby at Mc.Oracken's. It was the first baby and both parents had made careful preparation for its management by reading all the books of advice to young mothers, &c., that they could possess themselves of. They got along very well as long as the nurse was in the house, but when that necessary bat tyrannical individual had taken her departure they found themselves in a condition to test the value of the information they had acquired. The baby slept very sweetly until bedtime, but about the time its parents were preparing to retire it awoke; then fun com- menced. The baby cried; Mrs. Mac. said it was hungry, and was proceeding to administer the necessary lacteal when Mac. stopped her. "Don't you know that it will not do to nurse a child when it is crying ?" Mrs. Knowall's book says " never to feed a crying child, because it will give it a habit of whimpering." True enough. But the baby still cried. Mrs. Mac attempted to take it from the crib to her arms, but remembered just in time that "Sterling Advice to Young Mothers " said, "never take your child it year arms to stop its crying; if yen do it will always want to be in your arms." Mac. started to rock the crib, but was checked by Mrs. Mac., who reminded him of what was said in "How to raise children," which was, "Teach a child to lie in its crib without being rocked. The child soon becomes accus- tomed to the motion and will not lie in the crlb without it." The cry of the baby had by this time deepened into a pro- longed bowl. "Do you think it has th• 2 croup ?" said Mac. "I don't know," said Mrs. Mac., "but I will see." And getting her book on children and their ailments, she com- pared the appearance of her child with the symotnrns des- cribed in the book. The baby still cried. "I Con't believe It is sick," said Mae. "I'll walk it." "Don't," said Mrs. Mac. "Don't you know that all the books say that a child should never be walked under any circumstances. Men are such geese." Mac. subsided and the baby cried. "We will go to bed and put out the light," said the mother. "I read in some place that a light in the room makes a child wake- ful. When he finds himself in the dark he will go to sleep through force of habit." Mr. and Mrs. Mac. went to bed after putting out the light. The baby stilt howled. Mrs. Mac. waited awhile till she thought her husband asleep, amA then reached over him and cautiously lifted the baby into bed. The infant seemed to know what was coming, and stopped crying, and when it had received the nourish- ment that its mother could no longer refuse, it snuggled down in her arms and went to sleep. Mac. had been awake, and aware of what was going on; but man-like he never interfered. He would sooner spoil the baby than miss his rest. When the regular breathing of the child told him it was asleep, he said, " rely dear." " What ?" said his wife, starting from the dose into which she hdd fallen. " I have been thinking," said Mac., "that the books tell everything about the management of children except the way to stop them from crying, and I have come to the conclusion that no parent ever wrote a book of that character. In fact," said he, rising in bed to emphasise hie words, " I believe that the authors of such books are nothing more nor less than old maids." "Yes, dear," and they went asleep.— Jacksonville Courier.

div.head: FRIEND TO MEN AND ANIMALS
div.p: A FRIEND TO MEN AND ANIMALS

Jonathan Chapman was born at Boston, in the United States of North America, in the year 1775. The name of this good and noble man is still held in loving remembrance In the minds of the present inhabitants of the States of Pennsylvaaia, Ohio, and Indiana_ What are the great deeds of Jonathan Chapman? He planted fruit trees, and took care of sick, and of cruelly treated animals. By one of these good works he became the benefactor of European settlers, and of;their descendants, and thus contributed to the present prosperity of thousands.-By, his second work he set an example worth imitating, and exerci,ed an improving influence on :uncultivated minds. His life has therefore been a work of civilisation, and for the cultivation of both material and spiritual progress. c He was a " Kultar Ramp- fer," a combatant for:kimprovement in the most elevated sense of this word.

It is true that Jonathan Chapman was what -,was called an original; but en the road which everybody walks no one has ever done greater things, or more faithfully beaten the path to new ideas. No particulars are known of his child- hood, as he never gave any account of it; People irst noticed hits when he began his peculiar way ef life. In the year 1801 he started (at the age of twenty-five), with a sackful ef apple-seeds, into the iwildernees of Penn- sylvania, and there planted there. - Seen afterwards Euro- pean emigrants settled in the district, and Jonathan Chap- man removed farther Welt. His business increased. He looked for fertile tracts at land, ciavourably situated, near brooks, and there he rooted up bushes, and laid the founda- tion of his nursery, which he railed in with .stakes and in- terwoven branches.

Ther. lived, still, some twenty years ago, a colonist in Jefferson county, in Ohio, who had seen Jonathan Chapman rowing down the Ohio }liver, with two boats tied together, laden with appleBeeds, in order to do his work on the utmost boundaries of tnat settlement. When his provision of seeds was exhausted, he returned to the Fastern 'States to fetch new ones. Afterwards he gave up these voyages, and car- ried the seeds in sacks on his back. He also frequently carried his sacks on the back of an ill•treated horse, which he Bad delivered out of the hands of a hard-hearted farmer,

for a small sum of money. He let this :poor animal have its freedom in some rich pasture 'ground. "This release of old, badly used, and tormented:horses oonstitutes the second task of hie noble life. The hard work of elearing the wil- derness, the drives on uneven roads, and unmerciful treat- ment, had worn down many a poor horse. Whenever Jonathan Chapman heard of such cases of cruelty to horses, he endeavoured to buy the poor animals, and tried to place them into the hands of a more humanely-disposed farmer, on condition that they should only be employed for easier tasks; or he himself gained recovery to the overworked animal on some rich grazing plane. In this :way he some- times gathered a little flock of those animals, which he did not sell again when they had recovered, but gave them to settlers, from whom he expected kindly treatment of his proteges. .-Arat he kept his eye upon them, and during his journeys he often inquired whether they were still in good. hands.

When new colonists settled in the country where Jona- than had planted:his seeds, he sold them his apple trees, which had grown large enough to bear fruit, at a cheap price. If the new-corners were poor, which is gecerally the cue with pioneer settlers, he gave them a few stems, and when they were in better circumstances, he accepted from them clothing or produce in lieu of payment. In this manner he travelled for many years; working and toiling ever a large territory of the New World. His pre, severing work with his hoe, his Bowing seeds for useful fruit trees, soon made the wilderness blossom, and became the foundation of the extensive • apPle plantations in these States, which form a chief revenue of the present inhabitants. Hundreds of thousands ef barrels ef apples come at the pre- sent time yearly from these parts of the United States of North America to Europe. It has been oalczelated that the results of his work are now reaped on a surface of 100,000 Engli.h square /hike. Jona- than Chapman is consequently widely known in those countries to every child that rejoices in eating a savoury apple. They call him everywhere "good Johnny Apple. seed," and people there say with gratitude that few men have worked in a more unassuming manner for the benefit of the world, and for the generations to come. , We read in ea Greek history that the early settlers in the Peloponesus, and in the Merea, deified the men and women who first taught them the cultivation of corn and of the olive, so great was their gratitude toward those bene- factors of mankind. May not heartfelt thanks and wide- spread fame, therefore, well belong to the memory of Jonathan Chapman? Well may the present inhabitants of the United States of North America revere the name and cherish the memory of him who did such useful work, who was so kind-hearted and so merciful; who lived in the most simple manner, and afforded an almost unequalled example of frugality! Oat of the little money he earned, or received (he had always more than he wanted for himself), he was able to succour the needy and give to the poor. His food consisted only of fruit and farinacea, for he considered it sinful to kill any animal for the nourishment of man, because, he said, the earth produced plenty of healthy plants and tasteful fruit for the human-kind. He thought it, too, unpardonable to torment an animal, or to cause it pain, and he tried to spare and to save the life even of the smallest creature. Some anecdotes have been preserved whieh illustrate his kind disposition. One autumn evening, as he was sitting by the tire which he had made in the wood, he noticed that the wind blew the troublesome stinging mosquitoes into the Rre, and burnt them. As soon; as he saw this, he fetched water from the brook with his only cooking and drinking vessel, a tin pail, and quenched the fire, exclaiming, "God forbid that I should ever have a fire for my comfort in which these creatures should suffer a painful death !" Once he was bitten by a snake. When a friend spoke to him afterwards about this, he sighed deeely, and said. "That poor animal! It only touched me when, in a fit oLueholy passion, I was nehrly going to take its life." When a road was being repaired, it happened that e hornet's nest was thereby destroyed,:: r.cl one of the hornets was entangled in Jonathan's clothing. Although repeatedly stung by it, he caught it most carefully, and gave it its freedom. His companions laughed, and asked him why be did not kill the troublesome insect. "It would have been wrong to kill it," he replied, "for it did not intend doing me any harm." During the warns season he slept in the woods; in winter at some farmer's house, but always on the hard floor, never in a bed. He was a man of great energy, of great tough- ness in bearing pain and hardships; so much so that he was revered even by the Indians, who never troubled him in his lonely journeys; yea, even admired as a great "medicine- man," because he never complained of being tired or un- well, and they always saw him in good and robust health. Jonathan was rather small of stature, and thin; quick in movement, and lively in speech. His heard was black ; his eyes dark, yet brilliant. "Johnny Appleseed," as every- body called him' died in 1847, in the blockhouse of a farmer, near Fort Wayne, in the State of Indiaan. The physician, and the people who surrounded his coneh, said that they had never seen a man die so peacefully and pain- lessly. This happy death may be considered as the reward of the good and kind heart, and of the simple and useful life of this friend and benefactor of men and animals. As such Jonathan Chapman's name will remain fresh in the thankful remembrance of millioes of men, and his life, so fruitfully and nobly spent, deserves this one rneed of peace- ful fame.

FAMIG-N NEWS. • ENGLANYAND nuitivrAß:- GENERAL PREN'DERGAST'S OPERATI.ONS. . Caneurra, Stnen en.—The A ogle-Indian newspapers are all but unanimous in their approval of the annexation. The following was received at .the India Office on Satur- day from General prendergast:— Blialllo, DECEMBER 29,11.—1 left Mandalay for Bhamo on the 19th instant with the following force :—Half Batta- lion Royal Welsh Fusiliers, half 4th Battery Ist Brigade Royal Artillery, Hazara Mountain Battery. half Battalion 25th Madras Infantry, one company Sappers, 36 Mounted Infantry, and about 300 blue jackets Arrived at Bhamo on the 28th instant, delay being due to intricacy of chan- nel. Country along river bank quiet, and people generally express pleasure at our coming. The Bhamo Woon-duk sent a messenger to meet us et Sabatee, and came on beard himself two miles from Bhamo. He has kept the town and neighbourhood quiet, and was glad to see us. The head- Man of the Chinese, whom I met on shore, was equally friendly. After reading my printed notices, he remarked, ' the scene is the same, the actors only are changed.' The water is so shallow that steamers cannot approach nearer than two miles from Bhamo. Telegraph line in disrepair all the way up. Have arranged for its re-establishment from Mandalay to Tsengco, and will continue the line to Bhamo when operators and instruments have been received. Propose to leave at Male an armed launch and a company I4Yal Welsh FusAers on my way down to restore conli- deuce in district. Mr. Stevenson will be political officer. I leave the following force at Bhamo :—Two companies Royal Welsh Fusiliers, half 4th Battery let Royal Artillery, lianara Mountain Battery, half Battalion 25th Madras nfantry, one company Sappers and Mounted Infantry. Wain Adamson will be left as political officer." NEW TAXATION IN INDIA. CALCUTTA, MONDAY —At to-day'e sitting of the Legis- lative Council Sir Auckland Colvin, Finance Minister, Moved that the bill for the introduction of an income-tax should be referred to a Select Committee. Mr. Steel stated that he anticipated a surplus at the end of the year. He thought that the bill would to a great extent correct the inequality of incidence of the present license tax, but was of °Pinion that the necessities of the case would be more pro- PererlY met by increasing the salt tax by 4a. per maund. Mr. feel also proposed the abolition of the rice tax, which, he Stated checked produetion in that staple. The motion to .refer the question to a Select Committee was thee agreed tch The report will be presented to the Council on the 22nd inst. FIGHT WITH A HILL TRIBE IN INDIA. 13oemay, MONDAY.—A telegram from Lahore states that a sharp ergegement has been fought in the hills between the Guides and a party of a blockaded tribe. The latter eelvere driven from their position with heavy loss. Colonel eautchinson, of the Guides, was severely wounded, and one sower was killed and three wounded. EXPEDITION AGAINST DACOITS. MANDALAY, JaNuearn A, VIA MlNGlAN.—General White, hearing that a large body of deceits had gathered in the neighbourhood of Sagaing Fort, which is held by a British garrison, despatched a force thither with a battery of artillery. He gave instructions that part of the force with 'the runs should be landed under cover of the infantry, eWhile the remainder should disembark from the boats on the lollowing night and advance with the garrison to attack the • enemy's intrenched position. When the troops arrived at Sagaing three officers left the fort and went down to the • river side without an escort to witness the disembarkation. tirey were on their way to the landing place a party of 'Mounted deaths, who who had been hiding in the jangle, dashed forward and wounded Lieatenant Armstrong, 2nd Hampshire Reeiment. Dr. Heath lifted the wounded officer, and was'earrying him out of reach when he toe was shot. Captain Smythe, 2nd Battalion Royal Scots Fusiliers, bravely defendsd his wounded comrade until assistance came from the garifibri, *Then the decolts fled. The claims pat forward by the creditors of King Thehaw already amour tto 15 lees Of rupees. • • E(Nil3l' AND THE SOUDAN. CAIRO, SUNDAY.—The first meeting bstween the Khedive, • Sir H. D. Wolff, and Multhtar Pasha took place on Satur- day, and lasted an hour. Views were exchanged on all the subjects covered by the Convention, but all parties haying taken solemn vows of secrecy the results are Shrouded in mystery. General Stephenson is on his way back to Assouan. CAIRO, MONDAY.—ft has transpired that at the meeting of the Ottoman and English Commissioners on Saturday Sir H. Drummond Wolff informed Mukhtar Pasea that the eettlement of the Soudan question was entirely a question 01 finance. E rypt cannot, Sir Henry pointed out, meet the expense of a native army, ocficered by Turks, as the re- Sources of the country are temporarily exhausted, and as Turkey cannot send troops to co-operate, the work of reel- -fication must be left to the English. If. however, Turkey insists upon the formation of a native If, army she 1. must be prepared to forego payment of the tribute, which -. would enable something like an efficient Egyptian force to be formed. THE EASTERN QUESTION. COLLECTIVE NOTE FROM. THE POWERS. PHILIPPOPoLIS, SATURDAY.—An order has been issued by . the Ministry of War granting leave until the 19th proximo to nearly half tha men of the Reserves. The Shainoffeky Regiment left here this morning for Haskeni, where it evill be stationed during the armistice. SOFIA, MONDAy,—The representatives of the six Great Powers to-dayehanded a Collective Note to the Bulgarian Government, stating that in their desire for a pacific issue from the complications in the East, the Powers have agreed * to the proposal of the Russien Government to earnestly call on the Governments of Sofia, Belgrade, and Athens to agree to a general and simultaneous demobilisation. It is hoped that the Porte would not refuse to imitate this example. The diplomatic agents communicated the views of their respective Governments to the Minister for Foreign Affairs, , desiring to be infermed of Prince Alexander's decision, 'Which is not yet known. It is believed that Gaban Effendi tnis on his way from Constantinople with a special mission la'alrom the Porte. SERVIA. REFUSES PEACE. ar. CONSTANMNOPLE, MONDAY.—It is stated that England "• bao accepted the proposal of Russia, that the Powers -should make representations to the Governments of Greece, Servia, and Bulgaria, insiAing upon the disarmament of •these States. BELGRADE, TUESDAY.—The Servian Government has de- cided not to conclude peace with Bulgaria until the Eastern Roumelian question has been solved in a manner satisfac- tory to Serena. THE DEMAND FOR DISARMAMENT. CONSTANTINOPLE, TUESDAY. Inconformity with in- structions from Lord Salisbury, Sir W. White has declared to the Porte that England adheres to the ' Russian proposal to demand the disarmament of Servia, Bulgaria, and Greece, on condition that Turkey should also disertn. The Porte is disposed to agree to this course, proviled Servie and Greece first commence to give effect to the demand of the Powers. Kiamil Pasha, the Grand Vizier, has expressed a desire to several of the Ambassadors that the Conference should reassemble in order to finally settle the questions under clicpute regarding the Balkan States. ATHENS, WEDNESDAY.—The representatives of the six • Great Powers have presented to the Greek Government the Collective Note recommending Greece, Servia, and Bulgaria to disarnanand cease threatening the disturbance of peace in the Eaet.

A GRECO-SERVIAN ALLIANCE. BELGRADE, TliUßSDA.Y.—Negotiations are proceeding be- tween Greece and Servia for the coneusion of an alliance for the protection of their common interests, in view of at- tempts to establish a great Bulgaria, and of the injury . which would be caused to those countries by the union of Bulgaria and Roumelia. The amnesty to political prisoners, Which was granted entirely on the King's initiative and with- -out the knowledge of the Progressist Party, has been re- ceived with great joy by the people. ENGLAND AND SPAIN. MADRID, Suerretv.—The Spanish Minister for Foreign Affairs, Senor Morel, and Sir Clare Ford, the British sinister, have signed a protocol by which their respective Powers agree on the grounds of mutual friendship that the subjects of great Britain shall enjoy in the Caroline and Pelew Islands the same advantages and pzivileges in respect to commerce and trade as have been granted to Gler- manv. ATTEMPTED REVOLT IN SPAIN.—SEIZURE OF A FORT. MADRID, Moernay.—Near the stroke of midnight yeeter- day, a body of 40 soldiers and a lesser numb,: of civilians, commanded by 3. sergeant of regulars, surprised the fort and castle of St. Jalien, at Carthagena, Which is garrisoned by 60 men. They had. moreover, arranged with a further num- ber of insurgente in the town that the firing of the first shot should be taken as a signal for the extension of the rising to the town. Meanwhile, however, s)me inkling of what was on foot had come to the ears of General Fajat do, the Com- mandant of the garrison and military governor, who at once . proceeded to the harra6s. He also took a body of the gen- darmerie. He advanced alone to the insurgents and ad- dressed them. He was answered by a volley from the rifles of the insurgent!, and fell dangerously wounded. The in- surgents, finding themselves unable to resist the loyal troops, abandoned the cast'e and precipitately fled, taking refuge on board a small vessel, which sailed immediately, it is believed, for Oran. A war vessel has started in pursut. The insurgents are said to be Republicans. It is rumoured .that two sergeants and one corporal have been arrested. Artillery are posted in the streets of Carthagena. The town, however, 18 quite quiet. GERMAN AGGRESSION IN SAMOA..—FLIGHT OF THE KING. SAN FRANCISCO, MONDAY. The latest news from the Samoa group of islands in the Pacific is of a highly dis- quieting character. The Germans have made a pretext for interfering with the government of the islands oa the al- leged ground of protecting. the German traders. The King ' and Chiefs of the native tribes have Peen wantonly insulted by the German officials ; and so exasperated were the natives that, had it not been for the intervention of the British and American Consule, the German residents on the islands would undoubtedly have-Wen massacred. A force of German marines and seilore were landed direcrly after- wards from the German man of war Albatress, who forcibly took possession of the place, and before whom the King and his advisers have tied for eafety. The Samoan ceig was hauled down by the German Censnl in the presence of the • German forces. The British and American Consuls have protested energeticelly against these proceedings on the part of the Germans, but without any effect, and a formal written protest was afterwards lodged. the highest state of excitement, and a war is threatened, in which it is feared white men will suffer indisorimin- Count Hatzfeldt,. the' German Alnbaseacinr, &led upon Lord Salisbury at the Foreign Office on Tuesday afternoon. Tho visit was paid in accordance with the express instruc- tions of Prince Bismarck, and for the purpose of informing the British Government that the action of tbe commander of the Albatross at Samoa was taken withont the previous knowledge or sancticn of the Imperial German Government. Pending the receipt of full information from the German re- presentatives. at Samoa, and necessarily reserving entire liberty of action, the Imperial Government intimated through his Excellency, their wish and intention to ad- here to the treaty by which Germany, England, and the United States bad agreed to respect the independence of Samoa.

THE •I'ORM IN- AMERICA. PHILADELPHIA, MONDAY.—CoId continues to preYail ex- tensively on the Atlantic seaboard, but the temperature is rather higher in the interior. The tug Conffdence, with a lighter, bound to the relief of a wrecked vessel, founded in Massachuesetts Bay on Saturday last, and 40 men, it is believed, were drowned, as nothing has been heard concerning them. The schooner Millie has been wrecked near Boston, six lives being lost. The, wrechage and a large number of bodies were cast up by the waves along the shore. The steamer Brittanic arrived safely at New York yesterday after encountering a fearful storm.

RUSSIA AND THE VATICAN. WEDNIVDAY.—The Vatican yesterday received a request from the Russian government to s.Ancticn the des- patch of M. Boutenieff to Rome, with a view to the resump- tion of the neptiations between Russia and the Holy Sce. This step is regarded here as due to a desirer on the part of Russia to counteract the effect of the more intimate relations established between the Vatican and Prussia.....

POLITICAL AFFAIRS IN VICTORIA. MELBOURNE, THURSDAY.—The HOD. James Service de- livered a valedictory address to his conetithents in which, after explaining his retirement from public life was due to ill-health, be claimed that the coalition Ministry had been of immense benefit to the colony in securing the complete abolition of the political managemest of railways, tbat of political patronage. He therefore urged the coniirmance of the coalition under the Hon.- Duncan Geddes and the Hon. Alfred Deakin. Mr. Service's speech was very cor- dially received. FRANCE.—MESSAGE BY THE PRESIDENT. PARIS, THURSDAY.—President Grevy's Message to the French Chambers was read this afternoon in the Chamber of Deputies. M. Grevy declares that the Government of the Republic enjoys the high respect of Europe, and adde that in recent years France has contributed in no small degree to the malntenance of European peace. The Presi- dent concludes by rendering homage in wares terms to the army and navy. In the Senate to-day M. Leroyer was re-elected President by 140 votes out of 163. ASSASSINATION OF A FRENCH PREFECT. PARIS, TRURSDAY.—The Matira to-day announces that the Prefect of the Department of Eure was assassinated yesterday evening in a train near Evreux by some unknown Persons. The body was found on the Maison Lafitte Bridge, and there were two wounds on tbe head. It is believed that the assassins intended to throw the body into the Seine, but that, owing to their mistaking their whe'reabouts, it fell on to the road at Evreux. The Matin believes that the motive of the crime was robbery. An Exchange Company's telegram says it is snpposed that the murderers were interrupted, as they overlooked an envelope in which were 500 francs in notes and a purse con- taining 37 francs.

Mr. P. Gossett, the manager of the Jersey Banking Coln- I 3pan' (which suspended payment on Monday) and treasurer of the Jersey States, was last night arrested on a charge brought against him by a special committee of the Jersey States. FATAL ACCIDENT AT BLACKPOOL.—A joiner named John Whitetide, married, with a family of four, slipped from a plank while at work in re-decking the North Pier at Black- pool, on Thursday morning, and falling into the sea he was drowned. The water was rather rough at the time, and all attempts to save him were unavailing. FOUNDERING OF AN EAST INDIAMAN.—A special cable message received from Capetovnn on Thursday morning, dated 13th January, states that the splendid iron ship Hud- son Bay. of Glasgow, 1,641 tons register, homeward bound to Falmouth for orders, with a full cargo of sugar and other produce from Java,has foundered off the Cape of Good Hope. Part of the the crew have been landed at Table Bay, bat the fate of the remainder is at present unknown. The insurances are chiefly effected with London com- panies. RROPOSED LEGISLATION.—The Standard says notice will lie at once given from the Radical benches of a resolution in favour of free education. Mr. Jesse Collings's Allotment and Small Holdings Bill will be at once re-introduced, but the provisions relating to yeomen's holdings, which are felt to belong to a different class of legislation, will be drop- ped ; they may, however, be afterwards incorporated in a saparate Daily Telegraph says a bill for the abo- lition of the Viceroyalty will, it believes, be foremost among the Government measures for Ireland. OPENING OF TH ;4: NEW. PARLIAMENT HOUSE OF LORDS.-'-dlchtseasie • The eleventh Parliament of Queen Vietoria met to- day. Shortly before two o'clock the doors of toe House of Lords were thrown open. and 'a number of ladies were shown to seats on the Opposition side of the House. Soon afterwards Viscount Enfield, Lord Thurlow, Lord Sudely, Lord Rothschild, and Lord Bramwell entered, and at on the Opposition benches, On the Ministerial side there appeared the Duke of Richmond and Gordon, Earl Brownlow, and Lord , Harris, who eat on the front bench ; Lord Egertcrer, the Earl of Crawford and Balcarree, and the Earl of Limerick, who eat on other benches; and the Bishop of Hereford, who was the sele occupant of the Epis- copal Bench. Tbe Lord Chancellor, clothed as a Lord Commiseioner, entered at rive minoree past two o'clock.. lie did not, how- ever, take his seat on the woolsack, but passed out, to return almost immediately at the head of .the Lords Commis- sioners. who were, besides the noble and learned lord, Vie-- count Cranbrook, the Earl of Coventry,-the Earl of Icicles-- leigh, and V;scount Barrington. Tneir lordships having. taken their seats on a bench in front of the Throne, the , Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod was despatched to the- House of Commons to summons its members to the Honer of Lords. A crowd of Commoners sooit appeared at the I House of Lords' bar, conspicuous amongst whom were Sir M. Hicks-Beach, Lord J. Manners, Mr.. Chaplin, Sir R N. Fowler, Colonel Stanley, Mr. W. I. Smith. and Sir ' J. Ratnsden. , The LORD Catatecnoecae—My Lords and! Gentlemen,— Her Majesty, not tein•Sieg fit to be presort here this daY in her Royal Person, bath been pleased, in order to the opening and holding of this Parliament, to- cause letter's patent to be passed under the Great Seal, cootetirutiug us and several other lords therein named, to do, all things her Majesty's name on her part necessary to be performed in this Parliament, and this will more fully appear by the letters patent themselves, which will now be read. The Commission was then read by the Hon. Slingsbyo Bethel]. ' The LORD CILINCELLOD We have it in command hem her Majes.y to let you know that her Majesty witl, as soon as the members of your House be sworn, declare the causes of her calling of this Parliament; and it being necessary that a Speaker of the House of Commons shall be first chosen, it is her Majesty's pleasure that you, gentlemen of the House of Commons, repair to the place where you are to sit, and there proceed to the choice of some proper per- son to be your Speaker, and that you present such person whom you shall so choose here to-morrow at two o'clock for her Majesty s Reyal approbation. The Commoners then retired_ The Lords Commissioners- also retired; but the Lord Chancellor soon returned in le'es ordinary robes, and took his Best on the woolsack. Prayers were said by the Bishop of Hereford, after which the process of swearing in the Peers was proceeded with, the first being the Lord Chancellor s and amongst the others were V.eceunt Cranbrook, Lord Iddesleigh, Lord Sudelev, Lord Rothschild. Viscount Enfield, and Lord Bramwell. TETE NEW CLERK- OF PARLIAMENTS-. • • . The LORD CHANCELLOR said it was his painful 'duty to, communicate to the Reuse the sad intelligence of the deathi of Sir W. Rose, late clerk of the Parliaments. He had; also to announce that her Majesty had beet; pleased to ap- point Mr. IlenrY John Lowndes Graham to the office. Mr. Graham then entered the House in the usual wig and gown, took the oath, and, having shaken hands with the I Lord Chancellor, eeated himself at the table. Immediately after-yards the lortiel Cnancellor left the. Hou,e, which remeined empty for some time. ' His lordship returned twice, and on each occasion about a deem] peers were sworn, their Royal Highnesses the Prince • of %Vales, the Duke of. Edinburgh, the Duke of Connaught, and the Duke of Cinibridge being among the number. Lord ' Kenyon and the Earl- of Buckinghamshire also performed the ceremony—the former on attaining his majority, and the latter on succeeding to the title. At five minutes past four o'clock the House adjourned till two o'clock next day. HOUSE OF COMMONS —Densely. The doors Mahe House of Commons were opened at an early hour in the morning for the admission of members of the new Parliament—the eleventh of her Majesty's reign. The earliest of the arrivals was Mr. Thomas Blake, member for Forest of Dean, who represented Leominister in the Par- liament before last, and who now appeared on the vacant floor soon after ten o'cleek.
