SUMMONS OF THE HOUSE. Shortly after two o'clock " Black Rod" was announced. Sir J. R. DRUMMOND, Usher of the Black Rod, advanced to the table and announced that the Lords appointed by Royal Commission desired the attendance of the Commons in the House of Peers. Headed by Sir M. Hicks-Beach the assembled representatives went in irregular order to the Upper House. THE ELECTION OF SPEAKER.

On the return of the members from the -House of Lords, at a Quarter past two, Sir J. I‘IOWIREAY rose in a densely crowded House and said :—Sir Thomas Eriskine May,—ln obedience to the gra- cioss communication from her Majesty which we have just listened to in another place, it now becomes the first duty of the House of Commons, as it is its ancient and undoubted privilege. to proceed to the election of a Speaker. I feel it, Sir F.:seine May, to be a great honour and a great gratifica- tion that I have been requested on this occasion to propose as a candidate my right hon. friend the member for War- : wick and Leamington, with the confident assurance that the name of Mr. Arthur Peel will be received with cordial approval and will meet • with universal assent. (Cheers.) Two years ago the House of Commons sustained a serious and signal loss by the retirement of so able and experienced a Speaker as Sir Henry Brand. I believe its general impres- sion was Who among the members of the House is capable to sustain the unremitting toil, to bear the heavy burden, the immense responsibility of so arduous a post? I think I may say it wee a matter of congratulation that the choice of those who proposed a gentleman to fill the chair fell upon Mr. Arthur Peel. (Hear, hear.) The son of a great Ceinotoner, of a great Prime Minister, and a great leader of this HOUS3, bearing the name of England's most illustrious hero—Arthur Wellesley Peel seemed to have a double claim upon the confidence of this Hones. and upon the respect and affection of the British nation. But he had other and stronger claims, personal and in- dividual claims, which recommended him to the notice of the House of Commons, and which were his real recommendations to the high post to which he was elected. He was known for his high and indepen- dent character. for his spotless integrity, and for leis nn- wearying courtesy. (Laughter from some Irish members, and " No " from Mr. Biggar, followed by general cheering.) He was known to have experience of official life, and to be thoroughly conversant with all the work of the House of Commons. His name was received with acclamation. He was proposed by my hon. friend the member for Bedford (Mr. Whitbread) in a speech which still lingers in our memories. Mr. Peel was called to the chair by the unani- mous voice of the House, and we were at once assured of the wisdom of our choice, for, as soon as ever he was elected, the Speaker elect, standing on those sieps, before he proceeded to take his seat in the chair, addressed the House in words so striking, so weighty, so dignified, and 90 becom- ing his high station, that I believe every ono of us felt that he raised by that address the moral tone of the whole House. (Hear, hear.) The whole House is, I believe, per- fectly conscious of the high opinion entertainee. of Mr. I'eel. This much I may say, no one will deny this—that he has fulfilled to the utmost all the anticipations of his most sanguine supporters. (Cheers.) He has conducted himself in the chair with dignity. He has presided over over our deliberations with ability and impartiality, and he has exhibited ready decision, sound judgment, self-pesses- sion, and resolution. He has proved himself well ac- quainted with the rules and orders of the House, and he has

Ishown himeelf eepable of protecting all our privilews. I eiropose, therefore, to this-new House! Of Cotronons, come posed to so large an extent of new members, representiag'so man'y new conetitueticiem, ae old and- honoured Speaker, vied and approved by the last House of ,Commone. I feel assured that the House at large is well Ceativinced that there is not at the present moment, within these walls, any other man so pre-eminently qualified to guide and direct our de- liberations, to esaietain our privileges, and to band down unsullied tre:posterity all these lofty traditions which have ever apportarned to the anique position of the Speaker of the House of Commons. (Cheers.) Sir Erskine May, I beg to move that Mr. Arthur Wellesley Feel do take the chair as Speaker of the House of GYM moos. (Cheers.) Mr. Rumen, who was received witkcheers, said: Sir Erskine May, I 'rise for the purpose of seconding the nee- Lion which has been submitted by the right hon. member opposite. To members of the present Parliament now about te commence its' sittings, who have been in the last Parliament and the last Session, it seems absolutely unneceseaey to say a word in favour of this candidature; but to the new members, what has been said, by the right hone gentleman is of importance. I hnow not that I onght to trouble tbe , House with anything like a repitition of it. At the same time I feel disposed to add- two or three sentences to theme which he has uttered. illeary hear.) What qualities are required in the presiding officer of the House ot Common, have been to a certain extent &scribed. To new members it mat be, I think, clear, although they have no aoquaintance with what has been- done in the House heretofore, that it io absolutely necessary , that the Speaker should have a most extensive and minute ' knowledge of the procedure of the douse, and of Its- modes, of transacting its business. That, I think, we have found in our late Opeaker, and I doubt not we shall fin sl in our Speaker that is to come ample knowledge of that kind. (Heir. hear.) At the s- me time, with regard to the que:e- tion of courtesy, I have observed that the Speakers who have sat in that chair during the forty years I have been in this Efouse—(eheers)—have been themselves marked for their got:story to individual members (Elearohear.) There are ateundent cases in which members require to consuls the Speaker as to- little difficulties that arise, or as to points of their own procedure; and I have looked almost with wonder,. but with great admiration, at the manner in which applica- tions of this kind to the Speaker from every part of The House have been received by him. (Hear, hear.) I havere no doubt whatsoever that in future, in the Speaker we hope 1 we are about to elect, we shall find this courtesy as con- spicuous as-it has been displayed by those who have prece- ded him. In a House like this composed of more than 600 members, debating with a freedom not surpassed. The questions discussed are so great, they interest so many, the teeling of party is sometimes so strong, that it would be a deplorable and lamentable thing if we had in the chair of this House a feeble man, wanting in firmness and -courage on these occa- sions. (Cheers-)' Well, I believe, judging-by the past, that- in placing Mr. Peel in the chair we shall have a confidence that, whilst he wall do justice te every'party and every sec- tion in the House, he will be certain to do this—to uphold- the dienitY of his own office; and to support the authority of the House itselfe (Cheers.) (Cheers.)' I beg, sir, to second the nomination of Mr. Arthur Wellesley Peel to be called to the Chair of this House. (Cheers.) Mr.. JusoiNr McCeerrety : Sir, it will not be my duty, speaking on behalf of the party with- whom I have the honour to act, to-offer any opposition to what seems to be the general desire of the House to-day. But it would be the meanest affectation, and something like hypocrisy on my part, and on the part of those for whom I speak on this occasion, if I were to allow the language of unmitigated eulogy which has been poured out with regard to Mr. Peel to pass without some formal protest on my part. Mr. PEEL, who was received with hearty and general, cheering, said, speaking from his place as 'a member of the,' _House: Sir Themes Erskine May, I respectfully thank the .House for the manner in which they have received the men- tion of my name. I should be altogether wanting, sir,, in' the discharge of the obligations of courtesy, and, I. hope I may add, of friendship too, if I failed to thank the right hon. beronet the member for the University of Oxford and the right hon. gentleman the member for Birmingham, for the terms they have used towards me in respectively propos- ing and seconding my nomination to the chair of this House. Two years ago, sir, it was the pleasure of this House to elect me to fill that chair. They were two years of event- ful history. (Hear, hear.) I speak not,, sir, of the mere personal considerations which arise in connection with them. No Speaker can have occupied that chair fer two years without having the pe,sonal importance of those times- impressed heavily upon him individually. (Hear, hear.). But I may say that if I have learned—as I have learned— much during the occupation of that chair for two years, / , have above all things learned this—more deeply to appre- ciate and more fully to estimate the difficulties and the delicacies which surround the occupant of that chair- - (hear, hear,)---and, I say it unaffectedly,. I • :am more deeply conscious than I ,ever could have been before of my own shortcomings, and of failure to act up to the great traditions of that office. (Cheers.) Sir, those have been eventful years. They have resulted in a general elec- tion, conducted as it was under a Reform Bill, and a Redis- tribution of Seats Bill. The result has been that we are now met together in this House with an infusion of new members such as has never been paralleled for the last fifty years. (Hear, hear.) As one who has sat in this House for twenty years, may I remind those hon. gentlemen who, conversant asthey ' are with business of great importance outside this House, are yet taking their place in this Assembly for the first time, may I remind them—l em sure I do it without pre- sumption—that the rules and forma of proceeding of this House are wedded to remote antiquity, that many of them which seem to ,be new, are developments of the old, and that, while we have ailopnct new rules to suit the supposed requirements of the day, we have ever been influenced by a , regard for precedent and for old lines. (Hear, hear.) Many l Of our customs are old, some are new, and some are invested 1 with the prescriptive dignity of immemorial usage. Sir, if I am elected, if it is the pleasure of the House to elect me to that chair, I shall appeal with equal confidence to new members as to old. (Hear, hear.) I shall ask them to approach the rules. forms, and orders, with that generous and equitable spirit in which alone they ought to be ap- proached, whether they have to be interpreted and adminis- tered, on the one band, or have to be complied with on the other. I shall, above all ask for the forbearance of the House. No one knows better than I how much I shall stand in need of it. The position of a Speak. r, the moral strain upon him, to say nothing of the physical tedium— (ch ersl—are great calls and demands upon any individual. (Hear, 'hear.) Whatever these burdens may be, whatever these difficulties may be, they are lightened if one can feel assured that one will have the co-operation and support of the Houses (Hear, hear.) Without that support the posi- tion of a Speaker is untenable and intolerable—(hear, hear)—and there is ample reward for anything that may be gone through in the discharge of that offices—l would vay more, those difficulties I have alluded to vanish altogether if one can be assured that in some small measure at least one has won the confidence of the House of Com- mons. (Cheers.) I respectfully thank the House, and I very humbly place myself at its entire dispoeal. (Re- newed cheers.) Mr. PEEL was then, amid aeneral cheers, conducted by Sir J. Mowbray and Mr. Bright to the chair. Standing on the top step the Speaker Elect spoke as follows :—Stauding in this place I beg again most respectfully to thank the members of this House for the great honour they have done me, and for the dignified office with which they have been pleased to invett me. I shall remember all I have said, and I beg to assure the House that I shall above all try to exercise that virtue of impartiality to which allusion has been made. I shall strive to know no distinction of party, and shall appeal with the utmost confidence, not to one sec- tion of the House or to another, not to one party or ano- ther, but to the entire assembly of the House of Commons. (Cheers.) The hon. gentleman then took his seat, and the Ser- geant-at-Arms advanced and placed the mace on the table. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack shortly before two o'clock. Prayers having been said by the Bishop of Hereford, the Lord Chancellor retired to the Princes' Chamber to exchange his ordinary gown for the fuU scarlet and ermine robe of his rank. His lordship shortly returned, and with the other Royal Commissioners, via., Lord Cranbrook, the Earl of Iddesleigh, the Earl of Coventry, and Lord Barrington, seated himself on the tem- porary bench in front of the Throne, as is usual on such occasions, being uncovered. ROYAL APPROIATION OF THE SPENXER.--Mr. Peel, the Speaker-elect, accompanied by the Chancellor of the Ex- chequer and several members of the House of Commons, attended at the bar according to ancient custom and notified that the Commons had elected him to the office of Speaker. The Lord Chancellor assurrd the right hon. gentleman that her Majesty readily approved and confirmed him in the office. The Speaker then, in the name of the House of Commons, laid customary claim to their undoubted rights and privileges, and that the most favourable construction should be put upon their proceedings. Assent having been give' in due form, the Speaker and other members of the House of Commons retired, and several peers having, taken the oath and subscribed to the roll of Parliament, their lordships adjourned. At four o'clock their lordships, on the motion of Lord Tankerville, adjourned until two o'clock on Thursday. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY. The House met to-day at two o'clock, when there waa again a large attendance of members. APPROVAL,OF THE SPEAKER.

At ten minutes past two the Speiker-elect, preceded by the Sergeant-at-Arms bearing the mace, entered the House and took the chair. Mr. Peel was in Court dress, bu.t with- out his silk robe, and wore a tie-wig instead of the fall- bottomed wig which he wears as Speaker. Five minuter later Black Rod was announced, and having advanced to the table, he intimated that the Lords Commissioners desired the attendance of the House in the House of Peers. The Speaker-elect, accompanied by a crowd of members, there- upon proceeded to the Upper House.

. . At twenty minutes past two the Speaker returned, and having passed up the foor of the House, instead GI taking the chair, he proceeded to his room. liraying there assumed his silk gown pnd foill•bottommed wig,,he returned and took the chair. The SPEAKER then said : I have to report to the House that in the House of Peers Her Majesty, by Her Royal Commissioners has been pleased to approve of the choice made of myself for the office of your Speaker, and that I have in your name and on your behalf laid claim to all your ancient rights and privileges—freedom of speeet in debsto, freedom from arrest of your persons and servants, particularly a free access to Her Majesty whenever occasion shall require, and that the most favourable construction shall be placed upon all your proceedings. All this Her Majesty by Her Royal Commissioners has been pleased to grant and confirm in as ample a manner as they have ever been granted and confirmed by Her Maj,atz or any of Her Royal predecessors. It is MY duty to again thank the Nouse for the high honour they have done me in electing me to the chair of this House. It is now my duty to remind the House that the first duty of its members is to take the oath in the form prescribed by law. The Speaker then took the oath of allegiance, and was the first to sign the new roll of members. THE CASE OF MR. BRADLAUGH. DECISION OF THE SPEAKER. ADMINISTRATION OF THE OATH.

The SPEAKER, again rising, said :—Before hon. members come to the table to take the oath it will be my duty to in- form the House that I have received a letter from the right hon. gentleman the leader of this House with respect to the proceedings affecting the hon. gentleman the junior mem- ber for Northampton. I think it my duty under the very exceptional circumstances of the moment and inasmuch as by the nature of the case there can be no deb-aeon the sub- ject, to put the House in possession of the main facts of this letter, and also of another notice or letter which I have received from the right hon. gentleman the member for Cambridge University (Mr. Raikes), signed by himself and the bon, member for the Honiton division of Devon (Sir John Kennaway.) The letter of the right hon. gentleman for Bristol (Sir M. Hicks-Beach) contains an historical re- trospect of the case, which I do not propose to read to the House. (Laughter and " Hear, hear," from the Opposi- tion.) It is, as far as I know, a statement of mere facts, and it is not necessary for me to put the House in poses- don of those facts. The letter concludes by putting an im- portant question which it is my duty to read in the words the right hon. gentleman has wed. It is as follows It will thus be seen that the House of Commons consistently, and notwithstanding new writs and fresh elections of Mr. Bradlaugh, bas refusA to permit him to repeat the words which in his case would be merely an act of profanation. The Court of Anneal has decided by a judgment which the House of Commons cannot but recognise that Mr. Brad- laugh Was incapable of taking the oath.—(Cries of " No.")

No one doubts his identity—(laughter and " bear, bear ") —and I am advised that as a matter of law a state of facts once established is presumed to exist until the contrery is proved.—(Cries of "No, no.")—Until the House of Com- mons is fully constituted any action by the House is diffi- cult, it not impossible. I therefore respectfully submit for your consideration, in view of the facts to which 1 have deemed it my duty to direct your attention, that Mr. Brad- laugh should not be permitted to go through the form of ' taking the oath without an opportunity being afforded to the House of expressing its opinion upon a proceeding which, I believe, if fully constituted, it would decliee to sanctien." The other notice kcontiaued the Speaker) to which I re- ferred, from the member for Cambridge University and tile member for the Honiton Division of Devon, contains also an historical retrospect of the case—(laughter)—and differs very slightly indeed from the letter which I have just read, except in calling attention to the fact of the appearance of a newspaper styled the National Reformer, of January 10. 1886, and the right bon. gentleman and his colleague con- clude with a protest, and ask my opinion upon a point of order. I have deemed it my duty under the exceptional circumstances to mention these letters to the House, and it may be for the convekience of the House that I should, be- fore the House is constituted, and before members have come to the table to take the oath, state my views of what ought to be my conduct en this occasion. (Hear, hear.) It will be observed that the statements made by the right hon. gentlemen allude to proceedings in a former Parlia- ment.. (Hear, bear.) In no case cited does the Speaker take original and independent authority upon himself. It Is always by the action of the House in consequence of something that has occurred during that session and that Parliament. We are assembled in a new Parliament. I know nothing of the resolutions of the past. (Opposition cheers) They have lapsed, they are void, they are of no effect with reference ro this case. (Hear, heetr.) It is the right—the legal statutable obligation—of members when re- turned to this House to come to this table and to take the oath prescribed by statute. I have no authority. I hays no right, original or delegated,. to interfere between an hon. member and his taking of the oath. (apposition cheers.) I have been further asked whether when the L.Horise is complete and after a quorum has been constituted et weteld he competent for a motion to be made intervening between the member; for Northampton and his taking the oath. I have without hesitation come to the conclusion that it would neither be my duty to prohibit the hon. gentleman from coming nor to permit a motion to be made which would stand between him and the taking of the oath. (Opposition cheers.) The hon. gentleman takes that oath under whatever rises may attach to him in a court of law. (Hear, hear.) But it is not for me, arid I respectfully say it is'not for the House, to enter into any inquisition—(Op- position cheers)—as to what may be the opinionsnf a mem-, her when he comes teethe table to take the oath. lam honnd; and the Hoes& is bound, by the forma of the House and•by the legal obligations and rights of members. If a member comes to this table and offers to take the oath, I know of no right whatever to intervene be- tween him and his legal stttutable obligations. (Opposi- tion‘ cheers.) • The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER: I would ask the indulgence of the House while I make one observation. (Cries of " No' and "'Order.") The SPEAKER I must remind the right hon. gentleman that &debate is not in order. (Hear, hear.) No doubt the right hon. gentleman rose to a point of or tar. The CHANC.ELLOR of the EXCHEQUER, who sn acain ris- ing was received with murmurs from the Opposition, said : I understand, sir, your answer to the question which I, have ventured to put to you is that you will neither intervene yourself in this matter nor permit the intervention of another hon. member of this House with a motion. flow- ever much I and other members of this House--(Cries of

"Order.') The;Sreaxin: I must remind the right bon gentleman of the distinction I drew between calling my attention to a point order and making a speech. (Opposition cheere ) The right hon. gentleman has not himself taken the oath. (Renewed cheers.) The process of swearing-in the members was then begun. At the outset they were called upon in the alphabetical order of the countiesond the county and borough members for Bedfordshire, Berke, B'uckinghamshire, and Cambridge- shire were the first to advance to the table. Among those who in this group toolr the oath and subscribed their names were Mr..Magniac (he being the tirst to go through the cere- mony), Mr. C. Flower,, Mr. Whitbread, Captain Verney, Mr. Richardson-Gardner, Mr. Raikee, Mr. Beresford Hope, and Mr.Newnes. Baron Ferdinand de Rothschild took the oath in accordance vele h the Jewish custom. Each bon. member, after signing is name, WAS introduced to the Speaker by the Clerk of the House, and shook hands with him. The next counties named were Cheshire, Cornwall, and Cumberland. In this group, however, a large number of other bon members- advanced to the table for the pur- pose of taking the oath, and from this time the attempt to swear-in the members after the alphabetical order of the counties-, was abandoned. Accordingly a miscellaneous hatch of•gentletnen, comprising Dr. Forster, Mr. Elibbert, Viscount' Curzon, Mr..Coiartney, Sir R. Jardine, Mr. H.. C.. Howard, Mr. Borlase, and Mr. C-nybeare were the next to go through the ceremony. Mr. Herbert Gladstone was then seen at the table, and was sworn separately. The crush in the paseege between the front Ministerial bench and the Clerks table became so great that the Speaker suggested that those hon. members who had not been sworn should take' their seats in order to enable others to approach the table and subscribe their names. This appeal, however, had not much effect in relieving the block. Among those who for some time previoutly had been standing in the crowd in the mlddle of the floor, head and 'shoulders above most of his fellows, was Mr. Bradlaugh. His MOS. ments were watched with great interest. When the next group of members catneforward to be sworn the hon. gentle- man.was observed tohave possessed himself, like the rest of them, of a testament, and as the Clerk eoncluded the reading of tbe words of the oath Mr. Bradlaugh kissed the book—an action that did not appear to be noticed by the Clerk,. It was long after this, however, that the hon..neem- her for Northampton was able to make his way to the table. In the meantime the Clerk had begun to swear each mem- ber? separately as he get to the table. When at length Mr. Bradlaugh found himself there be told the Clerk—or ap- peared to be telling him—that he was already sworn. The Clerk (Mr. Millman). however, desired the hon. member again to go thro..egla the form, and this Mr. Bradlaugh at once consented to do, the Clerk slo wiy reading out the words of the oath, and the hon. member kissing the book. He then subscribed his name in the roll and shook hands with the Speaker. Thus for the present ended the great Brad- laugh controversy." Mr. John Bright made.an affirmation after the manner permitted by law to members of the So- ciety of Frienos. Shortly before the termieation of the Bradlaugh incident the oath was administered separately to I Mr Gladstone, Sir M Hicks-Beach, Colonel Stanley, Mr W H Smith, Sir R Cross, and Sir R Webster. Mr Gladstone signed the roll immediately after the Chancellor of the Ex- chequer. Lord R Churchill, Sir H -Holland,.Lord John Manners, Sir Charles Dilke, Mr Osborne Morgan, Mr Rit- chie, Lord Richard Groevesor, Sir W' -earcourt,.Mr Plunket, Mr A J Balfour, and other members of the present and late Government were afterwards sworn, but all of them did not I then subscribe their rames. On the motion of Mr AKERS DocroLas, the Nouse ad- journed at 25 minutes to six o'clock. HOUSE, OF LORDS.—TEMISDAY.
The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at two o'clock.

The only business. was the swearing in of peers, of whom during the afternoon twenty-three took the oath and sub. scribed to the roll Gi Parliament'. The Bishop of London took the oath, and the Bishops of Chester (Dr. Stubbs), and Southwell (Dr. Ridding), took the oath and their seats oas their accession to the peerage by rotation. The Bishops were introduced by the Bishops of London and Hereford. Their L-Erdshipa adjourned, at four o'clock until Tuesday next.
HOUSE OF COMMONS -THVRSDAY.

The Speaker took the chair at two o'cO.ock. After prayers, which were said to-day for the first time since the House met, the swearing in of members was at once proceeded. with. A small table was placed in front of the table of the House, and at this members took tl,e. oath in batches of four er five. Amongst the first to take the oath to-day were Mr. Isaac Holden, Mr. W. B. Denison, and Mr. R. W. Daff. The ceremony of- swearing in proceeded steadily for the first hoar of the sitting, until the number of those wanting to be sworn was exhausted. Baron H. de Worms took the oath after the Jewish custom with his hat on. When all the members in waiting had been sworn, Lord Arthur Hill called the attention of the Speaker to the fact that the member for Mid-Armagh was the Hon. Robert Torrens O'Niel, and not the Hon. Robert Frnest O'Niel as described in the return. By order of the tpeaker the Clerk of the Crown attended to amend the return accordingly. On the motion of Mr. Akers Dc:uglas, the House adjourned at half-past three until two o'clock next day. More than a hundred members took the oath.

THE new Parliament, whatever else it ins)' do, has made a good beginning in the rea - elec ion of Mr. ARTHUR PEEL as Speaker: It was at one time thought the Tories woula carry party feeling so far as to propose a nevi man for the new Parliament, although the)' had not a word to say as to the way in which Mr. PEEL had discharged the difficult and delicate duties of his high office. They did - contest Mr. PEEL'S seat; and they stror hard to beat him; but they failed in their determined assault. It was whispered that Sir MATTHEW WHITE RIDLEY was the per' son on whom Conservatives had their eye for the office of Speaker; but the fates , were against them in this respect, too. fo! while Mr. PEEL was a successful, Sir MATTHEW was an unsuccessful candidate. Then; again, when the Tories came to count heads at the close of the General Election/ they found that they could only hope to win in a contest for the Speakership by securing the solid Parnellite vote in conjunction with the support of every member of their own party. It is not unlikely tnat Mr. PateetE!, would have fallen in with a proposal to din place a Speaker who has shown atinsell strong enough to grapple with Irish obstruct' tion ; but what of the Tory members for - Ireland? Would they have taken kindly to putting a slight on Mr. PEEL because he via 9 disliked by the Irish Nationalists ? W. cant' not think so; and the chances are that the Government would have been beaten and, discredited on the first day of the meeting 01 the new Parliament. This was too much tc: risk; and it may be assumed, therefore, that in assenting to the re election of Mr. ARTNIM PEEL as Speaker of the House of Commong they have made a virtue of necessity. Sir JOHN MOWBRAY, as the mover on behalf of the Tories, was emphatic in his praise of Mr. PEEL---so emphatic that, if he was sincere, and we have no reason to doubt his sincerity, it excites the reflection that the Government would have committed a grievous wrong if they had gone further and fared worse. Mr. BRIGHT confirmed all that was said, and re' , marked that the election would not onit be a signal honour to Mr. PEEL. but a signal 1 honour to the House itself. The only dis' cordant note struck was that of the Irish party. Mr. PARNELL was not present; but, in his ab- sence,Mr. JusTua McCaRTHv entered a protest, a feeble protest, not against Mr. PEEL'S elec- tion ; but, as he himself expressed it, against the "unmitigated eulogy" of him as Speakers It was evident that his heart was not in hig task; and, as he had nothing: like a cases the incident served to bring into strong relief the high qualities which had in the past marked the conduct of the Speaker. Sir MICHAEL HICKS-BEACH, who followed, said ; Mr. PEEL had won the confidence and support of the House; and he added that, much as had been expected of him, "that expectation had been More than fulfilled." Mr. GLADSTONE I showed himself in good vein, and gentlY chaffed the Parnellites for assuming that it was possible that there could be such a being las a Speaker who would please them upofl all occasions. He congratulated Mr. PEEL upon having shown that he possessed that happy balance and combination of attributeS fahich enabled him to deserve and win the ' confidence. of the House. There can be nO question that the eulogy of the Speaker- great as it was—did not go beyond the feels ing of the House, speaking of it as a whole. When it was found that Mr. GLADSTONE, two years ago, had fixed upon Mr. PEEL to succeed Sir HENRY BRAND, it is not too much to say that there was something like a feeling of dismay. It was thought that the Premier had been carried away by his known regard for the late Sir ROBERT PEEL, the father of his nominee ; and there were those who pro- phesied that it was impossible for a man of whom so little was known to make a good Speaker of the House of Commons. But it was soon seen that Mr. GLADSTONE had selected the right roan. This indeed vva.S felt when Mr. PEEL returned thanks for lug election. His brief address was marked bl modesty, grace, and dignity—with the sugges' tion of power in reserve. It was not long before the Irish members tried a fall with him, and they were surprised to find that. - although they were grappling, as they thought, with a " prentice hand" they gc)t the worst of the encounter. The no/ Speaker showed that without heat and without haste, he was prompt to de- cide and quick to act ; and, as the Par-

ellites were the chief offenders they came in for the chief punishment. For this they bear him a grudge, and, if the circum- stances had been more favourable, they Would have gone further than the mild fling which they had at him on Tuesday. But they are just now on their good behavi- our; they are hoping to get something, and and if they happen to be denied we shall see .!omething more of the sprig of shillalah " " the sweet by and bye." The life of the Present Parliament may be long, or it may he short; the general impression is that it Will be the latter. In any case it is likely, to have a career which will exceptionally try the qualities of the Speaker. The physical tax is often enough great; but this is as nothing to the mental strain of incessant Watchfulness. Members who are tired of a g winded orator can leave the House, and eat, &rink, and be merry; the Speaker. nui.st remain at his post and look as if he enjoyed it. Indeed, he must follow every Word that is said, for at any moment some- thing may may be blurted out which may call for his interposition and instant decision. In exciting scenes, whoever loses his head, the Speaker must keep his, and guide .the House in a right direction. He is required to revise notices of motion and of questions; and if he makes the slightest mistake at any tune his conduct may be publicly challenged. The post is one of great, of historic dignity; and it is exceedingly difficult to find a man willo is equal to its requirements. The °llse of Commons has, however, been fortunate; it has a Speaker in Mr. ARTHUR PEEL worthy of its best traditions; and the 132, etnbers, therefore, did no more than their iduty on Tuesday in conferring on Mr. PEEL the stamp and seal of thorough and un- I bounded confidence."

•Mr. BRADLAUGH has had a long struggle wtth the House of Commons; he has been beaten back many times, but he has at last Proved victorious. He has .all along been a duly qualified member; but he took the oath °II Wednesday with the sanction of the Speaker, and is now both duly qualified and duly sworn, It seems that Sir MICHAEL HICKS- tEACII, and iwo othet Conservative members,

Put themselves in communication with the Speaker with a view to preventing Mr. BRAD- LAUGH taking the oath. The leader of the Tory Party in the House of Commons urged that it 'would be simply an act of profanation "; but the Speaker in reply said.:

We are assembled in a new Parliament; I know nothing of the resolutions of the late Parliament; they have lapsed, they are void, they are of no effect, in reference to this case. It is the right, the legal statutable obligation, of members when returned to this House to come to this table and take the oath prescribed by statute. I have no authority, I have no right, original or delegated, to interfere between an hon. member and his taking ni the oath. This is a clear and simple statement of issue; but it was not, of course, satisfac- tory to those who have so long over: ridden the law in order to perse- cute a political opponent. Sir MICHAEL Would have argued the point; but the Speaker cut him short by reminding him that he was bot entitled to make a speech, as the House Was not then constituted. 'Following this little passage of arms, in which the Gov- ernment got the worst of it. the swearing in of members commenced, and Mr. BRADL.4.UGH took the oath with the rest. Such an act of profanation," was, if the Tories were to be believed, what they would never tolerate; it would be a shock which would shake the very foundations of the Empire. But they have stood by and seen it done, and not even made a scene about it. How is it that such a Change has come over them? Does the pros- Peet of a struggle on the Bradlaugh question look different when they are in office to what it did when they were in Opposition? Or has the brief enjoyment of "the loaves and fishes" already had that peculiar benumb- ing influence on religious susceptibilities Which so frequently paralyses the efforts of officers of "Church and State ?" Raving gone so far, they ought, if they are Sincere, to go further. They have an Attorney General at their command ; let them set him to work to contest the decision of the Speaker, or the action of Mr. BRADLAIIGH If* they let the matter drop, it will be patent to everybody that they have throughout been _ _ _ _

_ actuated less by love of religion than hatred of the junior member for Northampton. . Our contention has always been that the House of Commons acted illegally in stepping in between Mr. BRADLAUGH and the oath. The Speaker proceeded on pre- vious occasions under the direction of the

Rouse; but in this instance—the House not . being constituted—he has been in a position to act on his own initiative, and he has done that which was warranted by sound law and common-sense. We grant that the oath is discredited; but it has for a long time been discredited. Mr. BRAD- LAUGH sought, in the first instance, to avoid giving offence by taking the oath—though he never refused to take it as is so often erroneously asserted. He asked to be per- 'flitted to affirm; and the Speaker haying a doubt as to his title to affirm brought the question before the House It was decided that he could not affirm—and then the Rouse put itself in the wrong by refusing to let him, as an alternative, take the oath. The House refused also to get itself out of the difficulty by passing an Affirmation Bill ; and if it now stands in a ridiculous posi- tion it is at any rate doing penance for its own sins. The lesson of the: conflict is obvious; the oath is unnecess ;itis in the Way, and should be abolished.

THE Runcorn School Board have recently erected a new school to meet the growing Wants of the community; and there has been Something like a tussle on the question of school fees. The point at issue was a small one on the face of it, and yet it is one which has caused a good deal of heart-bnrning in various places. It was proposed and carried by what we may call the denominational section of the Board that the fees should be 2d in the mixed school and girls' school, 3d for stan- dard two and standard three. and 4d .fo, standard four and upwards. Objection was taken to a fourpenny fee for the higher stan- dards; and, as the CLERK pointed out that the Motion was irregular from the fact that it was Passed at a special meeting which did not Pe(mit of school fees being considered, the Matter came up again at a meeting of the hoard held on Friday and adjourned to Saturday last. The result of the discussion Was that the fourpehny fee was set aside, the Majority of the Board being determined not to handicap children in the higher standards. 'Threepence will, therefore, be the highest fee Charged ; and we cannot but think the Board "kve acted wisely in coming to this decision. 17 may be, as Mr. LEA urged, that the \lies- Ityans, whose fees are higher, will feel the ti,e3sure of competition ; but it ,shorlid be Zt- membered, as the clerk pointed out, that

div.p: ' the outcome of the action of the school visitors has enabled the denominational schools to raise their fees from 33 to 50 per cent. They have had a sort of flood tide of late ; but tides are not always at the flood. It is unfortunate, we cannot but think, that on almost every School Board of importance in the kingdom there are members whose first thought is for the denominational schools with which they happen to be connected. They should remember that they are mem- bers of the Board as representatives of the ratepayers. It is their business to deal justly with all classes, denominational or undenom- inational. In this case, those who opposed the sliding scale of fees have the Educa- tion Department en their side, who may be regarded as impartial, and who have reached the conclusions they hold from long experi- ence extending over a wide area. They know that, other things being equal, the higher the school fee and the poorer the attendance. It is true that as children get older and more useful, parents sometimes grow indifferent to their regular attendance ; but it is alio true that the highest authorities are agreed that the weak point of our educational system is • that the bulk of our scholars spend too little time in the higher standards. To raise the fee for the higher standards is therefore to put up an extra barrier when I've ought rather to offer inducements to parents to allow their children to remain at school until they have passed the highest standard. The Runcorn School Board have taken the right course in making the way easy for the parents and better for the children.

div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."
The vicar of Christ Church, Latchford, prays for Parliament when it is not sitting. Query: What will he do now that it is sitting? —hurl the Athanasian Creed at it?

At St. Helens, a woman named Jane Nolan has been stealing a rug from a police cell She has been before he Wigan magistrates forty-four times. It would seem in this case that the ruling passion is strong in gaol, whatever it may be in death.

The ratepayers of Widnes have decided to bring the Free Libraries Acts into opera- tion; and Mr. BRUNNER, M.P., with char- acteristic generosity in matters educational, has promised £ oo towards the purchase of books. This is a good card—who will follow suit?

The death rate of Cad ishead for the past three months has been ro in the r,OOO only— abGut one half the average of the country, while the birth rate has been 30 in the r,OOO —a trifle under the average. It may be said of Cadishead, as the old woman said of Chorley Cemetery, that it is a healthy place to be buried in.

Skaters cannot be too careful. A large number of lives have been lost this season. A young lady, and a young soldier who went to her assistance, had a narrow escape at Wargrave on Tuesday. They had to be helped out of the water. There is no trusting ice when a thaw has set in, as was the case on Tuesday.

Miles Saul, a ganger in a Widnes chemical works, is not an over scrupulous man. He obtained some clothing from a St. Helens draper, and not only refused to pay, but swore in court that he had got the coat he was wearing elsewhere. Mr. Swift, plain- tiff's solictor, was not to be beaten; he described the maik of the firm on the coat, and insisted that the defendant should take the garment off. Defendant refused, where- upon the judge insisted; the coat was taken off, with the result that the mark was found, and judgment given for the plaintiff for the full amount. Here is a clear case of perjury, but who is to prosecute?

The Corporation of Bolton are up in arms, as the Warrington Board of Guardians were, against being taxed for the erection of a bridge across the rivm Ribble at Penwor- than-1. They have decided, if need be, to oppose the Caunty Justices Bill in Parlia- ment. This is going the right way to work; and they ought to be assisted by other author- ities who feel that an injustice is being done.

The Tories are going to bring in a bill "respecting the attendance of registrars at marriages at Nonconformist chapels." This means, it may be presumed, that they are going to dispense with the services of the registrar. Mr. W. E. Briggs is not now in Parliament, but he will be glad to hear that his friends the enemy are taking up the measure which he made his own. In a racy poem in the Daily News of Tuesday, entitled " A ,Dirge for the Departed," there is the following reference to the late member for Blackburn:—

"Where's Briggs? Who'd suspect 'neath his Cymon- like air A consuming desire to coquet with the muse hid? This is an allusion to the readiness which Mr. Briggs showed in introducing apt poetical quotations.

A London correspondent, describing the scene in the House at the opening of Parlia- ment on Tuesday. says : " Mr. Peter Rylands for a little season's space' was a striking object, bustling about in a marvel- lous smoking cap to initiate new members into the mysteries of the place."
Peter's prepared; he likes a little joke— A Tory Government must end in smoke.

The Tories have now been in office six months, and they themselves admit that things are going from bad td wOrse. Wages have been reduced in some trades, and in others reductions are being proposed. How is it? Is this what the Tories meant by Fair Trade?

The rumour is current in Conssrvative as well as Liberal circles that Lord Carnar- von as Viceroy of Ireland is about to resign, and that the resignation of Sir W. Hart- Dyke. the Chief Secretary, will soon follow. Poor Lord Carnarvon ! He was never tired of demonstrating, before he tried his hand, how the Liberals failed in dealing with Ireland.

THE MERSEY TUNNEL.—Mr. Cadstone will re- turn to ilaward.en to-day (Saturday), and will be the guest of the Duke of Westminister, at Eaton Hall on the Tuesday, to meet the Prince and Princess of Wales. He will accompany the Royal party at the opening of the Mersey Tunnel, and will return to London the following day to be present at the formal opening of Parliament: THE WEST LANCASHIRE RAILWAY.—.A. working agreement has been signed between the directors of the West Lancashire Railway Company and the Manchester, Sheffield and Lincoln, by which the latter take over the former so far as traffic is con- cerned, and incorporate it as a part of their system. The new junction railway, which unites the West Lancashire with the Southport and Cheshire Lines Extension, is likewise included in the arrangements. The new route. to Blackpool will also be speedily taken in hand.
LUCAL NEWS.
STREET MAKING AT WIDNES—.At the Local Board meet-

ing on Tuesday it was decided to serve notices upon owners of property to make West-street, James-street, and Par- sonage-road according to plans and specifications. ACCIDENT AT WIDNES. On Sunday evening John Brown, of Viaduct-street, Widnes, who is employed at the Liver Alkali Co's. works, Ditton-road, met with a serious accident. Brown was engaged at a hoist which was not in good working order, when the machinery started, and he we caught between the cage and the upright. Dr. Booth's assistant was called in, and it was ascertained that besides other injuries, the man's collar bone was broken. He was conveyed to Liverpool infirmary. Ha.vrcut PARISH Cuunca Citota.—On Tuesday evening . _

the members of this choir were invited to a supper, kindly provided by the wardens and sidesmen. A bountifully- supplied table was presided at by the vicar's warden, Mr. John Rutter and Mr. William Stokes, the parish warden. Various tfasts were proposed and responded to, being inter- si.ersed with several songs suitable to the occasion. The most pleasing part of the evening's proceedings was the presentation of an electre cruet stand to Mr. William Chrimes, ace of the choirmen, on the occasien of his mar- riage. It was the gift of his brother choristers.

SERIOIIS ACCIDSitT AT flarirosr.—An accident of a serious character occurred at Halton last night week. Two lurries belonging to Mr. Thomas Rigby, of Frodsham, were pro- ceeding down Halton-brow one behind the other. The second was " spragued," but owing to the slippery state of the road it had no effect on the lorry. The horses com- menced to run, and the driver, a man named Job Wright, of Frodsham, seeing that he must inevitably collide with the lorry in front rushed to the horses' heads and forced the lurry into the side of the road. Unfortunately he was un- able to get out of danger himself, and the wheel passing over his leg tore the calf away from the bone, and broke the limb. OPENING OF THE NEW ORGAN AT Dlrrox.—The new organ recently erected in St. Michael's Church, Hough Green, Ditton, was opened on Thursday night by a special Es vice. The instrument. which is handsome in appearance and beautiful in tone, was built by Mr. C. H. Whitley, of Chester, who erected the Cathedral organ in that city. It is a "two manual organ," has 18 stops, and 3 couplers, and cost £350. There was a large congregation at the auvice, the clergy present being the Revs. Canon Diggle, A. W. Wool, G. Bond, A. P. Hatnilton Wilson,S. A. Spooner, and J. Jones. The sermon was preached by the Rev. J. W. Diggle, rural dean of Childwall, from the:text "0 came let us sing unto the Lord." Mr. R. B. Woodward, organist at the Parish Church, St, iielens, presided at the clan, and played very effectively. MR. el., 1. BRUNNER, M.P., AT LIVERPOOL—On Satur- day, night there was a large gathering of members at the Liverpool Reform Club, the occasion being a banquet to members of the club who have been elected to the new House of Commons. Mr. Brunner, M.P., who was intro- duced by the chairman as the representative of manufac- turers, responded to the toast of the evening, and was re- ceived with loud applause. He remarked that the commit- tee of the club had shown exceedingly good taste in having decided upon that evening's proceedings, and for himself he felt peculiar gratification in being present. Though his name bad been coupled with their new county constituen- cies, as their chairman very well knew, he did not represent Hodge, but he should be proud if he did, because Hodge had done a good work in connection with the election. (App:auae.) Not least among the good works which Hodge had done had been the return to Parliament of Mr. Joseph Arch. (Loud applause.) He hoped it would be his pleasure to give a hearty welcome to Mr. Arch, as a member of the National Liberal CIO, before many days were over. (Applause.) He had very little to say about the new constituencies, but he Was clearly of opinion that the work which the new county constituencies had done had wrought a change in the spirits of the Liberal party when the election was over, and that it was a very grand monument to the skill and sagacity of Mr. Gladstone and his colleagues. (Loud applause.)

PREsENTATIONS AT RUNCORN MERSEY MISSIONS.—The annual teachers' tea meeting in connection with the Run- corn branch of the Mersey Missions was held on Tuesday evening, and there was a good attendance. Mr. W. Shaw, the missionary, preached, and in reviewing the work of the past year, said he was sorry he had lost the services of two of his oldest teachers, who had worked hard for the Mission, and he took that opportunity of thanking them for their valuable assistance. He referred to Miss Garrett, who had left the town, and Miss Owen, who had entered the married state. Mr. G. Howard, on behalf of the teachers, then pre- sented to Miss Eleanor Garrett, who acted for her sister, an album, bearing the following inscription :—" Presented to Miss Garrett, on the occasion of her leaving town, by the Sunday school teachers of the Mersey Miesions to Seamen, as a token of their esteem and well-wishes for her future spiritual and temporal welfare." The recipient appropri- ately aeknowledged the present. Mr. Greaves then presen- ted Mrs W. Pownall with an album bearing this inscription —"Presented to Miss Owen, on the occasion of her mar- riage, by the teachers in connection with the Mersey Mis- sions to Seamen, where she has laboured as teacher, with eafnest wishes for her spiritual and temporal welfare. Run- corn, Demmer 29th, 1885." Mr. W. Pownall, junior, de- livered a neat speech in responding on behalf of his wife. He fully 'appreciated and reciprocated the kindness which prompted that token of their regard to Mrs Pownall, and he felt sure she would never forget their kindness and would still endeavour to aid Mr. Shaw and the workers and friends of the Mission in the good work in which they were en- gaged- OPENING OF THE NEW BOARD SCHOOLS AT RUNCORN.— Without any formal ceremony Greenway-road Board schools were opened on Monday morning, when 104 children pre- sented themselves in the infant department, and 80 in the girls' school. The schools remedy a great deficiency of school accommodation in the town. For several years the schools of the town have been full to overflowing, and the School Board have been unable in consequence to carry out to their legitimate exteut the provisions of ths Education Act. Having now places for 452 scholars in the new schools, toe Board will be able to act with vigour: in com- pelling each child to attend and receive a sound elementary education, whilst the boat children will doubtless come in for a greater share of attention than they have hitherto done. Tue new building is admirably situated in the centre of a populous district, and is easy of access. Tne design of the exterior is very pleasing. The accommodation con- sists of two large rooms, the rower one for boys aid girls (mixed) and the upper one for girls. In the 'former there are desks for 130 children, and four class rooms, each capable of accommodating 32 scholars. In the upper storey there is room for 90 girls with three class rooms, providing 104 places. Messrs. F. and G. Holme, of Liverpool. were the architects for the building, which was erected by contract by Messrs. Brown and son, of Salford, for £3,112. The site ' purchased from the Runcorn Property and Invet2tment Co. cost an •additionel £l,OOO. Well ventilated, warmed, and lighted, and possessing every convenience, the schools are a great acquisition to the educational facilities of the neigh- bourhood. A fee of 2d per week per child in the infants' department, and 3d per week in the girls' department is charged. Rieteconer Bunter. BOARD.—The monthly meeting was held on Wednesday afternoon. Present, Messrs. William Littler (ctiairman), James Handley, J.P., H. Coleburn. G. MO3S, W. Whittaker, W. Mellor, E. Imison, and W. F. Salkeld (secretarY).—The Secretary reported that the num- ber of interments for the bine months ending December 25th was 244, being a decrease of 17 on the corresponding period last year. Ttae amount received for fees during the seine period was £246 Sc 6(1, being a decrease of £4B 9s 7d. Toe minutes of the Finance Committee, passed on the mo- tion of Mr. Moss, seconded by Mr. Handley, showed that £l2O bad been invested in the purchase of consols on sink- ing fund account. There had been £lOO received from the overseers on general account, and £27 fees. The com- mittee recommended that the mortgage with the Lily of the Valley Lodge of Oddfellows be repaid and re-borrowed at 31 per cent., being a quarter per cent, lower then the interest at present paid. The balance in bank was £ll2 103.—Mr Coleburn drew attention to the fact that at the recent volunteer funeral Yord, the ledge keeper, excluded a large number of people from the Cemetery', by closing the gates. Mr. Coleburn was of the number. The closing of the gate was insulting to the people, and a most unseemly scene took place which ought to have been impossible. The greatest decorum prevailed, and there was not the slightest need for I the gates being closed.---The Secretary alluded to the diffi- cult nature of Ford's duties, but said he was surprised at his behaving so disrespectfully.—After some discussion I Ford was called into the room. He stated that he had per- mission to close the gates whenever he thought necessary. On the present occasion he locked the gates while he went 1 to the chapel with the mourners, and returned in about ten Iminutes and opened ttie gates. 'There was a crowd of about i a thousand people in the Cemetery, arid he was afraid the funeral would he interfered with.—Mr. Coleburn said if Ford would take 700 from the thousand he would be nearer the mark. He stated that Ford did not come down to open ' the gate for the people, but to let the hearse out.—Ford nientioned the great damage done to the graves and head- ; stones by large crowds.—Mr. Moss said while they might respect the rights of the ratepayers they knew a cemetery I was not the place for a large crowd, because of the danger to the graves, for. which the Board was responsible. He thought they would make a mistake if they took out of the hands of the lodge keeper the power of closing the gates when be felt it to be necessary.—lt was decided, on the mo- tion of Mr. Mellor, seconded by Mr. 'raison, that the sec- retary be requested to attend the Cemetery on the occasion ! of large public funerals to superintend tire admission of the public—Time Secretary expressed his willingness to do so. •

div.p: THE.EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 16, 1886.

' LECTURE AT WIDNES—On Thursday evening the Rev. C. Ramat delivered a lecture on "The soul of a watch " to the members of the C.E.T.o. Toe Vicar presided, and there was a good attendance. BRUNSWICK !VICTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY, RUNCORN. —The 23rd annual meeting was held en Wednesday night, when Mr. T. Simister was re-elected president, Mr. J. D. Jones vice-president, and Mr. h. U. Kitto secretary. MALIN'S TEMPERANCE HALL, WIDNES.—In this building each evening dating the past we,.k a temperance mission has been conducted by Mr. Nichols, tbe temperance advo- cate. There have been good audiences, and a number of people have taken the pledge. FREE DINNERS FOR BOAT CHILDREN AT RuNconN.—On Monday and Wednesday Mr. W. Shaw, of the Mersey Missions, regaled about 100 distressed boat children ..vith a good meal of soup and bread. Many of the children were only partially clothed, and Mr. W. Shaw would be glad to receive can off clothing. LinErtAusu AT RUNCORN.—On Taesdav evening next, in Bethesda Lecture Hall, the Rev. W. Vause, will read a paper on our national expenditure. The meeting will be under the auspices of the Liberal Association, and a large audience of all shades of politics are invited. Particulars will be found in our advertising colamm. RUNCORN (IST) STARR-BOWKETT BUILDING SOCIETY.—

, The 26th appropriation took place in Mr. Handley's office, Runcorn, on Monday evening. Mr. W. Armstrong presided. The ballot resulted in Mrs. Ellen Clays, kf Fro4Bh3m, being entitled to £2OO, free of interest, for 12i years, Toe next appropriation will take place on the Bth February. LACEY-STREET BAND OF Hois, WIDNES.—Under the auspices of this organisation a singing competition and musical evening took place on Monday. Mr. Thomas Sadler presided, and an excellent programino was gone through. L. and A. Smith succeeded in winning the first priz., John Poulson the second, and Miss Kilsall the third.

ACCIDENT AT WIDNES.—Oa the arrival of the train da,i at Widnes Central Station from Warrington at 12-14 on Tuesday it was discovered that the connecting rods of the engine were badly bent, and that it would be unsafe to proceed further. After a delay of 40 minutes another en- gine was obtained and the train departed Much incon- venience was caused to the passengers.

ExcHAskas or PULPITS 4.. T RUNCJEM.—The good feeling existing amongst the various branches of Nonconformity was shown on Sunday, when the following exchange of pul- pits took place :—St. Paul's Wesleyan, Rev. W. Vause ; St. John's Presbyterian, Rev. E. Wood ; Bethesda Congre- gational, Rev. J. Cansland ; Hattori-road Wesleyan, Rey. J. D. Thomas; Greenway-road Primitive Methodist, Rev. T. Hackett ; United Methodist ',tee C!.u!ct;. Rev. E Williams.

A DANGEROUS DOG AT WESTUN.—Phte'M Barrow, of the Royal Oak Inn, Wertqn, appeared before tne Runcorn magi- strateB to answer a ch4tv,e of .tisobeying an order of the court •to keep a dangerous dog under control—lt was alleged by P.C. Breece that on the 280 December the dog was in the roadway and jumped at a girl and bit her.—The defendant stated that the dog in respect to which the order was made Ind been destroyed, and she called two witnesses, whose statements proved to the contrary.—The defendant was fined lOs and costs, 12s (id.,

CONCERT AT FROMHAM.—A concert in aid of the funds of the Frodsham Parish Church Bible Class Brass Band was given in the Town Hall, Frodsbam, on Monday evenipg, and was well patronised. The following ladies and gentle— men had kindly volunteered their services, viz.:—Mies Leila Bairstow, Miss Johnston. Miss Amy Benbow, Mr. Jos. Morrison, Mr. O'Connor. and Professor Lamb. Each of the soloists received frequent encores, and the audience fully recognized the marked ability disp'ayed by Miss Benbow in her pianoforte solos and concerted pieces. Mr. Lamb was applawkd fQr his skilful manipuletion of the musicAl belle aid ease'. • ODDFELLOWS' BALL AT RtiNcOati.—The tenth annual tea party and ball of the Loyal Wright's Pride Past Grand* Lodge took place in Runcorn Public Hall on Thursday night. The room had been decorated for the occasion. Mr. Arthur Riley, of Bridge-street. provided tea in good style, and about 150 persons partook of the repast. Suosequently the hall was cleared for dancing, which was kept on until a late hour on Friday morning to the strains of Bro. T. Wood's quadrille bind. Mr. Thomas Jones, of South Bank Hotel,supplied the refreshments. The arrangemews of tilt bell were under the superintendence of a committee, of which Mr. C. Cooke was secretary, and the affair passed if pleasantly. - - -

GREENWAY-ROAD NEW CHURCH, RUNCORN.—The third of a series of miscellaneous entertainments in aid of the building fond of this church took place in the National Infat.te School on Thursday evening. Mr. W. Mellor oc- cupied the chair. An interesting programme was gone through, and judging by the aoplause whick followed the various pieces, was highly appreciated. The Daresbury ringers fully sustained the high reputation they have ac- quired, and the first of their efforts was redemanded. In addition to the admirable concerted pieces •given by the Glee Class, songs were given by Miss Robinson, Messrs. F. Joule, Warhans, Gates, and R. C. Rosenberg. Valuible assistance was also rendered by Misses Sirnkin and Jones ; Messrs. Kay, Timmins. Nyman, Moss, Littler, and Rosen- berg, senr. THE UNEMPLOYED IN WIDNES.—A philanthropic scheme is.on foot for relieving Widnes of some of its surplus and unemployed population. A Widnes gentleman, who has business relations in many parts of the world, h4a the matter in hand. He is making arrangements for sending ta America at his own expense a number of the poorer unem- ployed of the town, and desires principally to give a new start in life to those whom slackness of trade is fast convert- ing into "corner men." It is his intention to send at an early date 100 in a batch, for the greater portion of whom he has obtained work. On Wednesday morning he received a letter from one of the largest iron producing firms in America, in which they state :—" Regarding men, we are not badly in want of them here at present, although pros- pects are more will be wanted as the year opens. We are having quite a revival is business, and prospects for the coming year are quite bright. Hope they will prove up."

THE WIDNES ORANGEMEN AND TRIER ANNUAL BALL. —At the St. Helens County Court, on Wednesday, before Mr. T. P. E. Thompson, judge, William Jones, of Widnes. on behalf of the committee of the Beaconsfield Loyal Orange Lodge. sued Alfred Parkes, proprietor of the Cen- tral Hotel, Widnes, for £2 100, and defendant put in a coun- ter claim for £2 Os 6i.-111r. Knowles appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Husband defended.—lt appeared from the evidence that Parkes was asked by Jones to supply refresh- ' meats at a ball to be held in November, and was told that he would have to ply £2 10s for the privilege. It was said that he agreed to this, but the ball proved A financial fail- ure, and he refused to pay. He was told that he would be sued for the account, upon which he said he would charge £2 lOs for tea supplied to the master of the ceremonies and expenses for fixtures and gas, which he expected would be found by the committee.—Defendant said it had been represented to him that there were 300 Orangemen in Widnes, and that at least 200 might be expected at the ball. He calculated from that number that it would be a success, but be was disappointed. He did not make definite agreement: he merely said if it was a success be would pay the usual £2 10s.—His Honour gave judgement for defendant on the claim, and for plaintiff on the counter-claim. I SINGULAR SCENE AT Sr. HELENS COUNTY COURT.— At the Ste Helens County Court, on Wednesday, before Mr. W. Tyrer, registrar, an action Will heard, in which Mr. James Highet, draphr, North-eared, St. Helens, sued Miles Saul, ganger in a Widnes chemical works, to recover £7 10e 9cl, balance of account owing for goods sold and delivered. Mr. J. 0. Swift appeared for plaintiff, and Mr. Knowles de- fended. Plaintiff's case was that on various occasions he supplied defendant with useful drapery goods, including a suit of clothes for defendant himself, made to order. De- fendant appeared in court attired in a black worsted over- cdat, which he swore he had purchased from Mr. Coop, Widnes, six months since. He also denied that he had ever purchased clothing from plaintiff. Mr. Swift remarked that on clothing supplied from Mr. Coop there was usually the maker's name to be found at the back of the collar; and as plaintiff marked his" Value Al," and felt certain that defendant was wearing the goods he supplied, he asked de- fendant to take off his coat. Defendant at first refused, but he was ordered to do so by the registrar, who said that judgment must go against him if he refused. Eventually he teok off his coat, and banded it to Mr. Tyrer, who found plaintiff's mark upon it. Mr. Know lea, defendant's solici- tor, hereupon threw up his brief. The Registrar gave judgmen for the full amount, and remarked that def- endant was deserving of prosecution for perjury. • LARGE REDUCTION OF ASSESSMENT AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Sessions on Thursday, before Mr. J. Brock and Mr. T. S. Timmis, the London and North-Western Railway Company, represented Mr Mr. Preston, jamor, solicitor, appeared to answer a summons issued by the Local Board to.show cause why they should not pay a district rate of £46 18s for the Widnes Dock, and of £ll 15s 6,1 for the St. Helens Canal. Mr. Allen, clerk to the Local Board, said the general district rate referred to was laid on July 22, 1884, and was based upon the poor rate laid on the 2nd of April in the same year. At that time the assessment of the Widnes Dock was £1.669, and of the canal £471, and ' the rate upon these two properties amounted to £5B 13s 6d. Subsequently the railway company appealed to the Assess- ment Committee of the Guardians for a reduction in the valuation, are' Mr. Allen was perfectly willing to take pay- ment based upon the reduced valuation. The amount claimed would therefore be reduced to £l7 3s 61.—Mr. Charles Whitfield, the collector, gave evidence in support of this statement. He deposed that the rateable value of the dock was brought down from £1,669 to £450, and the canal from £471 to £3o.—Mr. Timmis expressed astonish- ment at these reductions.—ln cross-examination Mr Whitfield said the rates upon the company's other property in the township were not reduced in accerdance with the reduction made in the assessments, because the Local Board had re- ceived a cheque for £B-13 10s in settlement of all the rates but these claimed for. Mr. Allen read a letttr receive! from the company supporting this contention.—Mr. Preston ar- gued that this cheque was only paid on account" of all the rates, and that not merely the rates upon the dock and canal should be reduced, but upon all the company's pro- perty of which the assessments had been reduced. He quoted a case in support of this contention, which after :ouch deliberation the magistrates upheld.—Mr. Brock said they were of opinion that when the assessments were altered it was the duty of the Local Board to have rendered new account, and although the money had been paid by the company. gives them credit for the amount overpaid. —.MG Edwards, the manager to the rats and taxes depart- ment of the company, said the total amount of the rates lor I 1884 upou the reduced assessments would be £579 3s, and there would be a balance due to the company.

Permission to sell at the George Inn, Pool-lane, Runcorn, was granted to Thomas Robinson on Monday. THE FLAT ROBBERIES AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Court, on Monday, John Carroll and John Heyes were brought up on remand charged with stealing various articles of clothing from the flat Washington. Lturence Keeting was charged with entering the fiat Clarence. On the application of In- spector Wood the prisoners were again remanded. TXEFT FROM A RUNCORN BEERHOUSE —On Thursday, at Runcorn Police Court, William Gregory, of Over, was charged with sleeting a pair of boots, worth 13s 6d, from the Cornwall and Devonshire Arms beerkouse, Church-st. The boots were missed from the house on Saturday morning after a visit by tbe prisoner, and they were subsequently pawned at Mr. Craddock's, Church-street. Police Clerk Wallace received tbe prisoner into custody front the Ove• , Police. Remanded. A HUNGRY THIEF AT RUNCORN.—At Runcorn Poiice Cour, on Thursday, before Mr. James Handley and Mr. U, L. Davies, Thomas Ankers,.eleven years of age, was charged with stealing a box containing two florins from the house of John A twood, Granville-street. Early on Tuesday morning Mrs. Attwood beard a noise downstairs, and sub- sequently she missed the box and the money. As the pri- soner had slept in a hayloft near the house on the previous night susp;cion fell upon him, and when charged he took Mrs. Attwoosi to a spot in the yard where she found 3s 6d
wrapped in paper. The boy &Aid he was hungry, and had spent sixpence at the Cocoa Rooms for breakfast. He wds apprehended by P.C. Wallace, and was now ordered to re-
ceive six strokes with the birch rod.

RECKIVERS AND STE,ALERS AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, Joseph Murray, a youth, was charged with having, about the 29th or 30th ult, stolen a piece of tarpaulin, value 10s, from the flat Alice whilst lying in Widnes Dock. 'rrtornas Perry, captain of the flat, ident.fied the article. John Barton, fish dealer, 60, Walessley-street, deposed buying the tarpaulin from the prisoner for 2,. The prisoner stated a Batman had given it to hint. When ap- prehended by P. C. Holbrook, the prisoner said he had found it on a wali.—He was sentenced to 14 days' hard labour. Barton was recalled into the box, and Mi. Cro,sage said the Bench were sfron!e!y of opinion that he was as kid as the thief himself. He ithist have known that the boy had not come honestly by the tarpaulin. It was peredle like Barton who made thieves by buying these stolen goods. STREET DANGEES AT WtDNES.—On Thursday, at Widnes Petty Sessions, Richard Tunkies, a youth with a wooden leg, who had served se-veral terms of imprisonment, was charged with throwing stones. P.C. Thomplen said the defendant ou the 4:h January was throwing cones and other missiles frem a catapult in Church-street, There were many people about at the time. A fine of 7s 6d and costs, 7s 6d, or 10 days' imprisoninent, was imposed,—Francis Kelly, a boy, was eiarged with a like offence. On the n,glit of the 3rd inst. the Salvation Army WAS passing along Mid- wood-street, wen I' C 1 089 saw the defendant throw two stones and a turnip wr,ongst Me procession. The defendant was fined 51 and c ,sts 7.4 61.—Henry Bulton and Aleert Ramsey, boys, were eAci fined 5s and costs. 7s 6d, for ob- structing dri.enYl au*ett by pi iy; ng a game called shinty." WtrE Thee:RIMS; Wtrnaree—.At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, Thema. </Note was charged with deserting his wife aged 22. arid a etlilA two yeara of age. On the 29th December tire tno-her applied to Mr. Scannell to be sent to the werkhouae, alleging that at Christmas her hus- band beat and kicked her, ana left her. The doctor said she was in a had star-, and as she Wes near her confinement he found her a sniper and a bed, and had her canveyed ti the Union next day. The prisoner said nis wife would not have been tome: out but for her drinking babita and "carrying on."—lnspector Wood said the pris-,ner had been 12 titr,es before the Bench, the last occasion for ler- ceny.—The prisoner WWI ordered to pay 21s 9d, the Oust QI tDilitt!tUttind in tire House, or go to geel br 14 days.

ALLEA3ED 'AftrOCILING AT RUNCWW.—B,fore Mr. Jam.. Handley, at Ruozorn l'o:ice Court, on Tuesday. P,oreo Andreses Fischer, Master of the 5.8. Mata Katrina, was charged that he on 9:h January, at Runcorn, concealed a of wham, with intent to defraud H.M. the Queen of the duties duo thereon. From the evidence gi-en by Mr. P. Quinn and Mr. T. Garner., Custom (louse officials, it ap- peared that the vessel aT'rived ot Runcorn on Saturday last. The captain was asked what tobacco or other goods ' liable to duty he had on board. He produced a quantity

of tobacco under seed which bad been allowed to him at Liverpool. The officers then wade a search, and concealed underneath a cupboard in the cabin they discovered a lb of foreign manufactured tobacco. Tr defensiant admitted
VW he kt-td denied the possession of this tobacco, but alleked that he had forgotten it.—He was ordered to pay the vslue of the tobacco and duty 6s 10d and the coati 7s

A RUNCORN MAGISMATE AND HIS WATER RATE.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions on ME,nday, Mr. W. D. Jolliffe, sJlicitor, appea,el on b-hal of the Runcttto Wat,etworks Corn wtny. HM apAied for the Issas of a digusa vwraut against Mr. Willia'n Blushes, J.P., of ir eston House, Weston, for the rict.v.ry of vriter rates a i?Tou.sting.to .£4B

is 2d.—The defendant did not appear.—Mr. Wm:Wright, the collector, stated the rates had been accumulating since 1882. He had Linataird the money frequently.—Mr. Davies thought the company should have taken steps earlier to recover the money, or have cut the water off.— Mr. Jolliffe replied that proceedings had been instituted, but withdrawn on Mr. Bankes undertaking to pay the money. The amount was reduced to £26 2s lid through the deduction of last quarter's rate, and an allowance upon the as.essinent.—rhe Bench grant,d a di.tress warrant for this amount, Mr. Joni& promising that execution should ue stayed for a fortnight. A. LESSON TO FOEEICINERS AT WIDNES. Before Mr. F. H. GossAge and Mr. J. Brock, at Widnes Petty Session, on Thursday, John Tharascovitch and John Pletchkitis, Poles, who Are employed as labourers, were charged on remand with assaulting Franz Vougart —Neither the prosecutor nor the prisoners could speak the English language, and Simon Butinski, a youth, acted as interpreter. It appeared that on Saturday night the prosecutor went into* house in Nelson-weer, in order to obtain lodgings. Whilst he was there the prisoners entered, and Hetchkitis fetched a quart of beer. They Asked the prosecutor to have a drink, but he declined " because it was tao cold," and the prisoners threatened that if he did not they would " take it out of hitn." Tharascovitch struck him on the face with his fist, and then together the prisoners dragged the man to the doorstep, where they kicked him, and battered his head with a drinking glass and a tin. He was seriously injured. It was alleged that the prisoners had attacked* hint in revenge, but ,they stated that the prosecutor would have beaten them if they had not beaten hina.—The prisoners were sentenced to a fortnfght's hard labour, and were ordered to each pay 9s costs to the prosecutor, and 2s 6d each to the interpreter.

THE CHESHIR,E LINES.—" The Liverpool Journal of Commerce" states that intimation has been given. to the employes of the permanent way and engi- neering department of the Cheshire Lines that a reduction equal to 7- per cent will be effected on all those receiving 20s. per week and over. This has been tradel rendered necessary by the depression in THE EDITORSHIP OF "THE DAILY NEWS."— " Truth" says :—" Mr. Lucy, who has just been ap- pointed editor of the Daiiy News, is a man not only of great literary acquiiements, but possesses that sort of energy and man-of-the-worldism which is requisite for an editor of a large London news- paper. Mr. Hill, the late editor, is a man of singu- lar power as a writer, but he lacks, in the opinion of the proprietary, that man-of-the-worldism which is so difficult to define, and the absence of *hich in no way detracts from the high estimation which his personal character and abilities inspire in all who know him." We may add that Mr. Lucy is the writer of the London •letter which appears in this Journal.

- HALTON AND THE SHIP CANAL. —The annual tea party of Halton Parish Church was held in the Girls' Schoolroom on Friday night last week. There was only a moderate attendance. In his address to the parishioners, the Rev. J. Lockwood, vicar, said he was sorry that their parish was not more thickly populated than it was a year ago. They had had no fewer than 31 deaths during the past year. Many of the largest houses in the parish remained unoc- cupied, which accounted for so many pews in the church being unoccupied. They, however, lived by hope, and trusted in God's mercy. If the Ship Canal was carried out., of which they heard so much, it would run through their parish, and would find work for any hands now idle. He trusted that the result would be the full occupation of their houses, and that they would have a very happy and. pros- perous parish. A MAN BLOWN INTO THE CANAL.—Yesterday, an inquest was held at the. Red Lion Inn, Moore, by Mr. J. T.. Ridgway, coroner, respecting the death of a man named Jellies Wilkinson, who was on the previous day blown into the Bridgewater Canal by a gust of wind and drowned. Deceased was 2:2 years of age, and a boatman. The principal evidence was given by his brother, John Wilkinson, of 53, Trafalgar-street, Bedford Leigh, also a boat- man, who said that on Thursday morning he and deceased were walking on the bank of the Bridge- water Canal near Acton Grange. When just past the bridge there a great gust of wind caught his brother, and blew him into the canal. Witness had swingletree with him, which he threw into the water, but deceased could not reach it. Deceased had a can used for holding corn strapped to his back. The can filled with 'water, sank deceased to the bottom, and he was drowned. The father of the deceased was in a boat ahead of the two brothers. A verdict to the effect that the deceased was blown into the canal and drowned was returned.
