CHURCH LiviNGs.--In consequence of the absence of Mr. Leatham, who is at present Qn the continent, Mr. Peter lands will take charge of the Bill which the lion, member for Huddersfield intro- duced last session for abolishing the purchase of chnrch livings. • DEATH OF Mn. THOMAS ISENNETT.—WO regret to announce that Mr. Thomas Bennett died at his Iresidence at Keckwick, near Warrington, og Wed- nesday morning. The deceased gentleman, who had been suffering from a complication of diseases for about two months, had been attended by Dr. Star- key Smith. He was in his 70th year, and (luring his lifetime filled many public offices, and for about 40 years was connected with the Court Leet,:at Hal- ton. Mr. Bennett was a Conservative in politics, and a member of the Wesleyan body. His death will be regretted by a large circle of relatives and , friends.

THE WATETiBURY WATCH. Our readers will have seen a new watch advertised in our columns, at the price of half a guinea ; and no doubt some of them will have smiled at the idea of spending so much in what they will have taken to be either a toy or a fraud. But the Waterbury Watch is neither. It is an average sized handsome looking watch ; and keeps time perfectly as we can testify from observation extending over several weeks. The secret of its cheapness is its simplicity of construc- tion, combined will the extraordinary turn-out as to number. As many as 600 watches are made I every day by the Waterbury Watch Company—that is one complete watch every minute that the men are at work. The Waterbury has fewer parts than any other watch known, and is the invention of Mr. D. A. Buck, an American who showed the smallest engine in the world at the Centennial Ex- , hibition. It is keyless, being wound up by the ' stem, a proceeding, which takes about two minutes, if the watch is wound up once a day. This is be- cause of the extraordinary length of the spring, but the long spring gives strength and ensures cheap- ness and accuracy. All the parts of the watch are interchangeable, and repairs can be effected at a small oost. The case is of nickel-silver. The Waterbury is what a watch should be—smart-looking, durable, and an accurate time-keeper. MARRIAGE OF MISS ANNIE COOK.—On Thursday a fashionable marriage was sokmnised at the Pen- keth Wesleyan Chapel, the contracting parties being the Rev. Frederick Parsons, Wesleyan minis- ter, of Kingston, Dorsetshire, and Miss Annie Cook, only daughter of Mr. R. Cook, East Bank, Penketh. The Revs. J. McTurk and Rev. Mr. Brooks, Stock- port, performed the ceremony. The bridesmaids were Miss Ingle, of Leeds, and Miss Cook, of St. Helens. Messrs. Alleyne Brown and Fred Brown, of , Southport, officiated as groomsmen. After the cere- mony the newly-wedded pair and numerous guests assembled at the house of the bride's father were entertained by Mr. Cook. The chapel was crowded by the villagers, and hearty good wishes were given to the 'worthy couple, Miss Cook being highly esteemed for her zealous labours as a teacher in the Sunday school. The teachers and scholars of the Penketh Wesleyan Elementary School made a very handsome present to Miss Cook on Wednesday after- noon, consisting of silver toast rack and marmalade dish. The presentation was made by Mr. Watson, the head master. Other costly presents were also received. The happy pair left for London duringl the day.. In honour of the occasion the scholars of the day and .Sunday school, as well as the teachers, were entertained to tea in the school-room by the kindness of Mr. Cook, and at 6-30 an excellent enter- tainment was given by the scholars, under the direction of Mr. Watson. DARRSBITRY IIIGHWAY BOARD.—A meeting of this Board was held in the Court Room, Daresbury, on Thursday afternoon. There were present Mr. E. Greenall, chairman, and a large number of members. —Finance : The Finance Committee recom- mended the payment of accounts amount- ing to .£659 14s 7d.—Mr. Bennet's Dcath: The Chairman. said that since his arrival there that ' day he had heard of the death of one of their 'colleagues, Mr. Thomas Bennet. Mr. Bennet, with the exception of one year, had been a member of that Hoard since it was instituted, and he (the chair- man) thought they could not do less than request the Clerk to write to Mr. Bennet's family condoling with them on the loss. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. Cliffe (vice-chairman) seconded the proposal, which was unanimously agreed to.—The Repair of Roads: The Chairman moved a resolution that a committee be appointed to inquire as to the advisability of the Board either buying or hiring a steam roller for the repair of roads.—Mr. Burgess seconded this propo- sal, which was, agreed to after a qiort discussion.— ' Alleged Boycotting : A letter was read from Mr.. Cox complaining of the condition of the road near Dut- ton Workhouse. It was his opinion that that road had been" boycotted by the surveyor." (Laughter.) —The Surveyor said that on receiving that com- plaint he inspected the road in question and found that it did not require repairs.—The Chairman: Are we to gather then that Mr. Cox's letter should not have been written ?—The Surveyor: Writing the letter did no harm. (Laughter.)—The matter then dropped. The Footpaths A.letter was read from the county authorities stating that the cost of the maintenance of the footpaths in the Board's district should not in the future be charged to the main- road account.—The Clerk Said he was not sure whether the Board could be called upon to pay for the footpath which had been taken over along with the highways, and it was decided that he should report on this point. This was all the business of public interest.

WARRINGTON PARISH CHURCH OLD CHORISTER'S ASSOCIATION.—The first annual meeting of this as- sociation, held at the Norton Arms Hotel, Warring- ton, on Wednesday week, proved an unqualified success. Upwards af 60 gentlemen sat down to dinner, and amongst those present were old choristers from Liverpool, Manchester, Burnley, Rochdale, Ormskirk, Stockport, Runcorn, &c., 1 eluding members of the legal, medical, scholastic, and musical professions. The chair was occupied by Mr. Chris. E. Rowley, late organist and choir- master of the Warrington Parish Church and first president of the association, and the vice-chair by Mr.A.J.Caufield. After dinner, the formal business of appointing the president, rice-presidents, and other officers for the ensuing year was proceeded with. Mr. Robert R. Grey, head master of the Rochdale Grammar School, and formerly choirmaster of the Warrington Parish Church and master of the schools, was unanimously elected president, and Messrs. C. E. Rowley (Manchester), Councillor J. E. Wright, Warrington; Forster Cunliffe, Manchester; John Scotson, Stretford; and Daniel C. Brown, Liverpool (organist of the Warrington Parish Chureh 43 years ago), vice-presidents. The retiring secretaries, Messrs, J. IL Clarke cud W. IL Harrison, and the treasurer. Mr. Bashford, were re-elected.— Amongst the usual loyal and other toasts. that of "The Church " was ably responded to by Mr. Coun- cillor R. W. Francomb, churchwarden of the Parish Church.—ln response to the toast of the president's health, Mr. Rowley profaced his remarks by re- questing the gentlemen present to drink in silence the memory of his immediate predecessor, the late Mr. Thomas Eaude, who had been organist for a period extending over 26 years. Mr. Rowley paid a feeling tribute to Mr. Eaude as a gentleman whose merit and simplicity of character had endeared him in the hearts of all who knew him, and concluded his remarks by thanking those present for the hearty way in which his own health had been drunk, and singing with much fervour, in which all joined, "Auld Lang Syne." The remainder of the evening was spent in a most agreeable manner.

The monthly meeting Wa`l 11,!;1 on Tnesday. Present: Mr. F. H. Onssage (chatrnaan), Dr. O'KeefTe ; Messrs. CArev, Handley, Wri4ht, Heyes, Taylor, H. Gaskell, junr, ,S. Sadler, Houghton, J. T. Ai!en (clerk), Hi:zginson (surveyor), 1. Carr (:ras eruziner.r).
THE FREE LIBRARY AND THE TOWN BALL QUESTION.-
GENEROUS GIFT.

The Chairman announced that at the meeting of rate- timvers held on Decemb-r 29th, the Free Libraries Acts were passed by a very large majority, and he congratulated Wid- nes on' the adoption of this measure. Speaking individ- ally, he thought the meeting was fairly a reoreFeut,tive one. .At the same meeting there was brought forward the subject of the completion of the Town gall, and as far as he could judge the meeting was not favourable to the ore- ject. It had been stated that the motion to erect the rii:w town hall was lost by a small majority, but he considered it a ' very substaniial majoiity —dr. Wright : The papers said there were 18 votes :igainst 15 votes.—The Chairman : That is not correct.—Mr. Wright: A gentlinan at:tne meettoz I said there were 18 against 15.—The Chairman replied tliat. Ihe took no part in the discussion at that meeting on eitLer subject, and he could assure them that what he had Said was

r his recollection of what took place. He did not pretend to be infallible.—Mr. Carey : The numbers were counted, were not they, Mr. Chairman ?—The Chairman : I believe they were, but there is no record here.—Mr. Carey: I think there were 16 for and 27 against.—Dr. O'Keeffe said the reportere printed the numbers as announced.—Mr. Carey : But both the numbers the newspapers announced were wrong.—The Chairman painted out that the decision of the meeting on the town hall question was not binding. Mt whole matter still rested with the Local Board.—On the motion of the. Chairman, seconded by Dr. O'Keeffe, the reioiution passed at the meeting with reference to the Free Library was ordered to be placed on the niinutes of the. Board.—The Chairman said Mr. Allen had infor.ned him that he met Mr. J. T. Brunuer, M.P. for the Northwich Division, a few days ago, and Mr. Brurmer expressed his pleasure that Widnes had adopted the Libraries Acts. At the same time he said he was willing to contrioute £lOO to wards baying books for the library. (Hear, hear, and ap- plause.)—Mr. Carey moved "That the generous offer of £lOO of Mr. J. T. Brunner, M.P., 'towards the purchase of books for the Free Library be accepted, and that the cerdial thanks of this Board ora behalf of the ratepayers of Widnes be offered to him." (Hear, hear.) Mr. Carey observed that he was very glad indeed to hear of Mr. Bruaner's kind and generous gift. Mr. Brunner had always been interested in educational movements' in the neighbourhoods with which he had been connected, and it was only like himself to make that offer.—Mr. Handley seconded the offer wi:h great pleasure. He was present when Mr. Brunner made the offer, and it was quite spontaraeous on his port.—The motion was carried utienimously.—At a later period in the proceedings a letter was read from Messrs. F. and G. liolme, architects, Liverpool, and the designers of the- town hall and public offices. Accompanying the communication was a sketch plan of a building for the free library in coanecrion with the town hall, and which could be erected separately. The letter also stated that the extra cost of adding the town hall to the public offices in course of constructioa would be £s2s.—Mr. Carey explained the sketch. The era:- side walls of the library would be the permanent walls of the town hall, so that that building if belt would not have to be taken down. The only thing that would have to be removed would be a temporary roof, which could tie accomplished without much expense. The room would he 42 by 37 feet, and would provide amply for the library and reading-room. There would also be a room for the librarian. The estimated cost NM £7OO —The Clerk ieformed the Board that it was their duty to find a build- beg for the library.—Mr. Geskell said they •,sould I either have to build a place or rent a place. Mr. Carey propos d that the Board adopt the suggestion of the architect.—Mr. Taylor seconded.--Mr. "right was glad the ratepayers had adopted the Free Libraries Acts, but he thought they ought to leave gone a step further, ard decided where they would have a library. He considered that to rent a place would be expensive, and contended that the public buildings ought.to be erfc'eti in their entirety. Ha moved a resolntrom that the plans of the town hall, which contained provision for the library, be carried out at once,—Dr. O'Keeffe seconded the motion. .t contractor, who was as well able to judge as the ardbitict, awl perhaps better, had told him that the cost of adding tbe town hall to the public offices if the latter were erected first would be £1,500, and the additional pulline down of the Free Library as now suggested would .11.4 perh,•ps another £2OO, bringing the extra coat to close upon £2,030. Me argued that if this amount were capitalised it would almost nay the interest upon the £9,00.3 required for the town hall. He contended that to erect the puelic buildings in the peacemeal fashion suggested was not creditable to the Board nor the town.—Mr. Taylor and Mr. Geekell stated that if this question were to be dealt with notize ought to have been given to the members. There were fire absent. —Dr. O'Keeffe contended that this motion wee qui•e in order, and he was supported by the Clerk, wh.) produced the minutes of the last meetinr.—After a desultory con- vessetion, the motions then before the Board were with- drawn, and Dr. O'Keeffe proposed that the whole scheme for the town ball and public offices be carried out at once Mr. Wright seconded.—Mr. Gaskell moved, and Mr. Taylor seconded, a direct negative. Mr. Gaskell thought this an unfortunate time to incur such an expense.—Dr. O'Keeffe's motion was defeated by five votes to four. The majority was composed of Messrs. Carey, Gaskell, Taylor, Sadler,

and Houghton.—lt was then (lidded, on the mption of Mr. Carey, seconded by Mr. Taylor, that the architect's scheme for the Free Library be adopted —Mr. Wright was the only dissentient, but several members did not vote.— The Clerk explained that a great deal of work would have . .
to be performed before the lirary and reading roam could be got into operation, and he suggPsted toe appo;ntrnent of a c)mmittee —Mr. Eleyes moved, and Mr. Wright seconded,
that the General Purposes Committee. consisting of Messrs. Gossage, Handley. Cry, Gaskell,_and Dr. O'ii,effe, carry
on the work for toe prese-oi,—Mr. Handley cootidered that the Library Committee should be formed independent of the _
Board, because there was a great deal of work to be done,
and to consist of members of the Board and other gentlemen. He proposed as an amendment that a Free Library Commit..

tee no constituted as follows :—Messre. F. H. Gjsage, Dr. O'Keeffe., E. Carey, H. Gasket', jun., S. Sailer, F. Heves, T. Handley, H. W. Deacon, R. H. Davies, T. Snipe, S. Robin- son, and ,J. Morrison.—Dr. O'Keeffe seconded.—Only the
mover and seconder voted for the amendment, and the

original motion vras carried.—lt was resolved on the propo- sal of Mr. Handley, seconded by Mr. Gaskell that the Cleric apply to the Local Government Board for sanction to bor- row money to erect the library as prolapsed by the archi- tects.

GAS AND WATER CaMMITTER. The Gas Engineer reported to this committee that the mean rainfall for December was 1 337 Inches. and that the water in stock on December 23rd was 7,894,187 gallons. There was a decrease of 414 per cent. in the amoJr_t of gas delivered during the past month compared with the corres- ponding month of 1884. The illuminating power of the gas daring the month had averaged 17.19 candles.—lt was recommended by the committee that the resignation of A. Redfern be accepted, and that an assistant manager be advertised for, salary to commence at £9O per annum.—" Mr. IG,skell, in moving the adoption of the minutes, expressed I the regret of the committee at the unfortunate occurrence bv which unpurified gas had been supplies' to the town. Steps had been taken to prevent a repetition of the nuisance, and one result had been that one employe had sent in his resignation.—Mr. Sadler seconded the motion.—Carriei.

div.head: TIM MAIN SEWER.
div.p: TIM MAIN SEWER.

Upon the minutes of the Highway Committee clrnin; zo for discussion, Mr. Handley aske4 how the main stwer was progressing.—Mr. Carey said he was glad to be able to re- port that their difficulties with the sewer, if nut absolutely an end, were at all events within a measurable distance. of the end. Last week the committee went through that part of the sewer that had. been reconstructed, and the ',fork was finished for the present. There was a length where the gtoure4 bad gone down some five inches or thereahou4.s, but in the opinion of the surveyor and the commitrae there was nothing in the appearance of that sewer to lead them to suppose that it would not stand for an indefinite length of time. The committee did not recommend that anything should be done at present. Messrs. Sayce and Randle's work app-ared to have been done in a satisfactory manner. The, surveyor had been instructed to have the dams removed. and the sewer flushed from end to end in order that the com- mittee might inspect the sewer thoroughly, which they proposed to do at an early date. When that was done the committee would further report to the Board, and they might have to make some recommendation, but he hoped. not.

Dr. O'Keeffe asked what steps bad been taken with re- gard to the bridle road to Ditton and the footpath from Widnea past Ditton Hall into Cow-lane.—Mr. Carey said he was sorry the Highway Committee were not so forward with this negotiation as they hoped to bare been, and it would be .i.eceesary to oppose the Railway Bill in order to n 1405 the Board in a proper position. div.p: HEALTH COMMITTEE : THE HOSPITAL AND ITS rsE.

To this committee the Medical Officer reported that du- ine,. December there were 111 births and 60 deaths, beinz at the rats respectively of 49.33 and 26.66 per 1,000. The deaths included 27 children under one year, and 14 between. one and five years. Zymotic diseases caused three deaths.. " Pigs," it was stated, "are still kept in a disgraceful con- dition in back yards." The Nuisance Inspector (Mr. Dick- son) reported there had been four cases of scarlet fever, and of these two (children) had proved fatal. Two of the cases were iv. Wilmer-'ane, and it was feared that the drain- age from the sewage farm might have been the cause of the outbreak. The committee gave instructions to the clerk to again write to the Local Government Board re Rainhill Sewage Farm, and it was recommended that legal proceed- ings be taken against two persons if they did not immedi- ately remove their pigs from the back yards. The receipts at the market for the month amounted to £2l 6s Bd, being an increase of £4 7s 3d on the corresponding month in 1884.. Petitions in favour of and against hand-selling outside Market, with correspondence respecting custom in neigh- bouring towns, submitted. It was recommended that the charges for "hand-selling" outside the market be increaeed froua Is 61 to 2s 61 for dealers in crockery, and to 3s 61 for dealers in clothes, and that no such selling be allowed in- side the market.—Dr. O'Keeffe moved. and Mr. Heugeton seconded, the adoption of the minutes.—Mr. Graskell said he had seen it reported that a man who was suffering from a. broken collar h-ne had been ordered by the docter to be ant to the Liverpool Infirmary. He snould like to know whether it was customary to send men from Widnes to Liverpoil, rather than to the Widnes Hospital ; and if so, why ? Was it through some deficiency in the Hospital, or the management, er did the doctors feel that they were no, capable of dealing awl]] a broken collar bone? It appeare; rather invidious to a first-class hospital, and every ber,, empty, that a man should have been sent to th" Liverpool Infirmary. It was calculated to do the Whines Hospital great injury, and that peoole woeide I lose faith in the hospital management —Dr. O'Keeffe re- p)ied that the ac&dent ‘lid not occnr in the township ef Widne., and therefore the man had no right to be roceived i into the hospital.—Mr. Gaskell : Bet he lived n Viaduct. 1 street.—Dr. O'Keeffe said the accident occurred at Divon ! and the man's employers sent him to Liverpoal. He cer- tainly thought that the medical men of Whines were as well able, to treat a Weaken collar bone as the surgeons at the ' Royal Infirmary.—The Chairman said the Board had no jurisdiction.—Mr. Gasket! remarked that it was rather hard ' if a man who lived in the town could not go to his own boa- pitch—Dr. O'Keeffe argeed that if a man lived ie the town he was entitled to i•zo into the hospital. There might have been a mistake.-1 he minutes we7e then passed. •

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. Satania.—Before Aldermen Burgess and Olandley. A DESERTER.—WiIIiam Riley (24), charged with absent- ing himself from her Majesty's 64th North Staffordshire Regiment, was remanded to await an escort. MONDAT.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison), ___ _ _

man Davies, and Councillor Greening. ON LE ATE.—Thomas McHugh, a convict on ticket-of- -leave, was charged with failing to report himself on the. 10th of May last year and monthly since. He was sen- tenced to be imprisoned until the completion of his original sentence. MISCELtANEOrS —James Kelly was fined 5s and costii for being.drunk and disordPrly in Bridge-street, and Thomas Humphreys, for being drunk in Wilderspool-read, was or- dered to pay costs.---William Plinston was fined 5s and costs for being drunk and disorderly in Winwick-street.— !Thomas Griffin, for committing n breach of the peace by assaulting his wife in Winwick-road, where the patties live, was bound over in his own recognieances to be of good be- haviour.—John Darwin, for being drunk in Tanners-lane 'whilst in charge of a horse and cart, was fined lOs and costs. —Michael and Henry Ashton were ordered to pay costs, 33 6,1 each. for playing at pitch and toss in Bath-street on the 3rd inst. case. " A SAVAGE DOG.—William Bradbury, 13, Hoyle-street, was summoned for keepitfg a dog said to ha ferocious and noLunder proper control. Mr. A. For the defence it was contended that the Children had teased the dog.—The Bench ordered the defendant to keep the animal under strict control. ' TUESDAY.—Before Mr. E. J. Guest and Councillor Broadbent.

A CONFIRMSD TEMP.—James Mooney, an aged man, was charged with being on the premises of, the London and North-Western Railway, on the previous night, with in- tent to commit a felony. Be was seen on the premises and to take some time tables out of a wagon.—The Clerk said that perhaps prisoner got better food in gaol than in the workhouse, and luspector James remirked that he could Conte out of the workhouse when he could not come out of prison.—Mooney, who has many times been convicted of petty thefts, was sent to prison for fourteen days with bard labour. Dr. White. FELONIES —Thomas Tray. and William Boyles were found guilty of stealing a pair of clogs and various articles, value 10s, from the marine store of Peter Taylor, Tanners- lane. Tray is 17 years of age, a forge labourer, living at 9, Berry's-yard, and Boyles is 19 years of age. and lives at Pinners-brow. Both were sent to prison for three months with hard labour.—Jcssph Litherland, a boy of fifteen, was charged with stealing a flannel petticoat from a clothes line in the backyard of the dwelling-house of Catherine Bell. Directions were given for him to receive twelve strokes with the birch rod. VarmaNcv.—William O'Neill was sent to gaol for a ninth for sleeping on the premises of Monks, Hall, and Co., Atherton's Quay, the same morning.

A DRUNKEN' DRIVER.—AIIen Hewitt was charged with haring been drunk whilst in charge of a vehicle on the 30th December at High Leigh. He was ordered to pay coats. ASSAULTS BY Buornsns.—William Chorlton, farmes, ugh Leigh, was charged with haying assaulted George horlton, his brother, and also described as a farmer, at • tilt. 7,-h Leigh. The Bishop of Peterborough will, early in the pr,sent session, introduce into the House of Lords a Bill which provides that churches shall be for the free use in common of all parishioners, and that it shall be unlawful for any archbishop, bishop, or other person to grant or appropriate any seat or pew in any parish church. ; The Bill, bowevar, preserves the rights of rectors in chan- cels and all existing titles to seats by faculty or prescrip- tion, and the rights to private aisles, chapels, or chantries kept in repair by their owners. Tbe Duke of Argyll, writ- ! ing from Inverary, says that having seen the draft bill for declaring the constitution of the Church of Scotland pre- ; pared by Mr. Finlay, M.P., be thinks it his duty to say at ' once that that Bill, or indeed any other bill drawn snbstan- tially on the same lines, would have his cordial and earnest support. These were the members of the commit- , ' tee, which was composed of the following gentle- . men, viz.':—President, Mr. Councillar John Pier-' point; vice-president, Mr. Thomas Jones; hon. treasurer, Mr. Thomas Morris; hon. secretary, Mr. Councillor Thomas Sutton; Mr. Samuel' Jones, Mr. Peter Chrimes, Mr. Noah Legge, Mr. Daniel Jones, . Mr. William Dooley, Mr. W. J. Horton, Mr. J. Smethurst, Mr. P. Caldwell, Mr. Councillor John Edward Wright; assisted by the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, Rev. S. Wilkinson, _Rev. J. McTurk, Rev. J. W. Drummond, Rev. G. Allton, Mr. D. Rankin, Councillor Francomb, Mr. G. Bliley, Mr J. Harrison, and others. The serving was admirably performed, there being a strong and indefatigable contingent of waiters and waitresses, in which were included Mrs. S. Wilkinson, Mrs. E. C. E. Carelton, Mrs. G. Allton, Miss Allton, Mrst Quekett, and the wives ' and daughters of most • of the committee men. The viands, which were of the most substan- tial and varied description, had been admirably pre- , pared by Mrs. Shackleton, of the Public Hall. The dinner having once fairly begun, those in waiting, like the carvers, found their office no sinecure. Age by no means had blunted the appetites of the guests,: and the silence, unbroken except by the clicking of knives and forks, which fell upon their ranks nn- mistakeably attested that the work of mastication I was being engaged in with a diligence and unan- imity of purpose worthy of so good a cause. It was nearly twoo'clock before all had been served. After the edibles had been freely partaken of, glasses of "nut-brown ale" and" the weed" were generally indulged in. Each of those present had been fur- nished with four tickets, and each of those tickets. was considered equivalent to half an ounce of to- bacco or a glass of beer-Or other beverage. Few present seemed to be members of the Anti-Smoking Society, and consequently the pipe" was very much in request. The after dinner scepe was by no , means the least pleasing of the whole affair. To see ' these Nestors of the tOwn reclining at ease on their seats, their countenances, all time-worn as they were, and in many cases bearing the unmistakeable impress of a life of struggle and penury, suffused with that air of general benignity which comes of a contented inner man, and apparently 'for the nonce forgetful of the vicissitudes and crosses of life, was a sight which is never seen except at a gathering of the "aged people." It ought to be mentioned that music, that accompaniment of luxurious feasts, was admirably. discoursed from the.organ by Mr. W. S. Woods at intervals during the dinner. Although the tea for the aged women was fixed to commence at six o'clock, five had barely struck when they began to congregate at the Public Hall. The tables were consequently soon appropriated, and so large was the number that came that the platform had to be utilised for the purpose of ac- commodating them, and even then two sittings had to be arranged. In all there were something like 440 present, nearly 100 more than had been provided for on any previous occasion. The serving and attendance was similar to that in the afternoon, and the tea passed off racist satisfactorily. After tea a concert was held, to which the public were admitted at a charge of threepence; and the 'gallery, which was set apart for their accommodation, was filled to overflowing. A suitable programme of song and music had been arranged, the comic element pre- Tailing, though judiciously interspersed with a little of the pathetic and sentimental. The comic songs were contributed by Mr. Mercer, Mr. Mullins, and also Mn Harrison, of the Gaiety Theatre,, whose services had been kindly given, and each of these' gentlemen won hearty recalls, Mr. Mullins being especially humorous and successful. Mr. D. Ikin excellently rendered the "Death of Nelson" and "The pilgrim of love," and Mr. Baylie, of the Gaiety Theatre, who also gave his services, sang severanautical songs with unusual expression and effect, and was boisterously recalled more than once. The lady singers were Miss L. Horton and Miss Harding, and their efforts were evidently highly appreciated. • Mr. Warburton gave an ad- mirable rendition of "The Friars Grey," while Mr. Whittaker's solos on the concertina were remark- able performances ,showing a wonderful proficiency in the handling of that instrument. Mr. Geo. Riley was the accompanist. During the concert several short addresses were given. • Mr. J. Piint POINT, who occupied the chair, mrtioned that the number o f the old ladies present on sions had never exceeded 360, but this year they had co i- enter- tained about 440. He had much pleas ' ' pleasure in wishing them al! "A Happy New Year." (Applause.) The Rev. S. WILKINSON said the chairman of the Old Men's Dinner and Aged Women's Tea Committee was Mr. John Pierpoint, wbo bad done mach towards the further- ance and success of that annual gathering. A ( pplause.) The labours which had been undertaken by the committee were by no means small. They had seen how much the members had done that day, and they most remember that the time of gentlemen engaged in various professions in the town was very-vahrable.- .Therdevoted a great deal of time year after year in making the aged ---p-e nen 1 happy and com- fortable, and their warmest thanks were, therefore, due is them tor the labours they had undertaken in getting up not only the dinner and tea but the entertainment which was shertli te be given. In conclusion be called for three cheers for the committee. The cheers were heartily given. Mr. PIERPOINT. in returning thanks, said that though the committee had worked hard, theirs had been a labour of love, and each member had devoted a considerable amount of time to his duties. He had been connected with the In- stitution for over 26 years, and year after year it gave him the greatest pleasure to see the number of old nie9 and women increase. They had had a greater number to dinner and tea than ever. caused no doubt by the slackness of trade, which had induced some not many months over 60 years of age to apply for tickets and to have the pleasure of being with them at the annual new year's festivities. The cohamitte had worked very had, and not only they were de- serving of thanks, but also the tradespeople of Warrington who had subscribed so liberally to the funds. (Applause.)

gM.AGISTRATES' DECISION. There was klarge attendance at the St: Helens ToWn Hall,Torihionday, when -before Mr. W. Pil- kington and Colonel D. Gamble, the 'extraordinary affiliation case of Janet Westhead against John Ed- wards again came on for hearing. About a month ago the defendant John Edwards a teamsman in the employ of Mr. Richard Pye, a farmer, at Rainford, was summoned to show cause why orders should not be made upon him to contribute to the support of a married woman named Janet Westhead with whom Edwards had undergone the ceremony of marriage. At the first hearing the summonses were dismissed for want of evidence that the first husband of the oenaplainant vale still alive. The complainant was again represented by Mr. J. 0. Swift, arid' Mr. H. L. Riley appeared for the defendant. Mr. Swift said he was. sorry- he and his friend Mr. Riley had not been able to save the Bench the trouble •of,hearing tigit case, but they had not been able to agree. As eir Worship would probably be aware the ease came before the Bench on the 21st December and was heard at some length.—Mr. Riley then took up several points, upon one of which the Bench held that he had 'failed to -make out his case. The ease was a peculiar-one, because the complainant was 'married ton min -named Westhead at Rainford in for about 12 years she lived with him. In April Itqt Westbeed left her, and she saw nothing of him for a considerable time afterwards. About eight Months, after he had left her she heard that a man had been killed at 3faghull, who was thought to ,be Westheacl. She went to see the body, but she was too late • the body was buried and she returned home. , During the whole of her married life with Westhead she lived at Crank, and continued to live there after Westhead's disappearance. She made the acquain- tance of the present defendant, John Edwards, and on the loth January 1877 she went through the care. mony •of marriage with him ; and there was no doubt they both thought they had be- come lawful • man and wife. Mr. Swift procee- ded to- speak of the birth of the four children, In 1877, 1879;1880, and 1883, and said the children had always been recognised by Edwards as his chil- dren. Shortly after the birth of the second child Westhead,' the first .husband,. turned up at Crank • where he slept ;with a man named -Johnson. He again_ disaßpeared .and had not since been seen,„ Until the beginning of last November they lived, .togethe, more or less comfortably. Edwards support- ing • the whole of the family, and recognising the ' whole of the four children as his. In the beginning of November he left Mrs. Edwards, and since then he had refused to support her or allow her anything in support of the four young children. She could not apply to the Guardians for assistance, because she was not his lawful wife. Westhead was undoubtedly alive when he went through the ceremony of mar- riage, and in the same way the Guardians could not interfere with Edwards as to the support of the four children. The only way in which he could,be com- pelled to maintain them was by the complainant ask- ing the Bench to.make an order upon him under the Bastardy Laws. He thought the facts were all clear and undisputable, and he hoped the Bench would see their way to make the order sought.; Janet Westhead, the complainant, was then called. She repeated her evidence given on the previous oc- casion, to the effect that in 1859 she married John Westhead, who left her in 1871. After marrying the defendant Edwards she met her first husband on Crank Brow. she did not speak to him, neither did he speak to her.—John Edwards, the defendant, was next sworn. He gave evidence as to his marriage with the complainant, adding that he did not know her first husband. He had heard that her first hus- band had . been seen in Crank —Charles Johnson, a resident of Red Cat, Crank, said he knew John West- heakwhen he lived at Crank. Witness saw him about six years ago at Crank Hotel, and that, night Johni Westhead slept with him (witness). He did not stay more than one night. Witness accompanied' him to Crank station on the following day. They spoke ,about Mrs. Westhead's marriage with Edwards. In reply to Mr. Riley, witness ,said Westhead did not tell him where he had been living all the time. He said he had been up and down the country.—Mrs. Rowlands, of Southport, said she used to live at Crank, and knew the parties to whom allusion had been made. She saw Westhead after Mrs. West- head's marriage with Edwards, and they talked to- gether for a quarter of an hour Before any of their witnesses were called Mr. Riley intimated that at the last hearing of the case he was bound to raise the points he did, because Edwards when he went through the marriage ceremoay with Mrs. Westhead believed he was entering into lawful 'matrimony, but that day, in face of the proof that had been given, he had instructed him to say that he was now satisfied. He had never heard that evidence be- fore to show that his marriage wAs an illegal one, and he was consequently -.able to Mrs. Westhead in the same way as if she was a single woman.. He spoke •of Edwards' present position, and remarked that in conversation with his friend Mr. Swift they had agreed that the payment of 5s per week, distributed over the four children would under the circumstances he just between the parties, and their Worships, he apprehended, with the consent of the parties, would make those orders. The Chairman remarked that the sum of ss was too small, bat if they had agreed upon it they would make an order for is for each of the two elder children, and Is 6d each for the two younger ones.

DISASTROUS COLLISION IN THE 'Dowtis.—Soon after 11 'o'clock on Monday night two vessels were in collision in the Downs, one Apparently an iroti barque, the other a large steamer. Both vessels made signals of distress, but it is feared that the steamer has gone down. A boat has returned to Dover and reports seeing nothing of the steamer. Ac- cording to the boatmen, the collision occurred nearly off Weimer Castle, about a mile and a half or two miles from the shore. The night was clear, and the crash of the col- lision was heard distinctly from the beach, this being fol- lowed by signals of distress. Two luggars at once put off to the scene of the disaster, when the vessels were made out to be a steamer and a barque. Before the spot could be reached, however, the lighte of the steamer were lost sight of, as above stated. It is believed she sank. EXECUTION IN IRELAND —On Tuesday morning John Cronin, who was convicted at the Sligo Assizes of the wil- ful murder of his father, Thomas Cronin, was executed in- side the prison of Mullingar District Prison, Berry being the executioner. The murder was committed in Longford town, on a Saturday night or Sunday morning in October, and some money the victim had was afterwards got in the postession of the murderer. The evidence was circumstan- tial but conclusive, but the unfortunate man, after being sentenced, became very defiant, and said that his ghost would haunt each juryman. He continued defiant and stubborn for a long time in goal, refusing to listen to the ministrations of the Roman Catholic clergyman. However, as the fatal hour drew near, he became penitent, and it is said he has made a confession of his guilt. The executioner did his work promptly and well. . CHAXBERLAIN, M.P., AND SMALL ALLOTMENTS The annual meeting of the Allotments' and Small Holdings' Association was held on Monday at the Westminster Palace Hotel, London, Mr. Jeese Collings, M.P., presiding. The report stated that the chief object of the society was the restoration of labourers and others to direct connection with the soil, as advocated in Mr. Collings' bill, and adopted by Mr. Chamberlain.—The Chairman urged that the time had come when they must keen faith with the agricultural la- bourer, and secure compulsory power for the purchase of land, which was the keynote of the position.—Mr. Jos. Cham- berlain, in supporting the adoption of the report, said be neither believed nor honed that this would be a long Par- liament, and if they did not do their best to redeem their promises, they would not deserve a continuation of the support given them by the rural population at the late election. The Tories had lied on the land question with vigour, persistency, and unanimity; but, nothwithstand- ing this, the labourer would not remain a helpless and hopeless dependent upon the land be had made productive. Already they had heard that landowners were. offering al- lotments by grace and favour, but that was not enough. They must give the principle legislative sanction, and no -settlement could be satisfactory which did not give the labourers direct and independent interest in the land. Local bodies might be left to control this matter, and they had a perfect. right to acquire lend at a fair value, wherever the necessity arose. He had little doubt of the result of the agitation. Ica AocIDENTs : EXCITING FORNES.—On Saturday after- noon there was a large number of skaters on Sefton Meadows' Liverpool The ice was slightly rough owing to the high winds. All went smoothly tin about a quarter to four o'clock, when the ice at the top part of the Meadows gave way, letting in several skater's. No fatalities have been re- ported, and it is believed that all skaters got safely to land. —On Saturday afternoon Regent's Park Ornamental water was crowded with hundreds of skaters. During the after- noon several immersions took place; but between four and five o'clock the ice in the south-west portion of the water, which is here very broad, suddenly broke up, without the slightest warning, causing the immersion of over 100 people. Fortunately, the water was shallow, having been made so ,after the great accident which took place some years ago at the same spot, when upwards of forty lives were lost. The major portion of those immersed scrambled out over the large pieces of ice which were floating ebeut, the ice having been cracked up in .all directions. A very exciting scene took place. A lad, in endeavouring to throw a rope, was himself immersed, but managed to get to the shore. One Cause for this alarming accident is stated to be the great rush which was made after the first few were immersed. A number of hats, kc., were lost, and many were seen to be floating about on the scrface of the water.—Whilst a large number of pelople were skating on some water near Leiees- ter, on Saturday, six persons were immersed by the break- ing of the ice, and three of thorn were drowned. Another fatal accident occurred at Leicester on Sunday. About a dozen people were grating. On a pond in a field near Abbey Park, when the ice gave way, and James Brewin. aeed 22, were drowned. Deceased leaves a wife and two children. Several persons were immersed at Wardsend, near Sheffield. on Sunday. They were all rescued with the exception of a boy, who disappeared under the ice and was drowned.—On Sunday evening a large number of persons were skating on a pool in Pig-lane, Rowley, when the ice gave way and four young men fell into water 21) feet deep, A long wire was procured, by means of which they were reecued in a very exhausted state, one being insensible. All four could swim, or they must have been drowned. A young man damed Pearson broke his leg when skating on a neighbour- ing pond.

div.head: MYSTERIOUS DItOWNING AT *ARRINGTON.
div.p: THE MYSTERIOUS DItOWNING AT *ARRINGTON.

On Monday morning the adjourned inquest as to the death of the young Irish farm labourer, named Michael Ward, whose body was found in a partially decomposed state in the Mersey, was held at the Black Bear Inn, Latchford, before the deputy- coroner, Mr. C. Blunt. The inquest had been ad- journed in order that John Byrne, another labourer, who was in Ireland at the time, might give evi- dence. Byrne was now called, and said that he left county Galway on Saturday to attend the iiNuest. Last summer he worked for Mr. James Davies, at Rollington, he and deceased living at the same farm- house. The evidence which witness gave before the magistrates when a youno- man named Scanlon was charged on suspicion with haVing caused the death of Ward, was read over, and he affirmed that it was correct. He then described the fight which took took place near Friars Green, Warrington, about midnight on the 10th October, between the two Scanlons, father and son, and the deceased. Ward ran away from the Scanlons, and he (witness) afterwards sought for but could not find him. He did not see any of the Scanlons during the time he was looking for Ward. He saw the Scanlons the day after the fight in the Star and Garter, Friars green, and in answer to his question, they said they knew nothing about Ward. Witness saw the elder Scanlon and his son Michael in Ireland on Tuesday last. He did not know that any ill-feeling existed be- tween the Scanlons and deceased.—Dr. Starkey Smith, Warrington, said the body of the deceased was so far decomposed that he could not make any satisfactory examination of it. He found several wounds and abrasions but it was impossible to say whether they were produced before or after death. He could not say whether death was due to drown- ing, or whether it had taken place before the body was put into the water.—Patrick Quinn, a labourer, living at Ormskirk, spoke to having seen the fight in October last. He remonstrated with the Scan- lons for their treatment of the deceased, bat he did not hear any flireats'usecl after the latter ran away. A verdict of " Found dead" was returned.

div.head: ALLEGED PERJURY AT WAR-
div.p: ALLEGED PERJURY AT WAR-
RINGTON.

At the Borough Court, on Wednesday, the magistrates heard a charge of perjury which arose out of a• case heard on the previous Friday, when a man named James Dicken- son was fined .£5 for assaulting Joseph Waterhouse. 4 bailiff of the Warrington County Court, in a brutal manner with a poker.—On that occasion a married woman named Ann Simpkin (27), sister to prisoner Dickenson, gave evidence in his defence, and swore on oath that she was present at the time of the assault and that she saw no poker need, and , also that Dickenson had not a poker in his hand. This evidence was so directly opposed to evidence given by other witnesses that application was made by the prosecution for a warrant against Mrs. Simpeins on a charge of committing perjury. The magistrates acceded. to the application, and the woman was taken into custody. On Saturday morning she was brought before two magistrates, and formally re- manded until Wednesdey, bail being allowed, On Weanet- clay.the was eharged wlth Nalailttiug wilful and corrupt perjury in an information in which Joseph Waterhouse was informant and James Dickenson defendant. Mr. J. L, Whittle, deputy town clerk, appeared to proeecnte on behalf of the police, and Mr. A. Browns, solicitor, Warrington, defended the nrisoner.—Mr. Whittle said that the case had arisen out of one that was before the magistrates on Friday. Ka believed that a poker had been used by tbe man Dicken- son, with which he assaulted Waterhouse, and prisoner, who was sister to the prisoner in the other case, was then a wit- ness for the defence. It was proved to the satisfaction of the magistrates that the prisaner Dickenson did in fact use a poker upon the bailiff, and it was sworn to by two bailiffs and was corroborated to some extent by the medical eVi- dence. On that occasion the prisoner swore that she was in the house at the time, if a poker had been used she would have seen it, that no poker was used, and that her brother never had a poker in his hand. The maeistrates were so satisfied that perjury ha r bsen committed that they then and there issued a warrant for her apprehension, and she was taken into custody. By the direction of the rnagis- strates' clerk notes were taken in shorthand of witness's evidence, and from the transcript he read, "When he Dickenson) got them out of the house the dark fellow (meaning a bailiff named Thomas) struck him with a stick and went away, and , he then turned round to defend himself and struck the man with the red whiskers (Waterhouse). He had nothing in his band. He never had a poker in his hand, but I saw the dark man strike him with a stick." Asked Will you swear defendant never had a poker in his hand," she replied ! -" Yes," and in answer to further questions said that had he had a poker in his hand she should have seen it. Mr. Whittle, continuing, said that he had a Witness who would swear to seeing prisoner take a poker from her brother's hand. He remarked on the great amount of perjury that was apparently committed in that court, and said that the magistrates had made up their minds to make an example of the first case of per- jury that they got held of. Evidence was then called.— Dr. Joseph stated that on Friday afternoon last Joseph Waterhouse, county court bailiff, came to see him. Witness found him suffering from bruises on the face, extending from the eyes to the jaw ; there was aleo two abrasions on the nose. The wound was not a dangerous one. ri e should not have thought of suggesting that it had been done by any instrument, but the wound was one that might have been caused by a poker, and the abrasions on the nose cor- responded with the square edges of a poker. It could have been caused by a fiat, but that was not 80 probable. Reply- ing to Mr. Browne as to whether a heavy poker would not have caused a more severe injury, the doctor said that he did not think so in the case of Waterhouse, who had a strang nasal bone ; the bones Were particularly firm. He still thought that the injuries could have been caused by a fist. but that they had more probably been caused lily a poker. Injuries of that kind were not so definite as stabs and gun- shot wounds.—Joseph Waterhouse, the bailiff assaulted, re- peated evideece given by him when the charge of assault was heard. He said that Dickenson had the poker in his hand when Mrs. Simpkin entered the house. John Thomas, County Court bailiff, and Alice OxlPy, wife of John Oxley, shopkeeper, lihilip•streetoleo gave evidence.—P.C. Neale said that he apprehended prisoner. He read the warrant. to her and charged her with having committed perjury. She replied, "I told them nothing only what I saw. That's all. He did not use a poker when I saw him."—Mr. Browne called a number of witnesses for the defence.—Mary Ann Williams, a married women living in Philip-street, said that Dickinson struck Waterhouse with his fists ; he had nothing in his hand at the time, and if he had had a poker she must Dave seen it, as she was only a short distance away.— Catherine Crearer, wife of Lawrence Crearer, Philip-street, 'said that she saw Dickinson throw Waterbease out of the house and thump him with hie lists; Dickenson had nothing in his hand at the time.—Elizabeth Dickenson, wife of James Dickenson, said that on the day in question the poker produced was in the kitchen fire-place at her house. Her husband picked it up, but she took it from him and put it in a back place. Prisoner 'never attempted to take the poker from her husband, and did not see the poker that day. —Mize Skelborn and Sarah Ann Cunniogharn, both of Philip-street, also gave evidence for the defence.—The mazistrates committed prisoner for trial at the next Liver- pool Assizes, bail being allowed.

EARLESTOWN (A. TItA M ) LOWTON ROVERS (IST TEAM )—These teams met on the ground of the first named, the Mesnes, on Saturday afternoon. A fairly goad game resulted in a victory for the home team by four goals to none. EARLEITOWN WANDERERS Y. HAYDOCK Sr. JAMES'S.— This match was played on the Wanderers' ground at New- ton Common on SatHrday afternoon, when there was cc fair attendance of spectators. Neither side was fully repre- sented. The result was : St. James's one goal, Earlestown Wanderers none.

• , EAILLIZSTOVfIi OLYMPIC V. GOLBOUNE Sr. JOSEPHS,* hif4 match was played on the ground of the Olympic on Saturday afternoon. Although the visitors had the assist- ance of Clarke and S. Cottam, of the Golborne Club first team, the Earlestonians won an exciting game by three goals to two. Clarke, Cottam, and Wheelan played best for the visitors, while Forster, Corcoran, W. It is stated that the Uolbornit4s played a rough game, and Cottam left the field about quarter of an hour from the finish in consequence of an injury to his arm.

EARLESTOWN. Wrisnavele BAND OF HOPE SOCIETY. The opening meeting in connection with the junior division of the-Wes- leyan Band of Hope was held in the Brunswick Wesleyan Schoolroom, Croes-lane, on Thursday evening. There was go xi attendance. and Mr. J. H. Graham, vice-president, occupied the chair. A capital programme of songs, recita- tons, and readings was gone through, and addresses were given by the chairman and Mr. Pearson (secretary.) EARLESTOWN RANGERS' CEICZET CLUB. A general meeting of the members of this club was held at the Wel- come Coffee Palace on Thursday evening. Mr. W. Whittle was elected to preside. The secretary's and treasurer's re- ports were read and passed, after which the Captain and other officers were elected, Mr. J. Jones, of 11, Chandos- street, being appointed secretary. A vote of thanks was passed to the officers for the past season, and a similar com- pli,nent to the chairman concluded the meeting. FOURTEEN DAYS ON HIS HEAD—At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, William Broughton, of Earles- town, was summoned for having been drunk and disorderly at Earlestown on the 31st December.—P.C. Hunt proved the case, and it was stated that it was the defendant's 23rd ap- pearance. He was asked where he got his money from, and he replied that he had been living on his means, and had had money given to him.—The Bench said he must go to prison for 14 days, whereupon the defendant exclaimed that he could stand on his head and do that. Fula, Taus AT THE VULCAN.—During the present week the hundreds of workmen employed at the Vulcan ironfoundry have again been started on full time. Some months ago, owing to the great depression, the works were run to the extent of only four days per week, but on Mon- day last a notice was posted on the board at the entrance gates to the effect that on and after Wednesday last work would be resumed on the old system with the exception of Saturday morning. This announcement created joyful feelings among the workmen and their families. HANGING RY THE NECE.—A singular " scene " was witneSsed in Back Market-street, Earlestown, on Wednes- day forenoon. A local farmer was on his usual round de-

livering milk, end for a short time stopped with his horse and trap in the thoroughfare mentioned. Ile left the trap, the only other occupant of which was a flue looking smooth- haired terrier dog. The dog was attached by a string, but it was subsequently noticed that the animal had leaped over thetside of the trap, with the result that it Was in the most uncomfortable position of being suspended with a string lround its neck, while its feet were some distance from the ground. Probably the dog would have met its death, but a passing stranger raised the animal to the cart, and the dog was not again seen to leave it in so hasty a manner. SAD END OF A GOLBORNE CHILD. Mr. W. 'r. Husband, the deputy coroner, held an inquest at the Red Lion Inn, Golborne, on Thursday week, respecting the case of a child whose death occurred under sad circurns,ances.— Mary Johnson said she was the wife of James JOhn:4,il, of Church-street, Golborne. Deceased was her child, and was four months old. It had been suffering from bronchitis, and about noon, on the 24th ult., she placed it in a roceine chair in front of the fire. The chair accidentally fell over, caught a pan of hot water which was standing netht hob," the contents of which ran over tne child's head and neck. Witness called in a neiekbour, and applied linseed oil and lime water to the child's injuries. She. sent for Dr. Dobb, who continued to attend until the 28th" ult , when the child died.—The jury returned a verdict of " Accidental death." GOOD TEMPLARY.—The weekly session of the Hope of Earlestown Lodge of Good Templets was held in the Lodge-room, Bridge-street, on Monday evenieg, when Bro. E. Newman, W.C,T., presided. There was a very good attendance, After one candidate had bseri initiated and two restored to membership, Bro. George Clarke gave a report on the New Year tea party, showing a balance in hand after the payment of eiperna s Bros. James Flaherty and jAIILICIS Mason, of the Old 40th Lodge connected with the Seatli Lancashire Regiment, gava instructive addresses on temper- ance work in the army; after which the evening's pro- gramme " Letter Box" was proceeded with. Interesting ' communications were read from Bro. J. W. Hall, D.M., of Warrington ; Bro. George Clarke, V.D , of Earlestosvn ; another was signed " A Member," and a fourth, a charac- teristic epistle, was signed" The Harmonium." The letters occasioned considerable interest, and the thanks of the lodge were tendered to the writers. Ileavnonse SICK AND BURIAL SOCIETY.—The annual meeting of this society was held in St. James's Church Schoolroom, Hevdock, on Monday evening. The event as celebrated by a tea, to which 200 persons sat down. The tea was of a most enjoyable character, the tables being presided over by Mesdames Kearney, Harrison, Hezeldine, Whitfield, Leyland, Owen, Tunstall. and others. After tea a meeting was held, when Mr. Waldron, the secretary, submitted his report for the year, in which he stated that although the club had been only recently established it was went.] £1 per member, and it had distributed during the year £2lin sick pay. As an inducement to members to join, he stated that the expenses of management had been less than one shilling per head, which contrasted favourably with the expenses of ether societies. Several songs, readings, were given by members of the society, under the presidency of the Rev. A. H. Kearney. Dancing was afterwards in- dulged in until 11-30, when the proceedings terminated. THE CHARGE OF STEALING A HUSBAND'S GOODB : A SEEKTEL.—A somewhat singular sequel to a recent charge against a hnarried woman named Haskins of stealing her husband's goods was heard at the Newton Petty Sessions on Saturday last, before Messrs. R. Houghton, T. J. Gillespie, C. Pilkington, and A. C. McCotquodale. Samuel Taylor and Frederick Haskins, young men were charged with com- mitting a breach of the peace by fighting on the 28th ult. P.C. Spencer stated that on Monday, the 28th nit, he found the two defendants fighting. He separated them. They were both on the ground, Taylor being on the tap M the other man. Haskins said he was fighting because Taylor was walking out with his (Elaskips') wife. The two de- fendants were bound over to keep the peace far six months. The defendant Taylor remarked that he was merely walking with Haskins' wife to Newton and they met the husband, who struck him. He (Taylor) merely took his own part. —The Bench remarked that they had nothing to do with that. A FAMIKY QUA.IIIIEL.—Before MeaSrg.'n.-Houghton, T. J. Gillespie, C. Pilkington, and A. C. McCorquodale, at the Newton Town Hall, on Saturday, Ellen Powell wa.s suin• moned for using threatening language to Mary Glynn, her step-daughter, on the previous Saturday. The coniplainent said the defendant come' to her house and threatened to break every window, and " run a knife throegh her." She also said be would "do" 12 months' for her and would also swibe. " for ber.—Defendant : When I married your father did I spoil your home ?—Complainant: No.—Defen- dant: Has your father kept me black and blue through you? —Complainant: I don't know.—The Chairman: That has nothing to do with this case.—Defendant admitted having, threatened to smash the windows of complainant's house if she would not allow her (defendant's) husband to come borne.—A sister of the complainant gave corroborative evi- dence.—the defendant said her husband kept up dancing, and singing all through the night, and he had frequently. kicked her on account of the complainant.—The Clerk: We have nothing to do with that.—Defendant: They have sent him out of the country' and he has taken his wages with him. She had never done the complainant nor her sister any harm.—The Bench ultimately ordered the defen- dant to be bound over to keep the peace. THE CONCEALMENT or BIRTH —At the St. Helens. Police Court, on Thursday, before Alderman Harrison, the young woman Mary Gavanagh, of Appleton-street, Peasley Cross, who was first suspected of having murdered her in: fent, but who was acquitted of such charge by a coroner's jury, was brought up in custody charged with coneealinie the birth of her child. Inspector Keighley stated that from three anonymous letters received by Police-constable Carter they proceeded to the house, and found the body concealed between the 'bed and laths, upon which prisoner had been sleeping. Gavanagh was arrested, and, being in a weak state, was remanded to the Providence Hospital. Evidence was given by Police-constable Carter, Mrs Bridget Purcell, Mrs Mellor, Mrs Blaney, Dr. Casey, and Dr. WNicoll. Mrs Martin said the prisoner left ser- vice to he married, and was afterwards deserted by her lover in the midst of her trouble. At this stage of the case the prisoner fainted away, and water and other reetoratives were applied Mrs Martin, having finished her evidence, left the box and sat down in court, and a few minutes later she was noticed in a faititing state, and was also attended by Dr. WNicoll. Prisoner, in reply to the charge, said it was all through fear. When committed to the assizes she cried bitterly. On Thursday afternoon she was removed to Wal- ton Gaol to await her trial. THIEI PLEASURBS or Imasteatermer."—A public lecture with thia tile was given by the Rev. T. W. Noble, 8.A., of Sheffield, in St. John's Schoolroom, Market-street, Eerlestown, on Thursday evening. There were about fifty persons present. The Rev. T. R. Matthews, vicar, presided', and he was supported by the Lecturer and the Rev. J. Lovett (curate).—The Chairman said he had a short but pleasing duty to perform, and that was to introduce their " noble" lecturer. He remarked that they sometimes in- dulged in imagination too much, but he did not know what they would do after hearing the lecture.—The Rev. T. W. Noble was well received. In the course of an instructive address, be said the imagination came under their notice only as an instrument to procure pleasure to the mind, and therefore pleasure was their principal theme. After remark- ing that pleasure came from heaven, he said the reality of pleasure few would deny, and yet a popular definition of it based their utmost ingenuity. It might be described as a pleasing sensation or feeling produced in the mind by the presence of some cherished object. Pleasure was the birth- right of every son and daughter of Adam's race, and people pursued different eleasures. The faculties comprising what they called imagination were conception, memory, taste, and judgment. Conception had to do with the recep- tion of ideas; memory had to retain and present those ideas in the council chamber of the mind ; taste had to do with the selection of taose ideas, and judgement had to consider the fitness of the ideas selected for the purpose. He explained that the imagination was the great constructive faculty of the mind for which we wets iadebted for the most valuable productions of art, science, id literature, and yet, be said, that faculty with all its aliehty and unknown capacities might lie dormant in the elite), yielding neither profit nor pleasure, or it might be- come the instrument of the most refined and excruciating ertures under certain conditions. He afterwards spoke at aonsiderable length of the pleasures to be derived from eature in the land, sea, and sky, and said true pleasures were ealculeted to nourish and strengthen the imagination and all :he kindred faculties of the soul, as well as calculated to devate and ennoble the character. At the close the meeting iccorded its hearty thanks to the lecturer.

NEWTON CONGREGATIONAL SCHOOLE.—On blonde? evening a supper was given to the elder scholars, to the number of about 80, attending the above Sunday scbools. A Musical entertainment was also gone through by several of the scholars, including Miss „Owen and Miss Both- well. Games of various kinds and dancing were indulged in. EARLEsTOWN GOOD TEXPLAES AT ASHTON.—A bout 25 members of the Hope of Earlestown Lodge of Good Tein.. plan visited Ashton and gave an entertainment in the British School. under the auspices of the Excelsior Lodge. on Wednesday, when there was a good number present, and Bro. George Clarke, V.D., of Earlestown, presided. Songs wele given by Bros. F. Urin and T. Gorse; readings by Bros. George Clarke and J. BAruard •, recitations by Bros. George E. Warburton, J. Clarke, 'l'. Gorse, and Sister Morris (Ash- ton) ; and duets by Sisters E. and J. Clarke and Mr. and Miss Jones (Ashton). Melodies by the choir were highly appreciated. An address was given by Bro. James Fla• berry. A cordial vote of thanks was paid to the enter- tainers on the motion of Bre. Willis, 'seconded by Bro J. It• Merry.

LIBERAL CLUB DISCUSSION CLASS. "OUR POLITINEAL DUTIES." The first meeting in connection with the recently-formed Debating Class for Earlestown was held in the Liberal Club. Fairclough-street, on Thursday evening, when Mr. Thomas. Morris, one of the principal promoters of the class, read an interesting paper on " Our Political Duties." There was a large attendance, and Mr. Lewis F. Foulkes was elected to preside. Among those present were Messrs. P. Hall, J• Clarke, J. Rutter, C. Kelly, M. Birklaead, jun., L. Maria' W. McEvoy, F. Willis, &c.

The Chairman said it was to be hoped by that class the 9 would be taught to appreciate the duties imposed upon theta as. citizens and subjects of the British empire. Our empire was such a large one, an the duties imposed upon earerY citiaen in tin) country were so great, it was to be hoped none of them would mare a mistake in thinking them small or important He called upon Mr. Morris to read his paper with the hope that those present would have no hesitation in discussing his remarks. (Applause.) Mr. Morris, who was well received, commenced by pointe ing out that the question of duty was a moat important one' and said it might be divided into three sections, namelh. religiousisocial, arid political duties. It was the latter section, with their permission and co-operation, he would disc.° that night. In the first place they must ask what wet! politics. The best explanation he could give was a deftn_h- lion recently given by Mr. Chamberlain when he describe. politics as being the science of human happiness. Liberal principles in politics had always been to give the greateet good to the greatest number, and on that assumption their ideal of duty as Liberals should be rather high. It ale important they should do their political duty, ae upon the result hung future prosperity or disaster to ihitieh trade and commerce. It was by the passing of just and equitable laws, by the repeal of unjust and bad laws, and by adoptiog a firm and st,ple foreign policy, that this country was 10 maintain its position in the markets of the world, and to be 'respected in the council chambers of different nations Wit.b whom we had dealinge. He briefly commented on the con' duct ef their Opponents when in oppoeition and in office' and alluded to undue influence exercised upon voters ill cot tam quarters, and proceeded to say that taking into con: elderation these and other influences brought to bcar agaioe' the Liberal party, the result of the general election `hal very gratifying to them, and gave them the hope that 1, they worked, organised, 'and otherwise did their politica) duty at the next general electicn, which he believed White not far dietint, they would win a most glorious victory- Ja! was confident they would set a good example in that non and return their esteemed candidate if they all their duty. He therefore appealed to all present to ne.e what influence they possessed to further the good canh2 and the party 7hinh. had done ,ale mush in the pet to 00'01 the mass of the people by ifs policy of advancement 011, reform. The most serious disadvantage they laboured mule' as a party, and, in fact; the great fault of the Litnral part' was the want of unity. He thought their list duty was 11) try and unite their forces. The friend who believed in disestablialmuent of the Church should try to convince those who did not so believe ; the free educationist, the local optionist, and even the Home Rulets, should oriO4 forward their cases, and by free discussion to try cas. vince his fellow Liberals and his political opponents of ell: justness of his cause, and not hold aloof from then, even vote against them, because everybody did not thine he might. Those were the reasons which had induced committee of that club to try the experiment of a disc°,,- sion class, feeling that by thoroughly ventilating those ail" kindred subjects it would benefit Liberalism in that divi‘ sion, besides helping to educate their members and improve their mental capacity. Ile observed that great cbanhee were necessary in the near future, and Ibis nation was n''t Progressing as fast as it shoula do, while other nations we'e heating us in our own markets, and it occurred to him there must be some remedy for the present state of affairs. Shu'e said the remedy was protection, but others said the reforin of the land laws would remedy the state of affairs. He clined towards the latter view; and in regard to the In.. question he said, in trusting the Tory party, the Irish p 4" pie were leaning upon a broken reed, as thNt party ave.'ree opposed to the Irish Land Act, and every measure of jusale` toe Lahore] party had conceded to Ireland. On the otbe hand, they could not expect to get a satisfactory solution the difficulty from the Liberal party after the manner which they had treated the Liberal party, and he believe' another appeal to the country would have to be made her.° it could be settled. With reference to the electoral Op: paign in this division, he thought they they had great COO' for self-congratulation in the moral victory they had and when they found their candidate running SUC:II minent politician as Sir Richard Cross, a Cabitet Ministe't so close a race, notwithstanding the influence of the l 0 11 gentry. He believed had the outlying districts been bette worked, had the orgalisatiOn of the party been more CO plete, the tables would have been turned and the seat $9.°P i: Knowing that it behoved everyone to be up and doin preparing for the coming fight, and as no dier could fight without weapons, neither cow, they argue or discuss without arguments. He there. fore appealed to them to make that infant discin aion class a success, and then if a Parliamentary Delliti`34 Society was afterwards formed they would have the ophar:i Utility of showipg their rivals the errors of their ways leading them to the right track ; bringing them froin taa dark, winding and antiquated path of 'Toryism to the Wahl_ and light turnpike road of Liberalism, and to follow in the footsteps of Gladstone, Cobden, Bright, and Sarauel Fl soil, the friends of suffering humanity, whose lives been spent spent in trying to benefit the nation by their bro.'hl and comprehensive legislation. Their duty -as Liberan clearly was to unite and work as one map for their cans" to organise and embrace every opportunity of spreadithl abroad the advantages of their creed, to study and make themselves masters of the questions of the day a'lhour, and when they bad grasped them to diffuse their knowledgbea among their less fortunate brethren. As a club, be thong they should make a greater effort to mutually iniPove thenaselves. (Applause.) The Chairman thought the warm applause showed tbe. paper had been appreciated, and asked for the criticising °I, the persons present—Mr. F. Willis asked for more info' mation in regard to foreign countries outrivalling this nart°; try in trade or workmanship.—After a few remarks fro- Mr. J. Clarke, Mr. W. McEvoy said be agreed with aorlIa: observations by Mr. Morris but disagreed with others. thought Lord Salisbury was compelled to carry out 0: negociations with Russia as honourably as they possibl, could. Lord Salisbury had a delicate and difficult questierf to contend with, and there were thousands lives at stake. As far as the trade of the CO, try was concerned, he thought they were able compete with any country in the world. He thought t"ei fault lay with the capitalists, who would not speculate, ar, that caused the great depression which existed.—Mr. disagreed with the remarks of Mr. Morris with regard t° the Irish question. He did not believe it was a Libera' spirit to say that the Irish could expect nothing W.)! the Liberals ft r what they did at the last election. Thbei', should not b,ar any malice. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. P. thought the first duty of Liberals was to consider their in its broadest sense, and then do what they could for taa party wherever they were situated. Liberals should nOt Liberals in name only, but in reality. They should preet., their Liberalism and support their party throngb local institunons. Mr. J. Clarke rehreth, some of the older members were ran present to give tb:', discussion on their duties an impetas. He commented uP!,j appointments to office, and in speaking of bad trade Oh they all hoped things would be better during the prese°o year than during the last year. There was no doubt a gree deal would depend on the people themselves whether it better or not.—The Chairman, in a lucid summing up of t'h paper and discussion, said political duty was to do the be! they could for their country and for themselves, and abe,e'l3; all for the good'and well-being of the British empire. aro country in which they lived demanded certain duties, 3 if they failed to do them they sinned against that countre", As politicians they must arise above party. Party was merel:.c, convenient instrument by which they gained ends. They We,' e Liberals, not because Liberalism was infallible, but beCeth. Liberalism combined within itself and its creed and of faith more in accordance with their beliefs and vie„h than Conservatism did. But political duties soared big 73, than that, and he hoped they would not go away with t idea that their chiefest duty lies in belonging to Liberalie as a party, but rather to do the best they could for the of the country. (Applause.) Mr. Morris then replied at some length, and he wag eft:f wards accorded a hearty vote of thanks on the motion ,e Mr. Jarrett, seconded by Mr. J. Rutter. On account of the severe frost last w-e-e-a, all the principal clubs in both Lancashire and Yorkshire cancelled their engagements.

Contrary to expectation, the match between Scotland and Wales was played on the ground of the Cardiff Club, every precaution having been taken to protect the ground against the frost. Wales did not show up as well as was expected, and was defeated by two goals, one try, and three minors to one minor.
