div.head: WIT AND HUMOUR.
div.p: WIT AND HUMOUR.

A witty critic, on hearing that a lawyer had composed a poem on "My Conscience," remarked, "It ought to sell well. The public are fond of novelties!" A wit says the times are so dull that it is difficult for him even to collect his ideas. Perhaps this is the man, said to be so lazy that he has worked but once, and that was when he was labouring under a mistake. "Jones died last night," remarked Smith to Brown. "Ah !" exclaimed Brown. "you surprise me. What's the complaint ?" "There is no complaint," responded Smith; everybody seems to be satisfied." UTAH-WARD.--" It has been revealed to us, mister," said the spouses of a Mormon elder to Artemus Ward, as he was standieg outside his show in Utah, 'that we can go in without paying." "You have read the revelation upside down," came the: ardent.; "you can pay without going in." A great writer says "A man ought to carry a pencil and note down the thoughts of the moment." "Yes," remarked a Yankee editor; "and one short pencil devoted maclasively to that use would last some men we know about two thou- sand years, and then have the original point on:" CORRECT.—" Don't you think," said Mrs. Keener, "that when Adani realised the vastness of the world into which he had been ushertd that he zaust have had a great deal on his mind ?" "Well," responded Mrs. Blunt, "from the photo- graphs I have seen of him I should say that what ever 'he did have on must have been on his mind." A HARD FACT.—" Just as BOOM as a man dies," remarked Brown, "everybody has something to say in derogation of his character." "Yes," replied Fogg; "and it makes you sad to think that the truth will be told about you one of these days, and you won't be present to hear it. It is rather hard, that's a fact." Encriesteerricat ham—Teacher : "What are the names of the seven days of the week ?"—Bey: " Monday, Tues- day, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturcay."—Teacher : "That's only six days. You have missed one. When does your mother go to church ?"—Boy: "When pa buys her a new hat." THE MODEIRN STLOR.—" SO you are -studying /or the stage, my dear?" "Oh, yes; I have been studying for several months." "I suppose it is very hard work ?" "Indeed it is. You have no idea how tiresome it is to sit around a dressmaker's all day long, having one new costume fitted on after another." JONRS'E MISTARE.—Mrs. Smithson (who 'flatters herself upon her youthful appearance): "That young lady over there is my daughter, Mr. Jones; would you believe it ?" Jones (lookieg in the wrong direction): " Your. daughter Is it possible? I should have guessed she was 'your! sister."—llre. Smithson: "Not the lady you are looking at, Mr. Jones: she is my mother."—Jones: "Oh !" At toe breaking out of the Crimean War, Rachel, the celebrated French actress, was in St. Petersburg. Just be- fore leaving the Russian capital, some of the Russian offi- cers gave a banquet in her honour. One of them, a noble- man of high rank, said to Rachel, in a bantering way. "We will not bid you goodbye, but merely say, Au r emir,' for we shall soon be in Paris to drink your health in Cliquot or Pommery." Monsieur," replied Rachel, "Trance is not rich enough to treat all her prisoners of war to champagne." Here's a hint for eating-houees--evidentiv there is some- thing to be learned from the Yankees. "1 beg your pardon, sir," respectfully observed a waiter in a New York restau- rant to a.gentleman who was laboriously sawing a tough piece of beef-steak with a dull knife; "but you have the wrong knife." "Eh ?" "Yes, sir," continued the waiter, as he handed him another knife, with an edge :that was al- most as keen as a razor's. "You ;have thatender loin knife. You see," went on the servitor, " most.people judge meats by the way they cut. When steak cuts easily, they say it's tender, so we keep a set of knives herelor each kind of meat. When a man orders fillet of beef we give him a dull knife.; when he orders sirloin, we give him one a little sharper; and, when he calls for round, we give him a razor- blade. We keep the sharpest knives for the toughest meat. In -this way we save lots of grumbling and please . every ore." We have before now heard of the dog that pointed a pike because the fish had swallowed a bird, and he was not a had dog; bet he was not of much account in comparison with the intelligent beast the story of which is published in the Paterson Press--US.A., of course !—" Sheriff McKee says that the intelligence or the nose of the dog referred to in yesterday's Press"—that is, the pike story—" does not amount to anything compared to the nose of a dog a friend of his owned. He thinks that any dog with a balf-wav decent nose otight,to be able to smell out a 'flock of wood-- cock, even if the birds are concealed in the stomach of a pickerel. The sheriff says he had a friend who had a won- derful dog for 'coons. If there was a 'coon within a mile of the dog, the 'aeon's doom was sealed, for the dog would cer- tainly smell him eut. One day the dog ergs out with his master after 'coons. They stopped at a small railway. station just as thatrain drew up. The dog came to a dead point on the train. The owner of the dog insisted that there mutt be a 'coon on beard the train, or that the train had run over a 'coon. His dog could not be mistaken. The train was searched.; but there was no 'coon. and no gore on the wheels. The man's faith in the dog did not waver for an instant Are yeti sure that there is no 'coon on board this train? 'he inquired of the bra.kesman. am sure there is not. The nearest thing to a 'coon is the conduotor, and his name is Coos.' 'That settles it! ' said the owner of the dog. I knew there was 'coon on this train some- where !' "

div.head: HE GAVE HIMSELF AWAY.
div.p: HE GAVE HIMSELF AWAY.

John Dolittle and Peter Indolence, two old cronies whose acquaintance and partnership in family secrets dated back almost to the landing of the Pilgrim Fathers, were .enjoying themselves immenEely while seated in front of Dolittle's cosy residence last Sunday afternoon, and the chief topic of converse ion was the ingenious manner in which they had pulled the wool over their wives' eyes during their declining years. "When I was younger," remarked:John, in a tone loud enough to be heard several 'rods away, for be it known, Mr. Indolence is somewhat deaf, •" I used to get op with the irk cock crew, light the fire and have the breakfast all ready for Mary when she had thrown off Morpheus and otirred herself downstairs. But as the years began to tell en me, and my limbs became just a little bit stiff, I learned:4 trick worth two of that." " You don't say ?" interrogatively chimegin his-com- panion. "Don't you light the fire no more "so sirre !"

"Hircla -servant girl, eh ?" "Not muchl You catch me spending my hard-earned money OR any fair daughter of Hibernia while VVO got an able-bodied wife in the house. That may be all very well for a bank treasurer or a millionaire, but I don't deal out of that pack; not this lend anyhow !" "You don't mean to tell me that Mrs. Dolittle does it herself, do you?" "Well, that's about the size ef it, Indolence, and she seems to get fat on it."

, "No !"- But I say yes—and mean it, tee. Why, old boy, I Laven't kindled a fire since Garfield was shot, and what's more, I have no intention of doing so either, on this aide of the Jordan. What I may have to do afterwards remains for the future or his satanic majesty to. reveal, but at present I draw the line at fire." But hew de you manage it? Hard work, eh ?" "No, not very after you got the thing going. You see in my extended matrimonial acquaintaace with my wife I came to the conclusion that she had a sort of a sneaking regsrd for the old fellow, and when eke thought I was the least bit sick would lo all in her power to alleviate my suffering. I realised this one cold winter's morning when I was tired and sleepy from having a night's lark, and so hit upon the idea of playing possum. So says Ito Mary when she' rive me her customary wakening punch in the ribs, Oh, wife dear, I feel awful sick this morning, and hardly able to.get up.' " What's the matter,ffohn ?' says she. "'I don't know, Mary, but my head aches, and I'm n.s cold as if someone had poured a dipper of ice water (loofa my back.' Well, lay in bed a little longer, John. I'll get up and make the tchildren's breakfast, and I'll br:ng you a sup of nice warm tea, it'll make you feel better.' "She seemed quite serious, too, and, cf. coarse, I felt pretty cheat. when I saw her ,putting on her stockings in a room where .the thermometer rregistered six be:ow. But I'd gone too far, and so let her go Well, old boy, that cup of good, strong tea went so fine that morning that I felt like having another on the morrow, and consequently, worked the same dodge with such success that I decided to keep the thing up, and I've been doing it ever since. Quite a bright idea, isn't it?" "No, it isn't, John Dalittle 7" yelled an angry woman's voice from a window overhead, " and now, you old hypo- onto, you are found out. 1 Mr. Dolittle had never dreamed that his wife wan .playing eavesdropper. He gets up with cock crow now, as e:n days of yore, and his friend has decided to profit by Ms expe- rience and hire a servant girl when the mornings ecome I unpleasantly chilly. I Fact.—Fall River ddvance.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER
LONDON, THURSDAY.

Considering that we are uponthe eve of a moment- ous political crisis, affairs in the House of Commons have gone forward through the week with strange quietude. The House met on Tuesday, and went through the ceremony of re-electing the Speaker. There was an enormous crowd, new members press- ing forward with great eagerness and as resolute not to lose anything of the spectacle,as if they were children at the pantomime. It is curious to note the air with which old members regard the new. They are inclined, in conversation with each other, to turn up their noses at the new comers. At the same time they take a great delight in patronising -them and showing them over the building. There are certainly some curious-looking men amongst them marking the new departure. In the Parlia- ment of 1874, there was only one low-crowned soft :felt hat, and that belonged to Mr. Joseph Cowen. In the last Parliament came .Mr. Lalor, who not only wore a low-crowned hat, but selected one white in colour, which added prominence to the innovation. Mr. Broadhurst, it is true, has a low-crowned hat, but he so far conforms to the usages of Parliament that he never brings it into the House. Immedi- ately upon arrival, he secretesfit in his loeker, and brings forth a respectable tall hat, in which he may be seen walking about the lobbies or seated in the House. When he is observed crossing the lobby with his billycock on it is a sure and certain sign that he is going home. The new members have brought several billycocks and soft felt hats with them, and Mr. Arch appears in a tweed suit, which quite puts in the shade Mr. Parnell s famous yellow ochre suit, which he is said to lend to Mr. T. P. O'Connor when not wearing it himself. Mr. Gladstone came down with thereat on Tues- day, and made the only decent speech in connection with the ceremony of. the election of Speaker. Sir John Mowbray is an elderly gentleman, who fitly represents a University. There is an antique flavour about him which, it is feared, will shortly altogether disappear from the House. He delivered an ornate oration of the old school type, to which the new =embers listened respectfully. Mr. Bright's ap- pearance was the signal for what the' French re- porters call a mouvement. But his speech fell very flat. There was, indeed, scarcely any occasion to rise to. It was a mere ceremonial without the exhilarating promise of a fight. It would have been very dif- ferent had the original intention of the Conserva- tives been carried out, and the re-election of Mr. Peel opposed.- Then Mr. Bright might have been expected to flame forth. As it was, he said a few words and sat down: On these occasions Mr. Glad- stone shows his great supremacy-. He can talk on all themes, in all moods.with or without provocation. He had special cause to be gratified by the occasion. Mr. Arthur Peel was his personal selection for the office of Speaker, a nomination the success of which -was much doubted at the time, Mr. Peel then little known, being regarded as rather a dull man, a foil to his brilliant 'and eccentric brother, Sir Robert. Mr. Peel has turned out the best Speaker since Mr. Shaw-Lefevre, and in congratulating him on his re- -election Mr. Gladstone had good reason to congratu- late himself: What he had to say in the congratu- latory vein he uttered with his usual felicity of speech, and thereafter dropped into one of those charming garrulous moods in which he discussed times of long ago amid the breathless attention of the new members. Mr: Bradlaugh was looked to, to supply some sensation at the opening of the session. This has been his pleasing duty every year since 1880. He has come forward as regularly as the Queen'sl Speech, and has been disposed of much more sum- marily. He was in his place as usual on Tuesday, though not now content to remain in the obscurity of the Gallery. He brought in his hat and deposited it on one of the benches like an ordinary member, and thereafter walked about and took his full share of the greetings that were going round.. Of course, nothing came of him on Tuesday, the business be- ing strictly confined to the election of the Speaker. But on Wednesday when the swearing-in commenced " the Bradlaugh difficulty" simultaneously ,presen- ted itself, and was happily disposed of. The Cabinet, among the cares that beset them have-had time to think of Mr. Bradlaugh and had prepared a little scheme for his discomfiture. First they were to call upon the Speaker to take note of the resolu- tions of the late Parliament and forbid Mr. Brad- laugh to take the oath. Failing that, Sir M. H. Beach was ready with .a new resolution to be sub- mitted as soon as a quorum was formed and before Mr. Bradlaugh could race up to th.; table and take the oath. But the inflexible Speaker stopped this little game. He ruled in accordance with the most obvious and elementary principles of justice and constitutional law that a resolution passed by the last Parliament was not binding upon the present. He might, if he had pleased, have gone further and shown how even a sessional order does not carry its jurisdiction into the next session • of the same Parliament. That being the case there was no power on earth to prevent Mr. Bradlaugh taking the 'oath with the rest of members, and he did it amid a quietude and general disregard, strik- ing by contrast with the fierce scenes that used to upheave the House in former times. This absence of excitement is indicative of what will follow. It was Lord Randolph Churchill and the then inchoate Fourth Party who made the future of Mr. Brad- laugh and., it must be added, their own. They ele- Yatea a not very desirable person 'into the position of a martyr. Mr. Bradlaugh became, as Wilks had been, the symbol of civil and religious liberty. For this, not for Mr. Bradlaugh, Liberals have stoutly fought, and now gratefully relegate Mr. Bradlaugh to obscurity. The tug of war begins next Thursday, when the queen will once more show her favour for a Conser- vative Ministry by opening Parliament in person. Much uncertainty exists as to the intentions of leaders and the issue of the fight. It is the old .story over again :

Lord ChathAm with his !word drawn Stood wsiiting for Sir Richard Strachan; Sir Riebqrd, lunginv to be at 'em, Steed waiting for the Earl of Cbatham. Only in this case the duel is triangular, like the famous one recorded in Midshipman Easy. Mr. Parnell takes part in it, and the three combatants stand watching each other waiting for the first move. Of necessity the Government must first take action. However carefully done, the Queen's Speech cannot fail to afford indication -more or less clear of the intentions of the Government with respect to Ireland. It is, I have the best reason to know, quite true that Lord• Salisbury has broken with the allies who helped him to turn out: Mr. Gladstone and reduce his majority at the General Election. After a long struggle, in which Lord Randolph Churchill fought for a bolder policy, it was resolved to give. up all attempts to satisfy the Parnellites. The#Qu'e ens Speech will announce the preparation of a bill dealing with local government in England, and will promise the later introduction of a simi- lar one for Ireland. That, of course, will not suit Mr. Parnell, and the only question now is whether the final and fateful battle will take place upon the Address, or whether it will be delayed till the Irish Bill is actually before the House. In either case it is equally certain that the Government will have to go, and then comes the question of resignation or dissolution. It is happily some time since we heard of any , attack upon the life of the Emperor of Russia. But a friend who has just returned from St. Petersburg tells me that none of the precautionary' measures are relaxed. When recently the Emperor and lm- press went to Kremsier elaborate preparation were made and a splendid suite of state apartments pre- pared for their occupation. But when bed-time -came the mighty Czar and his Empress, making a feint to enter their gorgeous rooms, turned aside and slunk away to. a modest spare room adjoining that of the Grand Duke George. Even now when at home they adopt the practice of frequently chang- ing their bedroom so that none of their personal attendants can say with certainty where they are sleeping. This is a kind of Imperial thimble-rigging which it is pitiful to hear of. A man earning thirty shillings a week who can peacefully go to bed without making a myst6ry of his apartment, or lying awake in apprehension of assassination, is surely a happier person than the Czar of all the .i.ussia.s. We have a travesty of this kind of thing in, England, where, when the Queen travels from North to South, all the railway stations are swept clear of the public, and her Majesty travels through the ranks of her loyal subjects as if they were in- fected with cholera. Something of this, I am sorry to say, will take place next Thursday when the Queen opens Parliament. These are proceedings as useless as they are ill-advised. But it is a differentthing with the unhappy Czar, who has more than once felt the breath of a would-be assassin hot upon his cheek. Princess Beatrice and her husband are about to pay a visit to Sandringham. It is understood that the invitation was procured by the direct interven- tion of the queen, the Prince .of Wales not having shown any absolutely overmastering desire for his new brother-in-law's company. But her Majesty

will not have anything of that kind going on, and ' so Prince Henry of Battenberg will be the guest of the Prince of Wales. Her Majesty, who has taken the Prince - under liar very special protection and cares for him with even embarrassmg solicitude, has not only artanged the visit, but it is said, super- vised the list of guests. It is on the whole likely to be a very cheerful house party. When Her Majesty opens Parliament, we shall probably have an opportunity, not Only of seeing I our Sovereign, but also of inspecting the hand- somest frock coat which the nation, as a nation, t ossesses. Lord Wolseley's administration has ratherreduced the brilliancy of the British soldier's dress. Tommy Atkins in grey or green, or blotting paper, has become less likely to be shot by an enemy with a good aim and vindictive nature. • Life insurance companies would deal with him op easier terms. But the bandsmen of our Household , Cavalry retain their unrivalled splendour of cos- tume. Instead of sendinWpatients to the great French expert, she has sent a doctor. • He arrived in Paris this week . arid studied the subject well'4 heard what M. If we can't afford to send a doctor to Paris, we might at least invite this Hun- garian to London, and as, since the dogs have, sheen ordered to be muzzled, the papers are full of cases of ' people being bitten. there would be no difficulty in finding a subject jot'. experiment. The police seem just now to run the greatest risk, and apparently to run them with impunity.

THE LIBERAL PARTY. Mr. Gladstone was visited,on Thursday by Lord Granville and the Marquis of Ripon, who remained in consultation with him for some time. Other members of the late Ministry are expected to visit the right hon. gentleman daring the day. The annual meeting of the Lancashire auxiliary of the Congregational Church Aid Society was held in Manches- ter on Wednesday evening, under the chairmanship of Mr. Henry Lee. The Rev. Dr. Macfadyen, Rev. Dr. Hannay, and the Rev. A. Mearns were amongst those who addressed he meeting. CONVOCATION for the province of Canterbury opened on Wednesday in St. Paul's Cathedral. The Latin sermon was preached by the Dean of Westminster, and the Archbishop age! wards held his Court in the Lady Chapel. In the Lower House Archdeacon Sumner was elected Prolocutor in sticresaion to Lord Alwyne Compton. Both Houses were prorogued to February 16. A SEntous POACHING CASE has Ipen tried at Maidstone Assizes before Mr.-Justice Stephen. At midnight on November 20 a number of poachers were surprised by keepers on the estate of C.olonel James, and on.) of the Poachers, named Je.saup, fired a gun and shot one of the keepers in the leg, and then all the men decamped. Jessup was sentenced to seven years' penal servitude, and two of his companions, named 'Jerry and Banco were each sentenced to 13 months' imprisonment with hArd labour.

div.head: 'TAKING TIME BY-THE FORELOCK."
div.p: 'TAKING TIME BY-THE FORELOCK."

Sir,---EvArvone naturally feels. apprehensive as to what may be the outcome of a Parliament which has been elected and which. meets -under -Tory auspices. .The unforttmate record of the last Tory Parliament makes this feeling in- evitable. It is, therefore, the plain duty of everybody who has any claim to patriotism to do all he can to ward off or to mitigate the evils which are—only too likely to happen: I am glad that this seems to be the opinion of those who regulate the services at Christ' Church, Latchford. Under ordinary circumstances it is, of course, not advisable to depart from the directions of the rubric to pray for the, High Const of. Parliament "at this time as- sembled," but when the leaders of Parliament are found in the Tory ranks, I think. the- innovation of praying for it before it has assembled which has been made at Christ Church is a judicious one, and shows forethought. The example might well have been followed by all who believe that prayer is efficacious In preventing those who seem naturally addicted to error from erring.—l am, sir, PATRIOT.

div.head: PEACE SOCIETY.
div.p: THE PEACE SOCIETY.

Sir,— I was much gratified in reading Mr. Ratbbone's able letter in vindication of this society from the attack made upon it by "Hodge." lam inclined to think that in- dividual will, after such a sound castigation as he has re:. ceiyed from Mr. Rathbone, be disposed to reflect a little before venturing on the time grounds again. For my own part I fail to see how a man can be found that possesses a Spark of humanity, much less Chritianity, about him, who is capable of denouncing the aims of such a society as the Peace Society, the object of which is one of the first tenets in oar Christian faith. We all are well aware that under the existing order of European government, it is impossible for us to carry its principles out to the full extent; but we can tiractice its teachings so far as the present-state Of things will allow. I trust that the time will arrive—it Must If we believe in our Christianity—when the principles 4, this society will ramify and be the guiding law of all civi- lized nations. Then Europe will Rot as now be.burthened by having to keep countless legions of armed men ready at Cue bidding of.one or two imdividuals to destroy each other In hundreds of thousands. Arbitration should be allowed to settle a dispute between nations as well as between mas- ter and man. We know that diplomacy is professedly in. tended to serve this end, but it, I think, has oftener prayed. a convenient and polite way of picking a quarrel than of preventing one.—Yours, &c., PLEBEIAN: Kingsley, Cheshire, Jan. 13th, 1886.

div.head: "TREAT TO AGED PEOPLE AT STOCKTON HEATH."
div.p: "TREAT TO AGED PEOPLE AT STOCKTON HEATH."

Sir,-1 observe in your issue of Saturday last a report with the above heading, and whilst being highly pleased with the acts of philanthropy and the charity of Christian ladies and gentlemen in and around our village in consider- ing the wants and enjoyments of the aged anti infirm, I could not help thinking that the account was very mis- leading. It seems to have been written by one who was ignorant of the real facts of the case, and anyone reading it would naturally come to the conclusion that it was a very one-sided affair. In the first place it is said to be given in connection with the Cottage Mission. Now, it so happens that we in Stockton Heath are favoured with about three kinds of cottage mission meetings, one of these being so select that no one but communicants at St. Thomas's Church are allowed to take part therein, though it is well known that the Vicar himself does not favour or support them with his presence and ability. These meetings are but very scantily attended—chiefly by a few aged men and women who frequently receive doles from the charities of St. Thomas's. Another series of cottage mission services is being held in the village by or in connection with the Wesleyan Methodists, and supported by other Christian workers, and very good meetings are the result betimes. The third, and what appears to be the most successful series of cottage mission meetings, have been held for about three years, and are known as the Stockton Heath Unsectarian Mission Services. These are the oldest mission services now being held in the village they are largely attended and supported by Christian workers of all denominations, and there is no doubt but that they have been the means of doing a great amount of good to the numbers who have at- tended them. . Now, sir, the treat was given, but in connection with which of the cottage missions? Certainly not the last which might rightly claim the preference, for the treat was provided by public subscriptions and was given, says the re- port, to members of all denominations. The first and second treat given here on a New Year's Day to the aged, was pro- vided by Christian workers in the Unsectarian Cottage Mis- sion, and would no doubt be given yet, but for an unchris- tian act of strategy which wrested it out of their hands de- signedly. by arranging to give a treat to the aged and infirm .on just the same day and the same time as had been arran- ged by the noble-hearted nnsectariau Christian workers. Certainly not by the Wesleyan friends, for they seem to know nothing about it. Neither bad any tickets been given to them or to the above Unsectarian Christian workers to distribute amongst any who might come under their obser- vation as recipients. Nor can I think it was given by those who call themselves St.lhomas's Cottage Mission, and who are so select that they could not think of meeting members of all denominations, and at a treat that bad been got up by public subscriptions, though 1 observe from the pro- gramme of the after meeting that not one member of any other denomination save those who attend St. Thomas's was allowed or even asked to take part. There were, however, several there whose voices or advice would have been most heartily received by the recipients of the treat, and done honour to the denominations they were connected with, and been more seasonable and profitable to the aged who are fast passing away from our midst than some items of the programme which were rendered.—Yours, &c., ALERT.. Stockton Heath, Jan. 14th, 1886.

"J. G. R." takes it upon' himself to remind the town authorities of an unperformed duty, and mentioned Inspec- tor Norman's name. We are ready to give that gentleman credit for possessing more common sense than permitting himself to become the servant only of the namby-pamby portion of the community. I have visited most of the rciddle-sized and larger towns in England and Scotland,and find that these potato-roasting machines abound everywhere, and in no single instance have I heard them spoken of as a nuisance; nor have I known of any attempt to put them down. Besides, so long as the chipped potato man is not acting illegally, so long as he plies his business and seeks to earn an honest living without offending against decency and order, without obstruction and without inconvenience to the public, he ought not to be swept from our streets to please the whim of some fine dainty gentleman, no matter who he may be.—Yours truly:" POLE OAT.

div.head: "A. STREET NUISANCE.'
div.p: "A. STREET NUISANCE.'

Sir,—in your last week's issue appears a letter headed "A street nuisance," signed "J. G. R."—apparently some meddling busybody, who is ashamed of his letter, or why not sign his name? so that the following information could be forwarded to him :—First, that for several months pre- vious to Christmas Inspector Norman has had every oppor- tunity to inspect, or obtain, a "sniff," without his holi- days (?) being curtailed at the wish of "J. G. It ;" secondly, that those "chipped potato vendors" have to pay a toll of 2s 6d Der week, or £6 lOs per annum, to Inspector Place, or his assistant, for the privilege of supplying4the wants of the panel • In answer to "J. G. R" I would simply remind him that Inspector Normaa has hitherto been able to perform his onerous duties to the expressed satisfaction of the Borough Council and ratepayers. and long may he continue to de so, without any gratuitous interference. If" G. B." has no dictionary, it would repay him to visit the Library in Bold-street and obtain the use of one, to enable him to write plain English, without misapplying those " crackjaws." Who ever heard of a " peripatetic chipped potato box " till his letter appeared ? I rather think he is a peripatetic masher" (vide Webster), or, like all other sensible people, he would enjoy the happiness of the cbildren when they have obtained a " hap'orth or pen'erth all hot," and not brand the cause of their pleasure a " nuisance," to the injury of yours. &c., JOHN PLINSTON. 53, Allen-street, Warrington, Jan. 140, 1886.

Sir,—Most sincerely do I pity your correspondent. with initials" J. G. R.," who rushes into print publicly to pro- claim that his olfactory nerves suffer dreadfully from sniff- ing the odours of a roasted potatoe. How refined must he his tastes, and how exalted his motives thus to invoke the power of the press to protect himself and others from the vulgar contaminations of every day life. His fellow-towns- men would, I am sure, be glad to know more of such an individual, who would appear to move in a lofty untainted sphere seldom reached by ordinary mortals. Sorry / cannot 'oblige them. But one cannot help indulging in a few sur- mises, guided by his pure, vigorous, and righteously indig- nant communication on the humble topic of chipped pota- toes. A man with such a delicate organism and highly strung nerves is completely out of place in Warrington addicted to such common-place pursuits as the manufacture of leather, chemicals, soap, and candles. So exquisitively eensitivs a plant is but ill adapted to breathe the vitiated atmosphere of our manufacturing towns. He should baste away to the neighbourhood of Shap, or apply for an appoint- ment with the next expedition to the North Pole. Fhat "J. G. R." is young and untravelled is probable, or his effusion would never have come to light. His education has not been neglected, otherwise he could not have com- pressed so large an amount of pedantic language into the short space of a baker's dozen of lines. That he is a keen observer is abundantly evident, as many stupid ordinary people pass these potato caravans, without once noticing the existence of the offensive exhalations complained of. At again I read his lines and between them and ponder them carefully the conviction forces itself upon me that he is fond of places of amusement and in the habit of keeping late houra or he would not be so frequently in close Proximity to the affecting whiffs of the perambulating Potato roasters as to cause them to disturb his equilibrium. Should this meet the eye of his anxious mother, she would act prudently by calling in the latch-key and slightly abridging her pretty son's liberty'.

div.head: MEASURES BEFORE MEN.
div.p: MEASURES BEFORE MEN.

Sir,—lf it he Mr. Rathbone's purpose ,to prove that the Peace society metes out Equal treatment to Tories and Liberals when they engage in war he has undertaken a hopeless task. Though be may rise to the heights or sink to the depths of Gladstonian sophistry, he will be utterly unable to convince those who have taken an interest in politics during the last few years that their own experience has entirely misled them. Everyone knows that for a con- siderable time before the general election of 1880 almost every city, town, and hamlet in the kingdom was invaded by the passionate pilgrims of the Peace Society, who de- nounced in unmeasured terms the evils of the warlike policy of the Tories. Since the Liberals went into power there have been wars, hut where have been our righteous denunciators of bloodshed and slaughter ? Have they made every platform ring as when their friends the Liberals were in opposition? Nobody can answer such a question in the affirmative. Mr. Rathbone maintains that mnrnbers of the Peace Society have protested against Liberal wars. They have; but they have protested as feebly and as rarely as the barest decency and the beggarliest rag of con- sistency would llow of. If they were sincere and con- scientious in all they said of war and makers of war when the Tories were in office, honest adherence to principle de- manded infini!elv more then has been said and done when Liberals were the war.mekers.

My main contention was that Mr. Rathbone in his previ- ous letter manifested that party spirit and narrow intoler? ant prejudice which have brought so many admirable schemes into contempt is this country. He has again gone Out of his way to afford evidence of this as "strong as proofs of holy writ." Whilst posing as the advocate of a principle which is above party and sectarian consider- ations, he takes occasion to drag from obscurity a calumny on L.rd Salisbury which, after hav- ing done most harm to the inventors of it, had been discarded by all judicious and prudent partisans. There is not another of our leading statesmen, except perhaps, Mr. Chamberlain, against whom a charge of "prevaricating utterance" could less easily be sustained than against Lord Salisbury. None of them have more effectually laid to heart Dr. Johnson's advice" to clear the mind of cant," and none are less under the influence of fantastic misleading senti- ment. What is the enigin of this one of the most odious charges that even political animosity ever fabri- cated ? If I am not mistaken it is entirely based upon the answer Lord Salisbury gave to an ill-timed query as to. whether what purported to be the terms of a convention be- tween England and Turkey, published in a newspaper, were accurate or not. Lord Salisbury replied that the document was not "authentic," and because it turned out to be sub- stantially correct this answer was fixed upon as an unparal- leled example of public mendacity. Yet Lord Salisbury's answer was verbally and absolutely true. The document was not an " authentic " but a surreptitious one, clandes- tinely pilfered from a State office. Teis is the foundation upon which Mr. Eathbone, who prides himself upon being "in good company," is content to base one of the most dis- honourable of imputations. If it be not party spirit which animates Mr. Rathbone, but a noble zeal for public morality, why does he never look at the other side for acts of official shortcoming ? Why, to give only one instance, does he never think of the Errington mission to Rome and of the miserable comedy of evasion, subterfuge, and equivoque consequent thereon in the House of Commons, in which Gladstone, the im- maculat-, was the principal performer ? In the case of Lord Salisbury national and perhaps world-wide issue!! de- pended on his answer, but in that of the Errington mission the issues were so trivial that they could be of no concern to any but a man who is really more of an ecclvsiast of the controversial hair-splitting type than a stateeman.—Yours, &c., HODGE.

div.head: BOOKS AND READING.
div.p: BOOKS AND READING.

Sir,—lt may not be amiss to say a few words to your readers respecting a subject that more than any other is fitted to convey a boundless satisfaction. It has been to the present writer a great pleasure to note the good attendance which the reading-rosin of the War- rington Public Library secures to itself, and if 'the Institu- tion can, as early as possible, be declared free a source of pleasure and knowledge will be placed before the public which it would be difficult to value. Of the history of books, or as Bacon so finely calls them "Ships of thought," it is not necessary here to speak ; it is rather as looking to them as conveying " results of life- times of patient thought " that I wish to draw your readers' attention. When Erasmus pointed to the treasured volumes which furnished his solitary cell, he was claiming to pos- sess "such great and goodly company" as few in his day and generation could boast the possession of. How differ- ent to-day! . For myself I rarely think ef books or reading without connecting with them the great benefit that was conferred upon Englishmen by the removal of all, restraints on the acquirement of knowledge. It was not enough to remove the burdensome taxes that lay upon the manufacture of paper or upon its distribution in the shape of books and newspapers; it was required that facilities should be provided whereby the people should learn their 'ABC,' and as be able to reap the full benefits likely to accrue from the removal by Mr. Gladstone in 1861 of the last remnant of the paper duty. Fifty years ago it must have been but the few arid the favoured who could possess a book and read it. To-day the Education Code is fast making the man who carnot read an object of pity. There are those. lam aware, who think that we may ererdo, and make the imparting of book lore a source of evil instead of good. lam not of these; I am convinced that we have less to fear from the educated than from the "uneducated devil.'' Therefore, I hail the day when with one voice the people will cry out for a Free School and a Free Literature, coupled with a uniform and , equalized taxation for support of the same. What may we expect will be the course taken by the peo- ple during the next few years in politics ? It would be difficult to give an answer to such a question; in fact. ire- possible; but we can do this—we can, by placing facilities for good reading before the people, educate them so that England obeli benefit and not lose by the extension of the suffrage. My intention in writing this is to point out that it is only by reading, and perhaps I ought to say the listening to lectures, that a man can honestly do his duty in the polling booth. What have we to guide no in the future? Is it not the history of the past ? We may be sneered at as " theoriete " on tl,e question of Free Trade, but when we take up our histories and look what social life was fifty years ago, we are satisfied that our "theories " are and must be the prac- tical part of English life in the future. In the biographies of Peel, Cobden, Palmersten, and Disraeli we have ample evidence that it would be unwise to make any attempt to turn the finger of time back. Books so varied in character are issued now that there is no valid reason at all why every working-man should not be thorooghly well versed in the departmental history of his country, arid by this means be enabled to judge every question that comes before hi.n from every point of van- tage.. . It unfortunately happens that while these splendid op- portunities are being placed before workmen, that another class, and that a most important one, the money-making and eapitalist class, is fast losing both time and taste for study. ' and we are, if not careful, likely to be at the mercy of those who are empirical in all hut money making. We have evi- dence of this one-sidedness of vision in our own town, a paper, to which Ido not care to ascribe any evil motive, weekly fritters its strength away by constantly charging. Quixote-like, the whirling sails of Free Trade. Had the editor of this paper time te read the speeches made by his own political leaders be would see how useless it was. Had he time to read the speeches made by experienced states- men be would see how criminal is his conduct. Had he time to read the report of the Education Commission be would not sneer at Technical Education; and above all, if he wenld find time to study the land laws of England, Ger- many, and Belgium he would at once know the panacea for all our bad trade, and Cease to support a man who will • eoneistently vote against redressing any evil, the re- moval of which would benefit the British working-man. A friend of mine has a saying that contains a lot of truth —" It you don't read you'll be roloe'd." The reverse of this must be—lf you read you can protect yourselves. There are few books printed but what contain some good., but it is not always necessary or desirable that we should. be hunting up "useful information." Books minister in a most wonderful fashion to the pleasures of life, and we may be sure that when we see the tables in the free reading- room in Bold-street well seated all round, that the eager students are enjoying a pleasure not obtainable in the eighteenth century. Professor ttogers says in "The Britieh Citiz-n :" "During the eighteenth century, the education of 1 the masses was•as scanty as it was is the darkest ages. II , do not believe that a hundred rears ago more than one man 1 in ten, or one .voman in twenty knew how to read and write. Church history during this period records very little that redounds to its credit. With the masses of the people it had little sympathy; a fox-hunting pareon sought the company of the sporting squire. Together they moulded the greatest debauchee of the age. George IV." Books and pamphlets are now being: issued in defence end in opposition to an established Church, and f urge upon ill the great necessity that exists for giving the subject a thorough study. Read both sides, for both sides are now on 1 Their mettle. Let us working-men remember the old saying ___,, When rogues fall out, honest men come by their own..' if working-men all strike, the nroof as to where Church revenue comes from will soon be seen. I say again—read, read, read. CLIFFORD DIX.

It is expected that Sir J. Grorst will shortly receive a valuable appointment in India. Information reached South Shields. on Friday, that the brig Quayside, of Whitby, has been abandoned in a sinking condition in the North Sea. DIvORCE CASE: £5OO DAMAGES.-1n the Divorce Divi- sion, on Friday, the jury awarded Mr. M'Cann. postal superintendent, Torquay, £5OO damages against a co-respon- dent named Martin, locomotive superintendent at Croydon, on the ground of his adultery with the petitioner's wife. Decree nisi also was pronounced. THE MYSTERIOUS TRAGEDY AT CHESTER.—An inquest was opened at t hester on Friday morning before the city coroner, Mr. Tatlock, on the bodies of the man and woman who were remeyed in a ca e to the Infirmary on Thursday afternoon. The man was found to be lying dead in the cab, and the woman died shortly after her admission. The bodies were now identified as Hannah Barnett and Abraham Barnett, mother and son. The mother has been lodging in Bridge-street, Chester, and the son in York-st:eet, Wrex- ham. The wife parted from her huebind on Tuesday even- ing after a quarrel. On Thursday morning Mrs. Barnett land her son were seen sober. Later they were found in a I dying state in the streets and taken to Chester Infirmary. Dr. Lees stated that he applied the stomach pump to the woman, and got nearly two pints of spirits out of her. She however died. The inquest was adjourned, the coroner ordering a post-mortem examination. THE ATTEMPTED EXTORTION FROM THE PRINCE OF WALES.—John Magee, a photographer, whc had pleaded guilty to sending a threatening letter, demanding money, to the Prince of Walee, was brought up on Friday Wore Mr. Justice Denman, at the Central Criminal Court, Lon- don, for judgment. The Judge, addressing the prisoner, said he had been well advised in pleading guilty to the charge. The learned Judge then referred to the contents of the letter, and said he had considered very carefully what sentence ought to be pronounced. The Prince of Willes, with his usual kindness of hear, desired that a lenient sen- tence should be passed, but the court could not regard the case in that light. He (the learned Judge) felt it to be his duty to pass such a sentence as would be an example to others. The Prince and everyone else must be protected from such proce,dings. He felt it his duty to sentence the prisoner to seven years' penal servitude.

div.head: IRISH QUES PION.
div.p: THE IRISH QUES PION.

It is reported at Sidcup that Sir William Hart-Dyke will be appointed Lieutenant-Governor of Madras. Sir William has left Dublin for London to arrange for his immediate retirement as Chief Secretary for Ireland. A London correspondent is informed that a circular has been sent to the heads of the Royal Irish Constabulary in- quiring as to their periods of service and pensions to which , they would be entitled on retirement.

The Dublin F2-eentan's Journal Parlitmentlry correspon- dent says :—There is no denying th,t for the present the tide runs high against Ireland. In fact, at this moment there is more anti-Irish feeling througheut England than there has been for a coneklerable time, and Home Rule is an obiect of loathing to most Englishmen.

To-day the Committee of Privileges and Public Exigen- cies of the Methodist Church in Ireland m9et at the Wesley College, Dublin, to consider what action is to be taken in the present crisis. The prevailing opinion with the Metho- dist community is against Home Rule. Mr. Jeremiah Jor- dan, Nationalist M.P. for West Clare, is a Methodist.

The London Evening News opens a leading article with the question—" Are we drifting to martial law in Ireland ?" and adds it is notorious that the policy of conciliation has been pnshed to its utmost limits with results which we frankly admit are disappointing and unsatisfactory. There must be a strong man at the head of the Irish Goverment armed with full power to make the law obeyed. We a.re not surprised that men should torn to Lord Wolselev for advice, or that he should have expressed an opinion that if he only had the requisite authority he would make the Queen's writ run in every corner of Conuaught in the course of 24 hours."

THE NEW BISHOP OF MANCHESTER. The Queen, on the recommendation of Lord Salisbury; has nominated the Right Rev. James Moorhouse, D.D., Bishop of Melhpurne, to the See of Manchester, void on the 22nd October last by the death of the Right Rev. James Fraser. Dr. Moorhonse is the third Bishop appointed since the constitution of tbe Diocese of Manchester, by an Order in Council, dated 10th August, 1847. The first Bishop, Dr. James Prince Lee, was elected to the See 17th November, 1847, and consecrated at Whitehall on January 23rd, 1848. His successor, Dr. Fraser, was nomi- nated to the • Sea on • January 18th, 18/0, confirmed at St. James's Church,, Picesdily, London, on the 31st January, and consecrated in the Manchester Cathedral on the 25th March following. Owing to various causes the delay in appointing a successor to the late prelate has been quite unprecedented. The nomination of Dr. Fraser to the see, it may he noted, was made very quickly—in little more than three weeks after the death of his predecessor, Bishop Prince Lee, while twelve weeks elapsed on Thursday since the death of Dr. Fraser. It is rather singular that all three prelates have borne one Christian name, that of James.

Dr. Moorhouse is essentially a north ctuntryman. His father was Mr. James Moorhouse, of the firm of Messrs. Moorhouse. Rushworth, and Steel, Sheffield cutlery mer- chants, and his mother was, previous to her marriage, Miss Jane Frances Bowman, of Whitehaven. Born in Sheffield in 1.828,.the new Bishop is now in his sixtieth year, boing somewhat older than either a his predecessors.

div.head: EARTHQUAKE IN GUATEMALA.
div.p: EARTHQUAKE IN GUATEMALA.

A telegram from the Panama states that intelligence has reached there that the town of Amatillan, in Guatemala, was nearly destroyed by an earthquake on December 18th last. There were altogether 131 shocks, but no fatal results are reported. THE FRENCH RAILWAY TRAGEDY.

PARIS, FRIDAY.—This morning the papers point to an in- dividual who alighted from the train at Nantes as the pro- bable murderer of M. Barreme, Prefect of the Eure. This person was seen to be carrying the Prefect's travelling rug, which was subsequently found in the stree't at Nantes/ One journal states that M. Barrel:tie had on the morning of the murder drawn a sum of 20.000 f., and that, therefore, robbery was probably the motive for the crinle.

FOOTBALL MATCH AT RUNCORN.. PROBLBLES v. POSSIBLES. Delightful weather per- vaded on Thursday at Runcorn on the occasion of the trial match pre aratory to the fixture at Warrington between West Lancashire and Border Towns Union and West Cum- berland on Siturdav next. The game excited a large amount of interest in the district, and notwithstanding the disad- vantage of its following so close upon the holidays there were close upon 2,000 persens present. Considerable difficulty was, hovrever, experienced by any of the selected play-:r.4 in getting away from business, and as a consequence numer- ous changes had at the last moment to he made in the com- position of the sides. The game terminated in favour of the Probables, who won by the large total of seven tries and two minor points to three touchdowns. Roberts in the first half, and Speakman throughout played well, the latter be- ing the best three-quarter on the field, although Lund ac- quitted himself most commendably. Warren showed well at half, as did aleo Hughes and LeadbPater, the latter make ing many good points. RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD. An adjourned meeting of this Board was held on Satin- day afternoon, for the purpose of considering the rate of fees that should he charged at Greenway-road Board school. A discussion on the subject took place on the previous day, and was reported, and it was adjourned in order that the Rev. Canon Barclay and the Rey. Father Fennelfey might be present. Canon Barclay presided, and the other members were Messrs. R. Lea, J Pritchard, G. S. Hazlehurst, W. Handley, and F. Rigby (clerk).

THE SCHOOL FEE 'MOTION. The Clerk explained the position of affairs, and in response to an inquiry from him, The .!,chool Visitor (Mr. Bowyer) said there was a worse per centage of attendance where the fees were higher, and he was having constant complaints from teachers about the irregular attendance of the upper standard children. W13,...n. they began to get useful parents kept their children at home. He was, of course, speaking snore particularly with regard to girls.
The Chairman said this statement merely implied that the children were more useful at home. Mr. Boyer: That is why they are kept away from school.
Mr. Pritchard: It is not difference of fees. Mr. Lea said the fees were the same now as they had been for years. _
Mr. Hazieburst said be quite agreed4with the Department that it was not advisable to raise the fees in the higher standards.

Mr. Handley moved that a uniform fee of 2d per child for the infant school, and 3d per child for the gins' school be- adopted instead of the sliding scale of 2d, 3d, and 4d, as passed informally at a previous meeting. The Clerk observed that they might consider the fee of 2d per child for standard one school settled. There was no difference of opinion about that. Mr. Hazlehurst had great pleasure in seconding Mr. Handley' s motion. Mr. Lea proposed an amendment that the fee in standard four and upwards be 4d per child. He anzued that if Mr. Handley suggestion were carried out the new schools would rob the denominational schools, and he thought they ought not to do that, especially this half-year. The fee, at the Wesleyan Schools were higher than any other school in the town, an they would be particularly liable to injury,. He asked was Mr. Hazlehurst aware of that, aud added that he would have no objection to the fees being modified at the end of the half year.
The Chairman : Father Fennelley spoke strongly upon this point the other day, not for any consideration of his own.
Mr. Lea In consideration of the whole denominational schools.
Tbe Chairman seconded the amendment, for which mover and seconder voted.
Messrs. Handley, H4zlehurst, and Pritchard voted for the original resolution, which was declared carried
Hazieburst remarked that if they could get good education on cheaper terms it would be a great public benefit.
RELIGIOUS EDUCATION.

The Board then considered the syitem of religious in- struction to be given !n the new schools, and on the motion of Mr. Pritchard, seconded by Mr. Handley, religious in- struction on the model 01 the Manchester School Beard, and which bad been satisfactorily carried on at Mill Brow, was adopted. There was no other business.

. RUNCORN' SAVINGS BAN K.—ANNUAL MEETING. The annual meeting of the Runcorn Savings Bank was held on Tuesday morning at the bank. The Rev. Canon Barclay presided, and there were present. Messrs. T. Brundrit, T.P., Joseph Handley, J.P., J. Sampson, W. Whittaker, J. 0. Jackson. S. C. Beckett, R. Forrester, and W. Handley (actuary). The Acteary read the report :—I respectfully- submit the following report, being an epitome or the transactions of the bank for the past year. During the year, ending Nov- ember 20th, 1885,.the number of deposits was 1,644, being. an average of £3l.s. BA-1, and the number of la itndrawals have been 642, an average of £9 12. 7d, making a total of 2,286 separate transactions. At the same date there were 740 accounts open with the bank consisting of personal de- positors 691, penny banks 3, charitable societies 18. friendly- societies 38. The amount due to depositors on Nov. 20th. 1884. was £23,877'16. 10d, the amount deposited during the year past being £5/813 131 7d, and the sum of £592 14e 2d was added as interest, making the gross total due to deposi- tors £30,284 4s 7d. From this amount must be deducted the sum of £6,182 4s Bd, being the amount of withdrawals of deposits during the year, thus leaving a nett liability to depositors of £24,101 19. s lid. To meet this the sum of £23,824 3s 5d is invested with the Commissioners for the Reduction of the National Debt, which was £328 16a 5d the balance in the hands of the treasurer makes a total asset of £24,152 19s 10d. showing a surplus in favour of the bank of £5O 198 lid. The interest allowed by the National Debt Commissioners on the amount invested with them was for the year £689.2t Td, and on the drafts £5 17'; and Adding thereto 11s received for fees, books, and sundries gives a total ince-me of £695 103 7d. Deducting therefrom £592 14s 2d as interest allowed to depositors, £9B Is 8d being management expenses, leaves a credit margin of £4 14s 9d on the year'i work. which, added- to the surplus as per last year's report of.X46iss 2d, makes a total of £5O 19s lid as above stated:. During the first nine months of the past year the amount withdrawn considerably exceeded the amount deposited, but it is satisfactory to note that the last three months of the year show a considerable increase of deposits over withdrawals, an improvement which still continues. The Chairman moved the adoption of the report and re- marked that he was glad to see they were in such good feather. Mr. Brundrit seconded the motion. The affairs of the bank were shown to be in a very satisfactory condition. The motion was carried.

It was pointed out by the Actuary that at present there were only 12 trustees and 17 managers, whilst according to the rules there should be 18 trustees and 33 mana-,ers. tie thought if they could raise up the list to its full streng h it would bean advantage to the bank. In examining the rules, Mr. Brundrit ascertained that a president and vice-president should be appointed, which had nct been the custom of the bank.

Mr. James Handl-y proposed that the Rev. Canon Bar- clay he the president. If not in name, he had in reality been .president for many Years. Mr. John Simpson seconded the motion. He was sure they were all pleased to see the vicar with them again. The motion was carried unanimously. On the motion of Mr. Whittaker, seconded by Mr. James Handley. Mr. J.
